123565.q: Which property of many DNA polymerases lowers the error rate during replication?
123565.e: Many DNA polymerases recognise wrongly inserted nucleotides and remove them with their exonuclease activity. This checking is called proofreading.

123566.q: Which enzyme prevents the DNA ahead of the replication fork from becoming too tightly twisted?
123566.e: Unwinding creates tension ahead of the fork. Topoisomerases briefly cut the DNA and so release the overwinding.

123567.q: Where does transcription take place in cells with a nucleus?
123567.e: In eukaryotes the DNA lies in the nucleus, so it is copied there. The finished mRNA is then exported into the cytoplasm.
123567.m: In eukaryotes, transcription takes place in the nucleus.

123568.q: What is the DNA region called where RNA polymerase begins transcription?
123568.e: The promoter is a recognition sequence in front of the gene. Transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind there.

123569.q: Which well-known sequence is found in many eukaryotic promoters?
123569.e: The TATA box lies just before the starting point of many genes. It serves as a binding site for transcription factors.
123569.m: Many promoters contain a TATA box.

123570.q: What is the DNA strand called that is read as a template during transcription?
123570.e: The template strand is read. The RNA produced therefore has the sequence of the other, coding strand, only made of RNA building blocks.
123570.m: RNA polymerase reads the template strand.

123571.q: What is removed from the pre-mRNA during splicing?
123571.e: Introns are non-coding sections and are cut out. The exons are joined to form the mature mRNA.

123572.q: Which two modifications does eukaryotic mRNA receive at its ends?
123572.e: A cap of modified guanine is added to the 5' end, and a tail of many adenine nucleotides to the 3' end. Both protect the mRNA from being broken down.
123572.m: The cap and poly-A tail protect the mRNA.

123573.q: What does alternative splicing make possible?
123573.e: Depending on which exons are joined, different mature mRNAs are produced. In this way one gene can code for several versions of a protein.
123573.m: Alternative splicing makes several proteins from one gene.

123574.q: What guides a ribosome with its growing protein chain to the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
a: A signal peptide at the start of the chain
A stop codon at the end of the mRNA
The poly-A tail of the mRNA
123574.e: Proteins for membranes or for export carry a signal sequence at the start. It is recognised and the ribosome docks onto the rough ER.
123574.m: A signal peptide sends ribosomes to the rough ER.

123575.q: How large are eukaryotic ribosomes, given as a sedimentation coefficient?
123575.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, bacterial ones only 70S. The difference matters for some antibiotics.

123576.q: What is the group of three on the tRNA called that attaches to the codon of the mRNA?
123576.e: The anticodon is complementary to the codon. This ensures that the correct amino acid is built in.
123576.m: The anticodon of the tRNA recognises the codon.

123577.q: Which bond links the amino acids during translation?
123577.e: The ribosome links the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next. In the process, water is released.

123578.q: What are the three tRNA binding sites in the ribosome called?
123578.e: The loaded tRNA arrives at the A site, the growing chain hangs at the P site, and the empty tRNA leaves the ribosome via the E site.
123578.m: The ribosome has an A, a P and an E site.

123579.q: Which enzyme loads each tRNA with the matching amino acid?
123579.e: There is a separate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase for each amino acid. Using ATP, it links the amino acid to the correct tRNA.
123579.m: Synthetases load tRNAs with amino acids.

123580.q: What binds to the ribosome when a stop codon is reached?
123580.e: There is no matching tRNA for stop codons. A release factor binds and releases the finished chain.

123581.q: What is an mRNA called that is read by several ribosomes at the same time?
123581.e: Several ribosomes can work one behind the other on the same mRNA. In this way many copies of a protein are made in a short time.
123581.m: A polysome is many ribosomes on one mRNA.

123582.q: What is different in bacteria compared with eukaryotes as regards transcription and translation?
a: They can take place at the same time
They only take place at night
123582.e: Bacteria have no nucleus. Ribosomes can therefore attach to the mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
123582.m: In bacteria, transcription and translation are coupled.

123583.q: Which amino acid is coded by the start codon AUG?
123583.e: AUG marks the start of translation and at the same time codes for methionine. That is why newly made proteins initially begin with methionine.
123583.m: The start codon AUG stands for methionine.

123585.q: How many stop codons does the standard code contain?
123585.e: The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. There is no matching tRNA for them.
123585.m: The standard code has three stop codons.

123586.q: Which codon is the usual start codon?
123586.e: The codon AUG marks the start of translation. At the same time it codes for methionine.

123587.q: For how many standard amino acids does the genetic code code?
123587.e: The sense codons are distributed among 20 canonical amino acids. In addition there are the stop codons.
123587.m: The genetic code specifies 20 amino acids.

123588.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is “degenerate”?
a: Several codons stand for the same amino acid
One codon stands for several amino acids
123588.e: Because there are more codons than amino acids, most amino acids are coded more than once. This is also called redundancy.
123588.m: Many amino acids are coded by several codons.

123589.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is almost universal?
a: Almost all living things use the same code
Every gene has the same code
The code is the same length in all proteins
123589.e: Bacteria, plants and humans translate codons almost identically. That is why a human gene can be read in bacteria; there are small differences, for example in mitochondria.
123589.m: Almost all living things use the same genetic code.

123590.q: Which circular table is used in biology lessons to read off which amino acid a codon codes for?
123590.e: In the codon wheel, a codon is read from the inside out. On the outside you find the matching amino acid or the stop signal.
123590.m: The codon wheel translates codons into amino acids.

123591.q: What is a mutation called in which a single base is exchanged for another?
123591.e: In a substitution, one base is replaced and the length of the DNA stays the same. It is a form of point mutation.
123591.m: In a substitution, one base is exchanged.

123592.q: What does the deletion of a single base in a gene usually cause?
a: A shift in the reading frame
123592.e: Because the codons are read in groups of three, all the following triplets shift. This usually produces a completely changed or shortened protein.
123592.m: If a base is missing, the reading frame shifts.

123593.q: What is a mutation called that does not change the amino acid sequence?
123593.e: Because of multiple coding, a new codon can stand for the same amino acid. The protein then stays the same.
123593.m: A silent mutation does not change the protein.

123594.q: What is created in a nonsense mutation?
123594.e: If a codon becomes a stop codon, translation breaks off too early. The protein is shortened and usually does not work.
123594.m: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.

123595.q: What is a point mutation called that leads to a different amino acid being built in?
123595.e: In a missense mutation, the changed codon codes for a different amino acid. The consequences range from harmless to severe.
123595.m: A missense mutation exchanges one amino acid.

123596.q: Which DNA damage does UV radiation typically cause?
123596.e: UV light links two neighbouring thymines together. If these dimers are not repaired, mutations and skin cancer can result.
123596.m: UV radiation creates thymine dimers in DNA.

123597.q: Which type of mutation is trisomy 21?
123597.e: In a genome mutation, the number of chromosomes is changed. In trisomy 21, chromosome 21 is present three times.
123597.m: In trisomy 21, the number of chromosomes is changed.

123598.q: What are substances or radiation that trigger mutations called?
123598.e: Mutagens increase the mutation rate. Examples are ionising radiation, UV light and certain chemicals in tobacco smoke.

123599.q: What are sections of DNA called that can change their position in the genome?
123599.e: Transposons are also called jumping genes. They make up a large part of the human genome.
123599.m: Transposons can jump around in the genome.

123600.q: Roughly what percentage of the genome do two people share?
123600.e: Two people differ in only about one in every thousand building blocks. Even so, these small differences account for a great deal of variety.

123601.q: What share of the human genome codes directly for proteins?
123601.e: Only a small part of the DNA consists of exons, which code for proteins. The rest includes introns, regulatory sections and repeats.
123601.m: Only a small part of the genome codes for proteins.

123602.q: Roughly how long would all the DNA in a human body cell be if stretched out?
123602.e: A diploid cell contains around 6 billion base pairs, which stretched out gives about 2 metres. The DNA is wound around histones and highly compacted.
123602.m: The DNA of one cell is around two metres long when stretched out.

123603.q: Which cell organelles have their own small genome?
123603.e: Mitochondria have a ring-shaped DNA with a few genes. This is seen as evidence that they originated from bacteria.

123604.q: What shape is the main chromosome of most bacteria?
123604.e: Most bacteria have a closed, ring-shaped chromosome. In addition, small plasmids may be present.
123604.m: Bacteria usually have a ring-shaped chromosome.

123605.q: Some amoebae and lungfish have much more DNA than humans. What does this show?
a: Genome size and complexity are hardly related
These animals are more complex than humans
123605.e: The amount of DNA says little about how complex a living thing is. A large part of many genomes consists of repeats and non-coding sections.
123605.m: A large genome does not mean a complex living thing.

123606.q: What is the field called that studies whole genomes?
123606.e: Genomics studies the structure, function and comparison of complete genomes. Proteomics, by contrast, studies the whole set of proteins.

123607.q: In which year did the public Human Genome Project officially start?
123607.e: The project was launched in 1990, mainly by US authorities. Research centres from several countries soon took part.
123607.m: The Human Genome Project began in 1990.

123608.q: Which researcher competed with the public project with the company Celera Genomics?
123608.e: With Celera, Craig Venter relied on fast shotgun sequencing. The race sped up the whole undertaking.
123608.m: Craig Venter challenged the public project with Celera.

123609.q: Which sequencing method was mainly used in the Human Genome Project?
123609.e: Frederick Sanger's chain termination method was highly automated. Modern high-throughput methods only came later.
123609.m: The human genome was sequenced with the Sanger method.

123610.q: In which year were the first draft versions of the human genome published in scientific journals?
123610.e: The draft was publicly announced in 2000, and the publications appeared in “Nature” and “Science” in 2001.
123610.m: The draft sequence of the human genome appeared in 2001.

123611.q: Who led the public Human Genome Project in its main phase?
123611.e: James Watson led the US part at the beginning; from 1993 Francis Collins took over. Collins led the project until it was completed.
123611.m: Francis Collins led the Human Genome Project to its goal.

123612.q: Roughly how much did the Human Genome Project cost?
123612.e: The public project cost around 3 billion US dollars. Today sequencing a genome costs only a tiny fraction of that.
123612.m: The Human Genome Project cost around three billion dollars.

123613.q: What did researchers achieve with the human genome in 2022?
a: The first complete sequence without gaps
The discovery of the DNA double helix
123613.e: The 2003 sequence still had gaps, for example at the centromeres. In 2022 they were closed with new long-read methods.
123613.m: Only in 2022 was a human genome sequenced without gaps.

123614.q: Which substance did the Swiss scientist Friedrich Miescher discover in 1869?
123614.e: Miescher isolated a new substance from cell nuclei and called it nuclein. Today we know that it was mainly DNA.
123614.m: Friedrich Miescher discovered nucleic acid in 1869.

123615.q: In which city was Friedrich Miescher born?
123615.e: Friedrich Miescher was born in Basel in 1844. He came from a Basel family of doctors.

123616.q: From what material did Miescher obtain his first cell nuclei?
123616.e: He used white blood cells from the pus on used dressings from a hospital. These cells have large nuclei.
123616.m: Miescher found nuclein in white blood cells from pus.

123617.q: In which city did Miescher make his discovery?
123617.e: Miescher worked in Felix Hoppe-Seyler's laboratory at Hohentübingen Castle. There he isolated nuclein.

123618.q: Which element was strikingly abundant in nuclein and distinguished it from proteins?
123618.e: Miescher's analyses showed a high phosphorus content. This made it clear that it was not an ordinary protein.

123619.q: At which university was Miescher later professor of physiology?
123619.e: In 1872 Miescher became professor of physiology at the University of Basel. There he continued to study nuclein, among other things in salmon sperm.
123619.m: Miescher later taught at the University of Basel.

123620.q: From what did Miescher later obtain large amounts of nuclein in Basel?
123620.e: Salmon from the Rhine provided Miescher with sperm cells with very large nuclei. From these he could obtain and study a lot of nuclein.
123620.m: In Basel, Miescher studied nuclein from salmon sperm.

123621.q: In which place in the Grisons did Friedrich Miescher die in 1895?
123621.e: Miescher had tuberculosis and sought a cure in Davos. He died there in 1895.

123622.q: Which protein is often used as “gene scissors” in the CRISPR method?
123622.e: Cas9 is an endonuclease that cuts DNA at a chosen point. That is why people speak of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors.
123622.m: Cas9 is the best-known pair of gene scissors.

123623.q: Which two researchers received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR/Cas9?
123623.e: In 2012 Charpentier and Doudna showed that Cas9 can be programmed precisely. For this they were honoured in 2020.
123623.m: Charpentier and Doudna received the Nobel Prize for CRISPR.

123624.q: What is the CRISPR system originally used for in bacteria?
123624.e: Bacteria store pieces of virus DNA in their CRISPR section. In a new infection, Cas recognises and cuts up the virus DNA.
123624.m: CRISPR is originally an immune system of bacteria.

123625.q: What steers Cas9 to the right place on the DNA?
123625.e: The guide RNA is complementary to the target sequence. It leads Cas9 exactly there.
123625.m: A guide RNA shows Cas9 where to cut.

123626.q: What does the enzyme Cas9 do to the DNA in the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors?
a: It cuts both DNA strands at a particular point
It translates the DNA into a protein
123626.e: Cas9 is an enzyme that cuts through DNA at a precisely chosen point. The cell then repairs the cut, and in the process the gene can be changed.
123626.m: Cas9 is the blade of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors.

123627.q: What can be achieved with the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors by cutting a gene at a chosen point?
123627.e: The cell often repairs the cut inaccurately. This produces small errors that frequently switch the gene off.
123627.m: A targeted cut with CRISPR can switch a gene off.

123628.q: What is CRISPR/Cas9 mainly used for in research today?
a: To change genes in a targeted way
To stain viruses under the microscope
123628.e: CRISPR/Cas9 is also called gene scissors. It can be used to cut and change genes at precisely chosen points.
123628.m: CRISPR/Cas9 is a pair of gene scissors for changing genes precisely.

123629.q: For which hereditary disease was the first CRISPR therapy approved in 2023?
123629.e: The therapy Casgevy was approved in 2023, first in Great Britain and the USA. It is also used to treat beta thalassaemia.
123629.m: The first approved CRISPR therapy treats a blood disease.

123630.e: Only someone who carries two changed alleles has the disease. People with one changed allele are healthy.

123631.q: Which organ is particularly affected in cystic fibrosis?
123631.e: In cystic fibrosis the body produces sticky mucus. It mainly blocks the airways and leads to frequent chest infections; digestive organs are also affected.
123631.m: Cystic fibrosis makes the mucus in the lungs sticky.

123632.e: A single changed allele is enough for the disease. It usually only appears in adulthood.

123633.q: Which organ is progressively damaged in Huntington's disease?
123633.e: In Huntington's disease, nerve cells in the brain gradually die. This leads to involuntary movements and to changes in thinking and behaviour.
123633.m: Huntington's disease is a hereditary disease of the brain.

123634.q: What advantage do healthy carriers of a sickle cell allele have in some regions?
a: They are better protected against malaria
123634.e: Heterozygous carriers fall seriously ill with malaria less often. That is why the allele is common in malaria regions.
123634.m: The sickle cell allele partly protects carriers against malaria.

a: With a diet low in phenylalanine
123635.e: In phenylketonuria, the body cannot break down phenylalanine. A special low-protein diet started early prevents brain damage; newborns in Switzerland are tested for it.
123635.m: A diet low in phenylalanine helps with phenylketonuria.

123636.q: Both parents are healthy carriers of the same recessive disease allele. What is the risk that a child will have the disease?
123636.e: Each parent passes on the changed allele with a probability of 50 per cent. Together this gives 0.5 times 0.5, so 25 per cent.
123636.m: Two carriers have a one-in-four risk for each child.

123637.q: What is a person called who carries a recessive disease allele but is healthy?
123637.e: A carrier is heterozygous and shows no symptoms. However, they can pass the allele on.
123637.m: Healthy people with a recessive disease allele are called carriers.

123638.q: What force acts on a proton (q = 1.6 · 10^-19 C) moving at 2 · 10^6 m/s at right angles to a field of 0.5 T?
123638.e: F equals q times v times B, so 1.6 · 10^-19 C times 2 · 10^6 m/s times 0.5 T. That gives 1.6 · 10^-13 N.
123638.m: The Lorentz force is the product of charge, velocity and flux density.

123639.q: Why does the Lorentz force not change the speed of a charged particle?
a: It always acts at right angles to the motion
It is always far too small
It only acts on charges at rest
123639.e: A force at right angles to the direction of motion does no work. It only changes the direction, not the kinetic energy.
123639.m: The Lorentz force deflects but does not speed up.

123640.q: What Lorentz force acts on a charge moving exactly parallel to the magnetic field lines?
a: A force in the direction of motion
123640.e: The force is proportional to the sine of the angle between velocity and field. At 0 degrees the sine is zero.
123640.m: Parallel to the magnetic field there is no Lorentz force.

123641.q: What is the radius of the path of a proton (m = 1.67 · 10^-27 kg) moving at 10^6 m/s at right angles in a field of 0.1 T?
123641.e: The radius is r = m times v divided by q times B. That gives 1.67 · 10^-21 divided by 1.6 · 10^-20, so about 0.10 m.
123641.m: In a magnetic field, charges travel in circular paths.

123642.q: What force acts on a 0.5 m long conductor carrying 5 A at right angles in a field of 0.2 T?
123642.e: For a conductor, F = I times l times B. So 5 A times 0.5 m times 0.2 T = 0.5 N.
123642.m: A force acts on current-carrying conductors in a magnetic field.

123643.q: Which quantity is determined with a fine beam tube from the circular path of electrons in a magnetic field?
123643.e: The Lorentz force forces the electrons into a circular path. From the accelerating voltage, the flux density and the radius of the path, the ratio of charge to mass is calculated.
123643.m: A fine beam tube measures the specific charge of the electron.

123644.q: How does the Lorentz force change if the velocity of the charge doubles?
123644.e: The Lorentz force is directly proportional to the velocity. Twice the velocity gives twice the force.
123644.m: The faster the charge, the greater the Lorentz force.

123645.q: Which device uses the force on current-carrying conductors in a magnetic field to produce motion?
123645.e: In an electric motor, forces in the magnetic field act on the wires of the coil. This produces a turning effect.
123645.m: The electric motor uses the Lorentz force.

123646.q: What does the orbital frequency of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field (non-relativistic) NOT depend on?
123646.e: The cyclotron frequency is q times B divided by 2 pi times m. Faster particles travel in larger circles but take the same time for one orbit.
123646.m: The cyclotron frequency does not depend on the speed.

123647.q: Which symbol is used for magnetic flux density?
123647.e: Magnetic flux density is written as B. H stands for magnetic field strength.
123647.m: Magnetic flux density is called B.

123648.q: What is B in a long coil with 1000 turns, 0.5 m long, carrying a current of 2 A (in air)?
123648.e: B is µ0 times N times I divided by l, so 4 pi · 10^-7 times 1000 times 2 divided by 0.5. That gives about 5.0 · 10^-3 T.
123648.m: In a long coil, B grows with the density of turns and the current.

123649.q: Roughly how large is the flux density of the Earth's magnetic field in Switzerland?
123649.e: In central Europe about 47 to 48 microtesla is measured. The Earth's field is therefore very weak.
123649.m: The Earth's magnetic field is only about fifty microtesla.

123650.q: What is B at a distance of 2 cm from a long straight conductor carrying 10 A?
123650.e: B is µ0 times I divided by 2 pi r, so 2 · 10^-7 times 10 divided by 0.02. That gives 1 · 10^-4 T.
123650.m: The field of a straight conductor decreases with distance.

123651.q: What kind of quantity is magnetic flux density?
123651.e: B has a magnitude and a direction. The direction points along the field lines.
123651.m: Magnetic flux density is a vector.

123652.q: Which quantity tells you by what factor an iron core increases the flux density of a coil?
123652.e: The relative permeability µr describes how much the material strengthens the field. For iron it can be well over 1000.
123652.m: An iron core strengthens the field by the relative permeability.

123653.q: How does B around a long straight conductor change if you triple the distance?
123653.e: B is inversely proportional to the distance r. Three times the distance gives a third of the flux density.
123653.m: The field of a straight conductor falls off with one over the distance.

123654.q: What follows from the fact that there are no magnetic monopoles?
123654.e: Field lines do not begin or end at single poles. Outside the magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole and back again inside.
123654.m: Magnetic field lines have neither a beginning nor an end.

123655.q: Who is the unit tesla named after?
123655.e: The unit of flux density honours the inventor Nikola Tesla. He worked mainly in the USA.
123655.m: The unit tesla honours Nikola Tesla.

123656.q: How can one tesla be expressed in SI base units?
123656.e: From F = I times l times B it follows that B = N divided by A times m. With N = kg times m over s², this gives kg/(A · s²).
123656.m: One tesla equals one kilogram per ampere per second squared.

123657.q: How many gauss equal one tesla?
123657.e: The gauss is the older CGS unit of flux density. One tesla equals 10,000 gauss.
123657.m: One tesla is ten thousand gauss.

123658.e: One tesla is 1000 millitesla. 0.25 times 1000 gives 250 mT.
123658.m: One tesla is a thousand millitesla.

123659.q: Which combination of units is equivalent to one tesla?
123659.e: From the force on a conductor it follows that B = F divided by I times l. So 1 T = 1 newton per ampere per metre.
123659.m: One tesla is one newton per ampere per metre.

123660.q: Which unit do you get if you multiply 1 tesla by 1 square metre?
123660.e: Magnetic flux is flux density times area. 1 T times 1 m² gives 1 weber.
123660.m: Tesla times square metre gives weber.

123661.e: One millitesla is 1000 microtesla. 0.05 times 1000 gives 50 µT.
123661.m: One millitesla is a thousand microtesla.

123662.q: What is Nikola Tesla mainly known for?
123662.e: Among other things, Tesla developed the three-phase motor and promoted the transmission of alternating current. This won out over Edison's direct current.

123663.q: In which unit is magnetic flux measured?
123663.e: Magnetic flux Φ has the unit weber, abbreviated Wb. The unit honours Wilhelm Eduard Weber.
123663.m: Magnetic flux is measured in webers.

123664.q: What is the flux through an area of 0.05 m² that is crossed at right angles by 0.4 T?
123664.e: Φ is B times A, so 0.4 T times 0.05 m². That gives 0.02 Wb.
123664.m: Flux is flux density times the area crossed.

123665.q: What is the magnetic flux through an area that lies parallel to the field lines?
123665.e: No field line passes through the area. The cosine between the field and the normal to the area is zero at 90 degrees.
123665.m: If the area lies parallel to the field, the flux is zero.

123666.q: What is Φ if B = 0.2 T and A = 0.1 m² and the field and the normal to the area make an angle of 60 degrees?
123666.e: Φ is B times A times cos 60 degrees. 0.2 times 0.1 times 0.5 gives 0.01 Wb.
123666.m: With a tilted area only the perpendicular part of the field counts.

123667.q: Who is the unit of magnetic flux named after?
123667.e: The Göttingen physicist Wilhelm Eduard Weber researched electromagnetism. With Gauss he built an early electric telegraph.
123667.m: The unit weber honours the physicist Wilhelm Weber.

123668.q: What is the total magnetic flux through a closed surface?
123668.e: As many field lines go in as come out, because there are no monopoles. This is Gauss's law for magnetic fields.
123668.m: Through a closed surface the magnetic flux is zero.

123669.q: What is the flux linkage of a coil with 200 turns if each turn is crossed by 0.003 Wb?
123669.e: The flux linkage is N times Φ. 200 times 0.003 Wb gives 0.6 Wb.
123669.m: In coils the flux through every turn counts.

123670.e: From the law of induction it follows that a change in flux of 1 Wb per second produces 1 V. So 1 Wb = 1 volt-second.

123671.q: What do you call induction in which the conductor stays still and only the magnetic field changes?
123671.e: In induction at rest the flux density changes, for example through an alternating current in a neighbouring coil. In motional induction, by contrast, the conductor moves.
123671.m: Even a conductor at rest experiences induction when the field changes.

123672.q: The flux through a coil with 100 turns changes by 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the induced voltage?
123672.e: U is N times the change in flux divided by the time. 100 times 0.02 Wb divided by 0.1 s gives 20 V.
123672.m: The induced voltage depends on how fast the flux changes.

123673.q: A rod 0.2 m long moves at 3 m/s at right angles through a field of 0.5 T. What voltage is induced?
123673.e: For a moving conductor, U = B times l times v. 0.5 times 0.2 times 3 gives 0.3 V.
123673.m: A conductor moving in a magnetic field becomes a voltage source.

123674.q: What voltage does a coil at rest deliver in a constant, unchanging magnetic field?
123674.e: A voltage is only induced when the flux changes. A constant flux produces no voltage.
123674.m: Without a change in flux there is no induction.

123675.q: In a coil with 500 turns the flux rises steadily from 0 to 4 mWb in 0.2 s. What voltage is induced?
123675.e: U is N times the change in flux divided by the time. 500 times 0.004 Wb divided by 0.2 s gives 10 V.
123675.m: Many turns and a fast change in flux give a high voltage.

123676.q: Why does a transformer not work with direct current?
a: The flux in the core does not change
Direct current does not flow through copper
123676.e: A constant current produces a constant flux. Without a change in flux, no voltage is induced in the secondary coil.

123677.q: What is the effect of doubling the number of turns of an induction coil, with everything else the same?
123677.e: Each turn makes the same contribution, and the contributions add up. The voltage is therefore proportional to N.
123677.m: More turns give more induced voltage.

123678.q: What peak voltage does a coil (N = 50, A = 0.02 m²) deliver when it turns at 50 Hz in a field of 0.1 T?
123678.e: The peak voltage is N times B times A times omega, with omega = 2 pi times 50 Hz. 50 times 0.1 times 0.02 times 314 gives about 31 V.
123678.m: A coil rotating in a magnetic field produces an alternating voltage.

123679.q: What kind of voltage does a loop of wire rotating steadily in a uniform magnetic field deliver?
123679.e: The flux through the loop changes with the cosine of the angle of rotation. Its derivative gives a sinusoidal voltage.
123679.m: A generator delivers a sinusoidal alternating voltage.

123680.q: A magnet is pulled away from a closed metal ring. How does the ring act on the magnet?
123680.e: The ring tries to prevent the flux from decreasing. Its induced current therefore creates a field that tries to hold on to the magnet.
123680.m: A ring also brakes a magnet that is moving away.

123682.q: How does a strong magnet fall through a vertical copper pipe compared with free fall?
123682.e: The falling magnet induces currents in the copper. According to Lenz's law, their magnetic field brakes it.
123682.m: A magnet falling through a copper pipe is slowed down.

123683.q: What does the minus sign in the law of induction express?
a: The negative charge of the electron
123683.e: The minus sign means that the induced voltage opposes the change in flux. This is the mathematical form of Lenz's law.
123683.m: The minus sign in the law of induction stands for Lenz's law.

123684.q: A north pole is brought near a closed metal ring. Which pole forms on the side of the ring facing the magnet?
123684.e: The ring tries to slow the approach and therefore repels with a like pole. A north pole forms.
123684.m: A ring repels an approaching magnet.

123685.q: What happens in Thomson's jumping ring experiment when the current is switched on?
123685.e: When switched on, the flux in the iron core rises. The induced current in the ring creates an opposing field, and the ring is repelled.
123685.m: In Thomson's jumping ring experiment the ring jumps up.

123686.q: Which basic principle does Lenz's law follow from?
123686.e: If the induced current strengthened its own cause, energy would be created out of nothing. That would contradict the conservation of energy.
123686.m: Lenz's law ensures the conservation of energy.

123687.q: Why is a metal ring with a slit in it hardly repelled by an approaching magnet?
a: No current can flow round the ring
123687.e: The slit breaks the circuit. A voltage is still induced, but no current can flow.
123687.m: Without a closed ring no induced current flows.

123688.q: What advantage does an eddy current brake have on trains?
a: It holds the train still when stopped
123688.e: The braking effect comes without contact, through eddy currents in the rail. There are no brake blocks to wear out.
123688.m: Eddy current brakes work without wear.

123689.q: Why are transformer cores made of many thin, insulated sheets?
123689.e: The insulation between the sheets breaks up large eddy current loops. This greatly reduces the heat losses.
123689.m: Laminated cores keep eddy currents small.

123690.q: How does an induction hob heat the bottom of a pan?
a: Through eddy currents in the bottom of the pan
123690.e: Under the glass ceramic, a coil produces a rapidly changing magnetic field. Eddy currents form in the metal bottom of the pan and heat it.
123690.m: On an induction hob, eddy currents heat the pan.

123691.q: Which device finds hidden metal objects with the help of eddy currents?
123691.e: An alternating field induces eddy currents in the metal. Their effect back on the search coil is measured.

123692.q: Into which form of energy is the energy of eddy currents mainly converted?
123692.e: Eddy currents flow through the electrical resistance of the metal. This produces Joule heating.

123693.q: Why can an eddy current brake not hold a vehicle still when it has stopped?
a: Without motion no eddy currents form
The current becomes too strong when stopped
123693.e: Eddy currents only form when the flux in the metal changes, that is when there is motion. The braking force therefore gets smaller as the speed falls.
123693.m: Eddy current brakes only work while moving.

123694.q: What does Waltenhofen's pendulum show with a slotted metal plate?
a: It swings through the magnetic field almost without braking
It swings faster than without a field
It is attracted by the magnet
123694.e: The slots break up the large eddy current paths. The braking effect is therefore much weaker than with a solid plate.

123695.q: How are aluminium parts sorted out with eddy currents during recycling?
a: They are flung away by a rotating magnetic field
They are attracted by a permanent magnet
They melt in the magnetic field
123695.e: A rapidly rotating magnetic field induces eddy currents in the aluminium. The repulsion flings the parts out of the stream of material.
123695.m: Eddy current separators separate aluminium from waste.

a: A coil induces a voltage in itself when the current changes
A coil produces current without an energy source
A conductor warms up by itself
123696.e: If the current in a coil changes, its own flux changes too. This produces a voltage in the coil itself.
123696.m: In self-induction a coil acts on itself.

123697.q: The current in a coil with L = 0.5 H falls steadily by 4 A in 0.02 s. What is the self-induced voltage?
123697.e: U is L times the change in current per unit time. 0.5 H times 4 A divided by 0.02 s gives 100 V.
123697.m: Fast changes in current produce high self-induced voltages.

123698.q: How does the current behave when a circuit with a coil is switched on?
a: It jumps straight to its final value
123698.e: The self-induced voltage opposes the rise. The current therefore approaches its final value gradually.
123698.m: Coils slow down the growth of the current.

123699.q: What is the time constant of a circuit with L = 2 H and R = 100 Ω?
123699.e: The time constant is L divided by R. 2 H divided by 100 Ω gives 0.02 s.
123699.m: The time constant of a coil is inductance divided by resistance.

123700.q: How much energy does a coil with L = 0.2 H store at a current of 3 A?
123700.e: W is one half times L times I squared. 0.5 times 0.2 times 9 gives 0.9 J.
123700.m: A coil stores energy in its magnetic field.

123701.q: Which part of a petrol engine uses self-induction to produce the ignition spark?
123701.e: When the current in the ignition coil is interrupted, a high induced voltage is produced. It is enough for the spark at the spark plug.
123701.m: The ignition coil produces the high voltage for the spark.

123702.q: What fraction of its final value does the current in a coil reach after one time constant?
123702.e: The current rises according to 1 minus e to the power of minus t over tau. After one time constant that is 1 minus 0.37, so about 63 per cent.
123702.m: After one time constant about 63 per cent is reached.

123703.q: In which unit is inductance given?
123703.e: Inductance L has the unit henry, abbreviated H. The farad is the unit of capacitance.

123704.q: Who is the unit henry named after?
123704.e: The American physicist Joseph Henry discovered induction at about the same time as Faraday and described self-induction. The unit henry is named in his honour.
123704.m: The unit henry honours Joseph Henry.

123705.q: What is the inductance of an air-cored coil with 500 turns, a cross-section of 4 cm² and a length of 20 cm?
123705.e: L is µ0 times N² times A divided by l. 4 pi · 10^-7 times 250,000 times 4 · 10^-4 divided by 0.2 gives about 6.3 · 10^-4 H.
123705.m: Inductance grows with the square of the number of turns.

123706.q: How does the inductance of a coil change if you double the number of turns (everything else the same)?
123706.e: L is proportional to N². Twice the number of turns gives a factor of 4.
123706.m: Twice the number of turns gives four times the inductance.

123707.q: How does an iron core change the inductance of a coil?
123707.e: The iron core increases the magnetic flux for the same current. The inductance grows roughly by the relative permeability.
123707.m: An iron core increases the inductance.

123708.q: What is the inductive reactance of a 0.1 H coil at 50 Hz?
123708.e: The reactance is 2 pi times f times L. 2 pi times 50 times 0.1 gives about 31.4 Ω.
123708.m: The reactance of a coil rises with frequency.

123709.q: Two coils of 2 mH and 3 mH are connected in series without coupling to each other. What is the total inductance?
123709.e: In series, inductances add up like resistances. 2 mH plus 3 mH gives 5 mH.

123710.q: Which combination of units does 1 henry equal?
123710.e: From U = L times change in current per unit time it follows that L = U times time divided by current. So 1 H = 1 volt-second per ampere.
123710.m: One henry is one volt-second per ampere.

123711.q: What is the resonant frequency of an oscillating circuit with L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF?
123711.e: According to Thomson's formula, f = 1 divided by 2 pi times the square root of L times C. The square root of 10^-8 is 10^-4, which gives about 1590 Hz.
123711.m: A coil and a capacitor form an oscillating circuit.

123712.q: What did Edwin Hall show in 1879 with the effect named after him?
a: That a magnetic field acts on the charge carriers in the conductor itself
That electric current heats a wire
That light can knock electrons out of metals
123712.e: Hall found a voltage across the current when a conductor lies in a magnetic field. This proved that the field deflects the moving charges in the conductor.
123712.m: Edwin Hall discovered the Hall effect in 1879.

123713.q: In which direction does the Hall voltage appear in a current-carrying plate in a magnetic field?
a: Across the current and the magnetic field
123713.e: The charge carriers are pushed sideways and collect at one edge. The voltage is at right angles to both the current and the field.
123713.m: The Hall voltage appears across the current.

123714.q: Which force causes the Hall effect?
a: The Lorentz force on the charge carriers
123714.e: Moving charge carriers are pushed sideways in a magnetic field. A voltage builds up until the electric force balances the Lorentz force.
123714.m: The Hall effect is based on the deflection of moving charges.

123715.q: What are Hall sensors mainly used for?
123715.e: The Hall voltage is proportional to the flux density. Hall probes therefore measure magnetic fields and detect positions or speeds of rotation.

123716.q: The Hall voltage is U = I·B/(n·e·d). How large is it in a copper plate with I = 10 A, B = 1 T, n = 10^29 m^-3, d = 0.1 mm and e = 1.6·10^-19 C?
123716.m: In metals the Hall voltage is very small.

123717.q: What does the sign of the Hall voltage reveal?
a: The sign of the charge carriers
123717.e: Positive and negative charge carriers are pushed to the same side but charge it differently. This is how, for example, hole conduction in semiconductors is recognised.
123717.m: The Hall voltage shows which charges are flowing.

123718.q: Why are Hall voltages much larger in semiconductors than in metals?
a: Semiconductors have far fewer free charge carriers
The magnetic field is stronger in semiconductors
123718.e: The Hall voltage is inversely proportional to the density of charge carriers. With fewer carriers they must flow faster, and the deflection has a stronger effect.
123718.m: Few charge carriers give a large Hall voltage.

123719.q: Who won the 1985 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the quantum Hall effect?
123719.e: In 1980 Klaus von Klitzing found that at low temperatures the Hall resistance appears in exact steps. This gives the von Klitzing constant.
123719.m: Klaus von Klitzing discovered the quantum Hall effect.

123720.q: The thumb of the right hand points in the direction of the current in a straight conductor. What do the curled fingers show?
a: The direction of the field lines
The position of the Earth's north pole
123720.e: With this rule you grip the conductor with your right hand. The fingers show the direction in which the circular field lines go round.
123720.m: The fingers of the right hand show the field lines around the conductor.

123721.q: The fingers of the right hand point in the direction of the current through the turns of a coil. Where does the thumb point?
a: To the north pole of the coil
To the south pole of the coil
To the positive terminal of the source
At right angles to the axis of the coil
123721.e: For coils, the roles of thumb and fingers are swapped. The thumb then points in the direction of the field lines inside, so towards the north pole.
123721.m: For a coil, the right thumb points to the north pole.

123722.q: In the three-finger rule (cause, medium, effect), which finger stands for the effect, that is the force?
123722.e: The thumb stands for the cause (direction of current), the index finger for the medium (magnetic field). The middle finger shows the effect, the force.
123722.m: In the three-finger rule the middle finger shows the force.

123723.q: What must you do if you want to work out the deflection of electrons with a rule made for positive charges?
a: Reverse the direction of the force
123723.e: Electrons are negatively charged, so the force points the other way. Alternatively, you use the left hand for electrons.
123723.m: For electrons the direction of the force is reversed.

123724.q: In which direction does conventional current flow in the external circuit?
123724.e: The direction of conventional current was fixed before electrons were known. The electrons actually move from minus to plus.
123724.m: Conventional current flows from plus to minus.

123725.q: For which application is Fleming's right-hand rule used?
123725.e: Fleming used the right hand for induction in a generator. For motors he used the left hand.
123725.m: Fleming's right hand is for generators.

123726.q: A proton is flying east and the magnetic field points straight up. In which direction does the Lorentz force act?
123726.e: The force follows from the cross product of velocity and field. East crossed with up gives south.
123726.m: The right-hand rule gives you the direction of the force.

123727.q: The current in a straight conductor flows away from the viewer into the page. Which way do the field lines go, as seen by the viewer?
123727.e: If the right thumb points away from the viewer, the fingers curl clockwise. That is the way the field lines run.
123727.m: A current flowing away from the viewer produces clockwise field lines.

123728.q: What does magnetic resonance imaging use to produce its images?
123728.e: MRI uses a strong magnetic field and pulses of radio waves. It works without ionising radiation.

123729.q: Which atomic nuclei is standard MRI mainly aimed at?
123729.e: The body consists largely of water and fat. Their hydrogen nuclei (protons) provide the signal.

123730.q: What is the Larmor frequency of hydrogen nuclei in a 1.5 tesla MRI scanner (42.6 MHz per tesla)?
123730.e: The resonant frequency is proportional to the flux density. 42.6 MHz per tesla times 1.5 T gives about 64 MHz.
123730.m: The resonant frequency rises with the field strength.

123731.q: What flux densities do clinical MRI scanners typically have?
123731.e: Most scanners in hospitals work at 1.5 or 3 tesla. That is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.
123731.m: Clinical MRI scanners usually have 1.5 or 3 tesla.

123732.q: What are the superconducting magnet coils of an MRI scanner cooled with?
123732.e: Superconductivity needs temperatures close to absolute zero. Liquid helium boils at about 4 kelvin.
123732.m: MRI magnets are cooled with liquid helium.

123733.q: Who won the 2003 Nobel Prize in Medicine for developments in MRI?
123733.e: Lauterbur and Mansfield showed how images can be obtained with gradient fields. Bloch and Purcell had already won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952 for nuclear magnetic resonance.
123733.m: Lauterbur and Mansfield won the Nobel Prize for MRI in 2003.

123734.q: Which element do most MRI contrast agents contain?
123734.e: Gadolinium is strongly paramagnetic and changes the signal of nearby hydrogen nuclei. Iodine and barium are used as X-ray contrast agents.
123734.m: MRI contrast agents usually contain gadolinium.

123735.q: Why is an MRI scan so loud?
a: The gradient coils vibrate because of Lorentz forces
The cooling pump runs very fast
The radio waves can be heard
123735.e: The gradient coils are switched on and off rapidly. In the strong magnetic field, forces act on them and make the coils vibrate.
123735.m: Vibrating gradient coils make MRI loud.

123736.q: Which ETH researcher won the 1991 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for nuclear magnetic resonance methods that also served MRI?
123736.e: Richard Ernst developed Fourier transform NMR. This technique is an important basis of imaging.
123736.m: Richard Ernst of ETH Zurich shaped nuclear magnetic resonance.

123737.q: Which UN specialised agency for food and agriculture is based in Rome?
123737.e: The FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) was founded in 1945 and is based in Rome. It collects data on hunger and agriculture and advises countries.
123737.m: The FAO is the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization.

123738.q: Which UN organisation, which provides food aid in crisis areas, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020?
123738.e: The World Food Programme received the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize for its fight against hunger. It is the largest humanitarian organisation distributing food.
123738.m: The WFP fights hunger with direct food aid.

123739.q: Which of the UN Sustainable Development Goals is called “Zero Hunger”?
123739.e: SDG 1 stands for “No Poverty”, SDG 2 for “Zero Hunger”. It calls for food security and sustainable agriculture by 2030.
123739.m: The UN's second sustainable development goal aims to end hunger.

123740.q: What is a lack of vitamins and minerals called, even though enough calories are eaten?
123740.e: In hidden hunger, micronutrients such as iron, iodine or vitamin A are missing. The people affected are often full but still malnourished.
123740.m: Even people who are full can suffer from hidden hunger.

123741.q: Which deficiency disease in children is caused mainly by a lack of protein and shows itself through fluid retention and a swollen belly?
123741.e: Kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition with a lack of protein. Oedema, which makes the belly look swollen, is typical.
123741.m: Kwashiorkor is malnutrition with a severe lack of protein.

123742.q: Which three cereals provide most of the plant-based food energy worldwide?
123742.e: Maize, rice and wheat dominate cereal growing worldwide. A large share of humanity's calories comes from these three plants, either directly or via animal feed.
123742.m: World food supply relies mainly on maize, rice and wheat.

123743.q: What is the concept of the La Via Campesina movement called, according to which peoples should decide their own agricultural and food policies?
123743.e: La Via Campesina, an alliance of small farmers' organisations, coined the term food sovereignty in 1996. It stresses local control over production and markets.
123743.m: Food sovereignty puts self-determination over a country's own farming at the centre.

123744.q: What is the figure called that shows what share of a country's food consumption comes from its own production?
123744.e: The self-sufficiency rate compares domestic production with consumption. In Switzerland it is about half of calorie needs.
123744.m: The self-sufficiency rate shows how much food a country produces itself.

123745.q: What is the index called, published every year, that rates hunger in countries by undernourishment, child mortality and stunted growth?
123745.e: The Global Hunger Index is published by aid organisations such as Welthungerhilfe. It combines several indicators into one value and compares countries.
123745.m: The Global Hunger Index measures how badly a country is affected by hunger.

123746.q: Which target do the UN Sustainable Development Goals set for food waste in retail and by consumers by 2030?
123746.e: Target 12.3 calls for halving food waste per person in retail and by consumers and for reducing losses along the supply chain.
123746.m: The UN wants to halve food waste by 2030.

123747.q: What does the best before date on a packet of pasta mean?
a: The manufacturer guarantees the quality until then; afterwards it is often still fine to eat
After that the product must be thrown away immediately
It gives the date of manufacture
After that eating it is dangerous to health
123747.e: The best before date is a quality guarantee, not a date for throwing things away. Many products are still perfectly fine afterwards if you check them (look, smell, taste).
123747.m: After the best before date, it is worth checking first instead of throwing away.

123748.q: Which date label do highly perishable foods such as minced meat carry?
123748.e: The use by date applies to products that are risky from a microbiological point of view. After this date they should no longer be eaten, for safety reasons.
123748.m: For risky foods, the use by date is a real safety limit.

123749.q: What is it called when people take food that is still edible out of supermarket waste bins?
123749.e: Skipping, also called dumpster diving, draws attention to waste in retail. Gleaning, by contrast, means gathering leftover crops from fields after harvest.
123749.m: When skipping, people rescue thrown-away food from waste bins.

123750.q: Which losses does the FAO call “food loss”, as opposed to “food waste”?
a: Food going off in consumers' fridges
123750.e: Food loss happens during harvest, storage, transport and processing. Food waste means waste in retail, catering and households.
123750.m: Food loss happens early in the supply chain, food waste in retail and consumption.

123751.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly produced when food waste rots in landfill without oxygen?
123751.e: Without air, microorganisms break down organic material into methane. Per molecule, methane is much more powerful than carbon dioxide.
123751.m: Rotting food in landfill releases the powerful greenhouse gas methane.

123752.q: In the hierarchy for using surplus food, which use comes top, directly after prevention?
123752.e: If food is already left over, it should first feed people, for example through social organisations. Only then come animal feed, energy and disposal.
123752.m: Surplus food should first benefit people.

123753.q: Why is a lot of vegetables sorted out in the field or during sorting, even though it would be edible?
a: It does not meet the trade standards for size and appearance
123753.e: Crooked carrots or potatoes that are too small often do not meet visual standards. So they are not sold as table produce.
123753.m: A lot of food is lost only because of how it looks.

123755.q: Which component of the water footprint describes the rainwater that plants take up in the field?
123755.e: Green water is precipitation that is stored in the soil and released by plants. Blue water comes from rivers, lakes or groundwater.
123755.m: Green water is rainwater used by plants.

123756.q: In the water footprint, what does “grey water” show?
a: The amount of water needed to dilute pollutants to below the limits
The water contained in the product itself
123756.e: Grey water is a calculated figure for pollution. The more fertiliser or pesticides get into the water, the larger it is.
123756.m: Grey water measures pollution as the need for dilution.

123757.q: What is the component of the water footprint called that covers water from rivers, lakes and groundwater used for irrigation?
123757.e: Blue water is actively taken and is then missing for other users. For irrigated rice or cotton in dry regions, this share is high.
123757.m: Blue water is taken from rivers, lakes or groundwater.

123758.q: Which of these foods has the largest water footprint per kilogram?
123758.e: On a worldwide average, about 15,000 litres of water are estimated for one kilogram of beef, mainly for feed crops. Vegetables and cereals are far lower.
123758.m: Animal products usually have a much bigger water footprint than plant products.

123759.q: Where does the larger part of the water footprint of the Swiss population arise?
123759.e: Because Switzerland imports a lot of food, textiles and raw materials, much of its water use takes place in other countries. This can make water shortages worse there.
123759.m: Through imports, Switzerland uses a lot of other countries' water.

123760.q: Roughly how many litres of virtual water are in a cup of coffee?
123760.e: According to estimates by the Water Footprint Network, about 130 litres of water are needed to grow and process the coffee beans for one cup. Most of it is rainwater on the plantations.
123760.m: Even a small cup of coffee carries a large water rucksack.

123761.q: Which Swiss sustainability researcher developed the ecological footprint together with William Rees?
123761.e: Mathis Wackernagel worked out the concept in the 1990s at the University of British Columbia. He later founded the Global Footprint Network.
123761.m: The ecological footprint comes from the Swiss Mathis Wackernagel and William Rees.

123762.q: Which organisation calculates Earth Overshoot Day every year?
123762.e: The Global Footprint Network compares the global footprint with the Earth's biocapacity. This gives the date of Earth Overshoot Day.
123762.m: The Global Footprint Network sets the date of Earth Overshoot Day.

123763.q: Roughly how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the Swiss population?
123763.e: Switzerland's footprint per person is almost three times as large as the biocapacity available per person worldwide. CO2 emissions make up the largest part.
123763.m: The Swiss way of life needs much more than one Earth.

a: The ability of ecosystems to produce raw materials and absorb waste such as CO2
The number of animal species in an area
The storage capacity of a biogas reactor
123764.e: Biocapacity is the supply side of the calculation. If the footprint is larger than the biocapacity, nature is being overused.
123764.m: Biocapacity is what nature can provide each year.

123765.q: In industrialised countries, which part usually makes up the largest share of the ecological footprint?
a: The carbon footprint from fossil energy
123765.e: For the CO2 component, the forest area that would be needed to absorb the emissions is calculated. In rich countries it is the largest item.
123765.m: Fossil energy makes the footprint of rich countries especially large.

123766.q: What does it mean if a country has an ecological deficit?
a: Its footprint is larger than its own biocapacity
It exports more food than it imports
It has more forest than farmland
123766.e: A country with an ecological deficit uses more than its nature provides. It covers the gap through imports or by overusing global goods such as the atmosphere.
123766.m: An ecological deficit means a country is living beyond its means.

a: Applying ecological principles to farming and food systems
123767.e: Agroecology is a science, a practice and a social movement all at once. It relies on diversity, natural cycles and local knowledge.
123767.m: Agroecology shapes farming on the model of natural ecosystems.

123768.q: What is it called when several crops are grown at the same time on the same area?
123768.e: Mixed cropping makes better use of light, water and nutrients. It can confuse pests and spread the risk of a failed harvest.
123768.m: In mixed cropping, different plants grow side by side.

123769.q: What does it mean if an agroecological growing system is considered particularly “resilient”?
a: It can cushion disruptions such as droughts or pests and recover
It gives exactly the same yield every year
It needs no sunlight at all
It consists of only one single variety
123769.e: Diversity of crops, varieties and living things spreads the risk. If one crop fails, others can partly make up for the loss.
123769.m: Diversity makes farming systems more resilient.

123770.q: Why are legumes such as clover or peas deliberately included in crop rotations?
a: Their root nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air
They make the soil much more acidic
They need no light to grow
123770.e: Legumes live in symbiosis with root nodule bacteria (rhizobia). These make nitrogen from the air available to plants and so fertilise the soil.
123770.m: With the help of bacteria, legumes bring nitrogen into the soil.

123771.q: Which traditional form of land use in Switzerland is an example of agroforestry?
a: Traditional orchard of tall fruit trees in a meadow
123771.e: In traditional orchards, large fruit trees stand in meadows that are mown or grazed. Agroforestry combines trees with crops or livestock in this way.
123771.m: Traditional orchards combine trees and grassland on the same area.

123772.q: What is the method developed in East Africa called, in which desmodium drives pests out of the maize field and border plants such as Napier grass attract them?
123772.e: Desmodium gives off repellent scents (push), and the grass lures stem borers to the edge of the field (pull). The method works without insecticides.
123772.m: The push-pull method steers pests with plants instead of poison.

123773.q: Which animals are often used in biological pest control against aphids?
123773.e: Ladybirds, and especially their larvae, eat large numbers of aphids. Such beneficial insects are a key part of agroecological systems.
123773.m: Ladybirds are important helpers against aphids.

123774.q: Which research institute, based in Frick in the canton of Aargau, is one of the world's leading institutes for organic farming?
123774.e: The Research Institute of Organic Agriculture (FiBL) was founded in 1973. Today it has sites in several countries.
123774.m: FiBL in Frick does research into organic farming.

123775.q: Which use is the most important direct cause of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest?
123775.e: Most of the cleared land in the Amazon region becomes cattle pasture. Soya growing, mining and road building also play a part.
123775.m: In the Amazon, the rainforest is giving way mainly to cattle pasture.

123776.q: For which crop were particularly large areas of rainforest cleared in Indonesia and Malaysia?
123776.e: Indonesia and Malaysia are the largest producers of palm oil. Rainforests and peat swamps were destroyed for the plantations, with consequences for orangutans, for example.
123776.m: In South-East Asia, palm oil plantations have replaced a lot of rainforest.

123777.q: What does the term slash-and-burn mean?
a: Burning forest to gain land for farming
Burning crop remains in an oven in a controlled way
123777.e: In slash-and-burn, vegetation is burned and the ash fertilises the soil for a short time. A lot of stored carbon is released as CO2.
123777.m: Slash-and-burn turns forest into farmland using fire.

123778.q: What does the UN programme REDD+ stand for?
a: Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation
123778.e: REDD+ rewards countries financially for keeping forests and so avoiding CO2 emissions. The plus stands for additional measures such as sustainable forest management.
123778.m: REDD+ pays for forests to stay standing.

123779.q: Which principle has shaped Swiss forest law since the revision of the federal forest police law of 1902?
a: The area of forest must not be reduced
Every forest belongs to the Confederation
All trees must be felled after 50 years
123779.e: After heavy deforestation and floods in the 19th century, the Confederation laid down a ban on clearing forests. Anyone who is exceptionally allowed to clear forest today must in principle plant new forest to replace it.
123779.m: In Switzerland, preserving forests has been laid down in law for over a hundred years.

123780.q: What do researchers fear if too much of the Amazon rainforest is cut down?
a: Large parts could tip into a savannah-like landscape
The Amazon would become a glacier region
The sea level would fall immediately
The rainy season would last twice as long
123780.e: The rainforest produces a large part of its own rainfall. If too much forest is removed, a tipping point could be passed, after which it dries out.
123780.m: The Amazon has a tipping point beyond which it could become savannah.

123781.q: Which coastal forests in South-East Asia and Latin America are often cleared for shrimp farming ponds?
123781.e: Mangroves grow in the tidal zone of tropical coasts. They protect against storm surges and are a nursery for many fish species, but are cut down for aquaculture.
123781.m: Mangroves protect coasts and are still cleared for shrimp farming.

123782.q: What are the streams of moisture called that carry rain from the Amazon rainforest to other parts of South America?
123782.e: Trees release large amounts of water, which is carried on as water vapour. Deforestation weakens these “flying rivers” and can make droughts worse in the south.
123782.m: The rainforest sends rain onwards through flying rivers.

123783.q: What is the first Fairtrade label called, which was created in the Netherlands in 1988 and is still well known in Switzerland today?
123783.e: The label is named after a character in a novel that denounces exploitation in the Dutch East Indies. In Switzerland the Max Havelaar Foundation has been active since 1992.
123783.m: Max Havelaar was the first Fairtrade label.

123784.q: What does the Fairtrade minimum price guarantee producers?
a: A lower price limit even if the world market price falls lower
A fixed price that may never rise
123784.e: The minimum price is meant to cover production costs. If the market price is higher, the higher market price applies.
123784.m: The minimum price protects farming families from price crashes.

123785.q: What are specialist shops called that sell only fair trade products?
123785.e: World shops appeared from the 1970s onwards and are often run by volunteers. They combine selling with providing information.
123785.m: World shops sell fair trade goods and inform people about trade.

123786.q: Which Swiss women's group campaigned for fairer banana prices with campaigns from the 1970s onwards?
123786.e: The Banana Women from Frauenfeld drew attention to the poor pay on banana plantations. They are considered pioneers of fair trade in Switzerland.
123786.m: The Banana Women were pioneers of fair trade in Switzerland.

123787.q: For which product does Fairtrade have a particularly high market share in Switzerland?
123787.e: In Switzerland a very large proportion of the bananas sold carry a Fairtrade label. This puts Switzerland among the leaders for fair bananas.
123787.m: In Switzerland, fair trade is especially widespread for bananas.

123788.q: Which two countries does most of the world's harvested cocoa come from?
123788.e: Together the two West African countries supply well over half of the cocoa. Low incomes and child labour are big problems there.
123788.m: Most cocoa comes from Ivory Coast and Ghana.

123789.q: Which title can municipalities and towns receive if they actively promote fair trade?
123789.e: Fair Trade Towns meet criteria such as fair products in the administration, shops and restaurants. Several municipalities in Switzerland hold this title.
123789.m: A Fair Trade Town actively supports fair trade.

123790.q: What is a plant protection product against fungal diseases such as mildew called?
123790.e: Fungicides stop fungi from growing. They are used a lot in vineyards and orchards, for example.

123791.q: Which organisms are herbicides aimed at?
123791.e: Herbicides control weeds that compete with crops for light, water and nutrients. By quantity they are one of the largest groups of pesticides.

123792.q: Which goal did the Confederation set itself with the 2017 action plan on plant protection products?
a: To halve the risks of plant protection products
To only import pesticides from now on
123792.e: The action plan aims to reduce the risks to people, waters and beneficial insects significantly. This includes alternatives to chemical plant protection and less spray drift.
123792.m: The Confederation's action plan aims to halve pesticide risks.

123793.q: What is the required minimum period between the last use of a pesticide and the harvest called?
123793.e: The pre-harvest interval makes sure that residues fall below the permitted maximum levels by harvest time. It is set for each product and each crop.
123793.m: After spraying, the pre-harvest interval must be kept before harvesting.

123795.q: Which plants does the natural insecticide pyrethrum come from?
123795.e: Pyrethrum is obtained from the dried flowers of certain chrysanthemums. It acts as a nerve poison on insects and is allowed in organic farming with restrictions.
123795.m: Pyrethrum is an insecticide made from chrysanthemum flowers.

123796.q: What is it called when a long-lasting substance such as DDT builds up in living things, increasing along the food chain?
123796.e: Birds of prey at the end of the food chain had such high DDT levels that their eggshells became thin. The concentration rises from level to level.
123796.m: Long-lasting poisons build up along the food chain.

123797.q: Why do pesticides often lose their effect when used frequently?
a: The pesticides become stronger in light
The plants turn them into fertiliser
123797.e: With every use, a few resistant individuals survive. Through selection their genes spread until the population is resistant.
123797.m: Frequent use of pesticides breeds resistant pests.

123798.q: In integrated plant protection, what does the “damage threshold” mean?
a: The level of infestation at which control makes economic sense
The highest amount of pesticide allowed per year
The temperature at which pests die
The distance between a field and a body of water
123798.e: Below the damage threshold, the loss of yield is smaller than the cost of treatment. This way pesticides are only used when needed.
123798.m: Integrated plant protection only sprays once the damage threshold is reached.

123799.q: Which receptors in the nervous system of insects do neonicotinoids bind to?
123799.e: Neonicotinoids occupy the acetylcholine receptors and overstimulate the nerve cells. Insects are much more sensitive than mammals.
123799.m: Neonicotinoids disrupt signal transmission in the insect nervous system.

123800.q: What does it mean that neonicotinoids work “systemically”?
a: They are taken up by the plant and spread to all its parts
They only work on the leaf surface
They break down immediately after spraying
They only work in the soil
123800.e: Systemic substances get into stems, leaves, pollen and nectar. This protects the whole plant but also reaches pollinators.
123800.m: Systemic insecticides are found throughout the whole plant.

123801.q: In what form were neonicotinoids often applied in farming?
a: As a seed treatment on the seed
As an additive in animal feed
123801.e: In seed treatment, the grain is coated with the active substance. When sowing, contaminated dust can be produced, which can endanger bees.
123801.m: Neonicotinoids were often applied directly to the seed.

123802.q: What effect of the neonicotinoid imidacloprid on bumblebee colonies did a study published in “Science” in 2012 show?
a: The colonies produced far fewer new queens
The bumblebees grew twice as big
The bumblebees became immune to mites
123802.e: Bumblebee colonies exposed to realistic amounts of imidacloprid grew more slowly and raised about 85 per cent fewer queens. As a result they found fewer new colonies the following year.
123802.m: Neonicotinoids can also weaken wild bees such as bumblebees.

123803.q: Which active substance was the first commercially very successful neonicotinoid?
123803.e: Imidacloprid came on the market in the 1990s and quickly became one of the best-selling insecticides in the world.
123803.m: Imidacloprid was the first big neonicotinoid.

123804.q: Which measure did the EU decide on in 2018 for three widely used neonicotinoids?
a: A requirement to use them in organic farming
123804.e: The ban affected imidacloprid, clothianidin and thiamethoxam, after the food safety authority EFSA had confirmed risks to bees. Switzerland followed with similar restrictions.
123804.m: In 2018 the EU banned three neonicotinoids from fields.

123805.q: What effect of even small amounts of neonicotinoids has been proved in honeybees?
a: They find their way back to the hive less well
123805.e: Sublethal doses do not kill the bees immediately but disturb learning and orientation. Foraging bees then return less often, which weakens the colony.
123805.m: Even small amounts of neonicotinoids disturb bees' sense of direction.

123806.q: What did a study by the University of Neuchâtel, published in 2017, show about honey samples from all over the world?
a: Only honey from Europe was contaminated
123806.e: The researchers examined 198 honey samples from every continent except Antarctica. The levels were mostly below the limits for humans, but in a range that is worrying for bees.
123806.m: Neonicotinoids can be detected in honey all over the world.

123807.q: Why do plants treated with glyphosate die?
a: They can no longer make important amino acids
They can no longer absorb light
123807.e: Glyphosate blocks an enzyme that plants need for certain amino acids. Without these building blocks they can no longer make proteins and die.
123807.m: Glyphosate shuts down the production of important amino acids in plants.

123808.q: Why does the main way glyphosate works not affect people and animals directly?
a: Animals do not have the blocked metabolic pathway
Animals immediately turn it into sugar
123808.e: Animals get aromatic amino acids from their food instead of making them themselves. However, other possible effects are being discussed, for example on gut bacteria.
123808.m: Glyphosate targets a metabolic pathway that only plants and microorganisms have.

123809.q: How is glyphosate classified by its effect on plants?
123809.e: Glyphosate works on almost all green plants it hits. That is why it is used before sowing or after harvesting.
123809.m: Glyphosate kills almost every plant it touches.

123810.q: Which US company brought glyphosate onto the market in the 1970s under the name Roundup?
123810.e: Monsanto later also developed genetically modified plants that tolerate glyphosate. The patent on the active substance expired long ago.
123810.m: Glyphosate was originally marketed by Monsanto.

123811.q: Which German company took over Monsanto in 2018?
123811.e: With the takeover, Bayer inherited many lawsuits in the USA over alleged cancer risks from Roundup. The court cases cost the company billions.
123811.m: Since 2018, Monsanto has belonged to Bayer.

123812.q: How did the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classify glyphosate in 2015?
123812.e: The IARC placed glyphosate in Group 2A. Authorities such as EFSA, however, concluded that no cancer risk had been proved when it is used correctly.
123812.m: Expert bodies disagree about the cancer risk of glyphosate.

123813.q: For how many years did the European Commission extend the approval of glyphosate in 2023?
123813.e: Because the member states could not agree, the Commission decided. The new approval applies until 2033 and includes some conditions.
123813.m: Glyphosate remains approved in the EU until 2033 for now.

a: Genetically modified varieties that survive glyphosate treatment
Varieties that only grow with glyphosate
Plants that break down glyphosate in the soil
123814.e: Such soya, maize or cotton varieties carry a gene for an insensitive enzyme. The field can be sprayed without harming the crop, which increased glyphosate use.
123814.m: Glyphosate-tolerant plants survive spraying, but weeds do not.

123815.q: What is the main goal of regenerative agriculture?
a: Building up humus and soil health
Making maximum use of mineral fertiliser
123815.e: Regenerative agriculture aims not only to protect the soil but to improve it. More humus stores water, nutrients and carbon.
123815.m: Regenerative agriculture builds fertile soil back up.

123816.q: What is sowing without ploughing or other tillage beforehand called?
123816.e: In direct drilling, the seed is placed in untilled soil. Soil life and structure are preserved and erosion falls.
123816.m: Direct drilling protects the soil because it is not ploughed.

123817.q: Which soil problem arises when heavy machinery drives on wet farmland?
123817.e: The pressure squeezes the pores in the soil together so that water and air get in less well. Roots and soil organisms often suffer for years.
123817.m: Heavy machinery on wet soil compacts it.

123818.q: Why is building up humus considered a contribution to climate protection?
a: Humus stores carbon that was previously in the air as CO2
Humus cools the Earth's surface by several degrees
Humus produces oxygen like a forest
123818.e: Plants take up CO2 through photosynthesis and release part of it into the soil as organic matter. If this becomes stable humus, the carbon stays stored for a long time.
123818.m: More humus in the soil means less CO2 in the atmosphere.

123819.q: What does the “4 per 1000” initiative, launched at the 2015 Paris climate conference, call for?
a: Raising the carbon content of soils by 0.4 per cent a year
Cutting pesticide use by 4 per cent a year
Planting forest on four in every thousand hectares
Limiting meat consumption to 4 kilos a year
123819.e: Such an increase in soil carbon could offset a significant part of annual CO2 emissions. The initiative was started by France.
123819.m: The 4 per 1000 initiative relies on soils as carbon stores.

123820.q: What is grazing called in which many animals graze a small area for only a short time and then move on?
123820.e: In mob grazing, the grass is used briefly and intensively and then left to rest for a long time. This is meant to encourage root growth and humus formation.
123820.m: Mob grazing lets pastures rest for a long time after brief use.

123821.q: Why should farmland in regenerative agriculture be covered for as much of the year as possible?
a: To protect it from erosion and drying out
So that nobody can walk on it
So that birds cannot find worms
123821.e: Bare soil is carried away by rain and wind and heats up a lot. Plants or mulch protect it and feed the soil life.

123822.q: What is the very fertile dark earth enriched with charcoal called, which people in the Amazon region created centuries ago?
123822.e: Terra preta was created from charcoal, pottery fragments and organic waste. Today biochar is used on this model to improve soils.
123822.m: Terra preta shows how charcoal can make soils permanently more fertile.

123823.q: Which soil animal is considered an important indicator of healthy, living soil?
123823.e: Earthworms loosen the soil, create pores for water and air and mix in organic material. Lots of worms suggest gentle farming.
123823.m: Lots of earthworms show that soil is healthy.

123824.q: What is meant by vertical farming?
a: Growing plants on floors stacked on top of each other in buildings
123824.e: Vertical farms stack growing areas in halls or tower blocks. Light, temperature and nutrients are completely controlled.

123825.q: What is growing plants without soil, with the roots standing in a nutrient solution, called?
123825.e: In hydroponics, a circulating solution supplies all the nutrients. Many vertical farms work on this principle.
123825.m: In hydroponics, plants grow in nutrient solution instead of soil.

123826.q: Why is the yield per area of ground much higher in vertical farms than in a field?
a: Crops are harvested on several floors and all year round
The plants grow ten times bigger there
They are only harvested once a year
123826.e: Several growing levels stacked on top of each other multiply the area. On top of that there are many harvests a year, because weather and seasons play no part.
123826.m: Stacked floors and harvests all year round give high yields per area of ground.

123827.q: Which system combines fish farming with growing plants in one cycle?
123827.e: Bacteria turn the fish's waste into nutrients that the plants take up. In doing so, the plants clean the water for the fish.
123827.m: Aquaponics links fish and plants in one cycle.

123828.q: Which colours of light do LED lamps in vertical farms mainly use?
123828.e: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light, while green light is reflected more. That is why many facilities glow purple-pink.
123828.m: For photosynthesis, plants mainly use red and blue light.

123829.q: What is considered the biggest disadvantage of vertical farming?
a: The high energy use for light and air conditioning
The large amount of land needed
123829.e: Because sunlight is replaced by artificial light, running the farm needs a lot of electricity. This makes the products expensive, and their climate impact depends on the source of the electricity.
123829.m: Vertical farms need a lot of energy because they replace the sun.

123830.q: Which plants are especially suitable for vertical farming?
123830.e: Lettuces and herbs grow fast, stay small and are almost entirely eaten. Staple foods such as cereals would be far too expensive to grow indoors.
123830.m: Vertical farming mainly grows lettuces and herbs.

123831.q: Why does vertical farming often need much less water than growing outdoors?
a: The water is reused in a closed cycle
The plants are smaller and drink nothing
The building collects fog from the city
123831.e: Evaporated water is condensed and excess nutrient solution is fed back. So hardly any water is lost.
123831.m: Closed cycles make vertical farming save water.

123832.q: Which advantage of vertical farming is particularly interesting for cities?
123832.e: Vertical farms can stand in the middle of cities. Lettuces and herbs reach the shops fresh and without long lorry journeys.
123832.m: Vertical farming brings growing close to the city.

123931.q: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
123931.e: The enzymes of glycolysis are dissolved in the cytoplasm. That is why it can also take place in cells without mitochondria.
123931.m: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.

123932.q: Which end product is formed from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
