125525.e: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for fight or flight. Heartbeat and breathing speed up, and you sweat.
125525.m: The sympathetic nervous system controls the fight-or-flight response.

125526.q: Why does avoidance behaviour strengthen a fear in the long run?
a: You never experience that the danger does not happen
You move too little in everyday life
It makes you sleep too much
It makes you eat too much sugar
125526.e: Avoiding a situation brings short-term relief. But you never find out that what you fear does not happen, so the fear remains.
125526.m: Avoidance brings brief relief but keeps the fear alive.

125527.q: How does the WHO classify burnout in ICD-11?
a: As a psychosis in its own right
125527.e: In ICD-11, burnout appears as a phenomenon linked to work, not as a medical illness in its own right. It is explicitly related to chronic stress at the workplace.
125527.m: The WHO describes burnout as a result of chronic stress at work.

125528.q: Which dimension is one of Christina Maslach's three core features of burnout?
125528.e: Maslach describes emotional exhaustion, a detached attitude and reduced performance. Exhaustion is considered the central feature.
125528.m: Emotional exhaustion is a core feature of burnout.

125529.q: What is the well-known questionnaire for measuring burnout called?
125529.e: The Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) was developed by Christina Maslach and colleagues. It is used in research all over the world.
125529.m: The Maslach Burnout Inventory measures burnout.

125530.q: Which psychologist coined the term “burnout” in the 1970s?
125530.e: In the 1970s, the psychologist Herbert Freudenberger described the exhaustion of people in helping roles. In doing so, he made the term known in psychology.
125530.m: Herbert Freudenberger made the term burnout known.

125531.q: What does “depersonalisation” mean in Maslach's burnout model?
a: A detached, indifferent attitude towards others
125531.e: It means a cynical, numbed attitude towards clients, patients or colleagues. It often serves as protection against being overwhelmed further.
125531.m: With burnout, people often become detached and cynical.

125532.q: In which professions was burnout originally described above all?
125532.e: The first descriptions concerned people in nursing, social work and counselling. Today we know that burnout can occur in all professions.
125532.m: Burnout was first described in caring professions.

125533.q: According to the job demands-resources model, when does the risk of burnout rise particularly?
125533.e: The model distinguishes stressful demands from supporting resources such as freedom to make decisions or support. If resources are lacking under high strain, the risk rises.
125533.m: High strain and little support encourage burnout.

125534.q: Which measure is considered important for preventing burnout?
a: Being available on your mobile at all times
125534.e: Breaks, holidays, sleep and a clear separation of work and free time help to rebuild strength. Social support also protects.
125534.m: Recovery and clear boundaries protect against burnout.

a: Too little exercise in everyday life
125535.e: PTSD develops after a traumatic experience such as a serious accident, war, violence or a natural disaster. Not everyone who experiences a trauma develops PTSD.

125536.q: What is the sudden, unwanted reliving of a trauma as if it were happening right now called?
125536.e: In a flashback, images, sounds or feelings of the trauma come back very vividly. Experts also speak of intrusions.
125536.m: A flashback is an unwanted reliving of the trauma.

125537.q: In PTSD, what is meant by “hyperarousal”?
a: Lasting overexcitement and being easily startled
125537.e: Hyperarousal means the body is constantly on alert. Those affected sleep badly, are irritable and startle easily.
125537.m: In PTSD, the body often stays on alert.

125538.q: Which therapy method for PTSD uses targeted eye movements?
125538.e: EMDR stands for “Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing” and was developed by Francine Shapiro. Memories are processed with the help of eye movements.
125538.m: EMDR is a trauma therapy using eye movements.

125539.q: Which English term was used in the First World War for the psychological effects of war on soldiers?
125539.e: “Shell shock” refers to the shock of exploding shells. Many of the symptoms described at that time would be classed as PTSD today.
125539.m: Shell shock was an early name for war trauma.

125540.q: What is the short-term reaction directly after a trauma called, which usually fades within hours to days?
125540.e: The acute stress reaction is a normal, temporary reaction to an extreme event. If the symptoms last a long time, PTSD can develop.
125540.m: An acute stress reaction usually fades quickly.

125541.q: Which diagnosis was newly introduced in ICD-11 for the effects of long-lasting, repeated trauma?
125541.e: Complex PTSD includes the PTSD symptoms plus problems with regulating emotions, self-image and relationships. It occurs, for example, after long captivity or war.

125542.q: What is a stimulus called that triggers memories of the trauma in people with PTSD?
125542.e: A trigger can be a sound, a smell or a place that reminds the person of the trauma. Many of those affected try to avoid such stimuli.
125542.m: A trigger sets off memories of a trauma.

125543.q: Which three core symptoms characterise ADHD?
a: Sadness, lack of drive, sleep disorder
125543.e: ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Typical are problems with attention, a strong urge to move and acting impulsively.
125543.m: ADHD shows itself through inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.

125544.q: Which active substance is often used to treat ADHD with medication?
125544.e: Methylphenidate is a stimulant that strengthens the effect of messenger substances in the brain. In many people affected it improves attention and self-control.
125544.m: Methylphenidate is a common ADHD medicine.

125545.q: In which Swiss city was methylphenidate first produced by the chemical company Ciba?
125545.e: The chemist Leandro Panizzon produced the substance at Ciba in Basel. Basel is still a centre of the pharmaceutical industry today.

125546.q: What is the form of ADHD without marked hyperactivity often called in everyday language?
125546.e: In the mainly inattentive type, the strong urge to move is missing. Those affected seem more dreamy and distracted.
125546.m: ADD is a form of ADHD without strong hyperactivity.

125547.q: At what stage of life does ADHD begin?
125547.e: ADHD is a developmental disorder. The first signs appear in childhood, even if the diagnosis is sometimes only made later.

125548.q: According to current knowledge, which factor has the greatest influence on the development of ADHD?
125548.e: Twin and family studies show that ADHD is highly heritable. Environmental factors can play a part, but sugar or upbringing alone do not cause ADHD.

125549.q: Which messenger substances are particularly in the focus of ADHD research?
125549.e: In ADHD, signal transmission with dopamine and noradrenaline is altered. These messenger substances are important for attention, motivation and self-control.
125549.m: Dopamine and noradrenaline play an important role in ADHD.

125550.q: What is true of ADHD in adulthood?
125550.e: In many people affected, symptoms remain into adulthood, often in a changed form. Hyperactivity then often becomes inner restlessness.

125551.q: Which character from Heinrich Hoffmann's “Struwwelpeter” is often seen as an early portrayal of ADHD-like behaviour?
a: Augustus who would not eat his soup
125551.e: Fidgety Philip cannot sit still at the table and finally pulls the tablecloth down. That is why people sometimes speak of “Fidgety Philip syndrome”.
125551.m: Fidgety Philip is seen as an early portrayal of hyperactivity.

125552.q: In which two areas do the core features of an autism spectrum disorder show themselves?
125552.e: Autistic people often have difficulties with social interaction and communication. In addition, there are restricted interests and repeated behaviours.
125552.m: Autism affects social communication and repeated patterns of behaviour.

125553.q: Which former diagnosis was merged into autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5?
125553.e: Asperger's syndrome is named after the Austrian paediatrician Hans Asperger. Today the different forms are grouped together as a spectrum.
125553.m: Asperger's syndrome is now part of the autism spectrum.

125554.q: Which child psychiatrist described early childhood autism in the 1940s?
125554.e: In the USA, Leo Kanner published a well-known description of children with autistic features. Early childhood autism is therefore also called Kanner's syndrome.
125554.m: Leo Kanner described early childhood autism.

125555.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist introduced the term “autism” into technical language?
125555.e: Eugen Bleuler was a professor of psychiatry in Zurich and used the word in 1911. He originally meant a withdrawal into one's own inner world.
125555.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the word autism.

125556.q: What does research show about the claimed link between vaccinations and autism?
125556.e: Large studies with millions of children found no link. The study that spread this claim was withdrawn because of falsified data.

125557.q: Why do people speak of a “spectrum” today?
a: The characteristics and the need for support vary greatly
There are exactly three fixed types
125557.e: Autistic people differ greatly in language, abilities and need for support. The term spectrum reflects this variety.
125557.m: Autism shows itself in very different ways.

125558.q: What is self-stimulating, repeated behaviour such as rocking or hand-flapping called?
125558.e: Stimming helps many autistic people to calm down or process stimuli. It is usually harmless and should not simply be suppressed.
125558.m: Stimming helps autistic people regulate themselves.

125559.q: Which special feature of perception is common in autism?
a: Over- or under-sensitivity to sensory stimuli
125559.e: Many autistic people experience sounds, light or touch as very intense or hardly noticeable. Loud, crowded rooms can therefore be very stressful.
125559.m: Autistic people often perceive sensory stimuli differently.

125560.q: Which term describes the view that neurological differences such as autism are natural variations of human beings?
125560.e: The term neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains. It aims to make strengths visible and reduce exclusion.
125560.m: Neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains.

125561.e: The Viennese doctor Sigmund Freud developed psychoanalysis around 1900. It stresses the importance of unconscious processes.

125562.e: Carl Rogers put the person and their ability to grow at the centre. The therapist accompanies rather than prescribing solutions.

125563.q: According to Carl Rogers, which basic attitude is one of the core conditions of helpful therapy?
a: Rewards in the form of presents
125563.e: Rogers names empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness. These attitudes are meant to make change possible for the client.
125563.m: Empathy is a core attitude of client-centred therapy.

125564.q: What is especially at the centre of systemic therapy?
125564.e: Systemic therapy looks at problems in connection with family, partnerships or other groups. Relatives are often included in the therapy.
125564.m: Systemic therapy looks at people within their environment.

125565.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist founded analytical psychology?
125565.e: C. G. Jung worked in Zurich and coined terms such as “collective unconscious” and “archetype”. He later broke away from Freud.
125565.m: C. G. Jung founded analytical psychology.

125566.q: What changed in Switzerland with the prescription model in 2022?
a: Psychological psychotherapy is paid for by basic health insurance when prescribed by a doctor
Only doctors may hold therapy sessions
Therapy is now only available online
125566.e: Before, psychological psychotherapists had to work under a doctor's supervision for the health insurance to pay. Now, on a doctor's prescription, they can bill basic insurance independently.
125566.m: Since the prescription model, basic insurance pays for psychological psychotherapy prescribed by a doctor.

125567.q: Which factor does research consider one of the most important active factors in any psychotherapy?
a: The size of the therapy room
The length of the journey there
125567.e: A trusting relationship between client and therapist helps success across different schools of therapy. This is also called the therapeutic alliance.
125567.m: A good therapeutic relationship is central to the success of therapy.

a: Feelings from earlier relationships are directed at the therapist
Passing files on to the health insurer
125568.e: In transference, the patient unconsciously experiences the therapist in a similar way to important people from the past. These feelings are worked through in therapy.
125568.m: In transference, old relationship patterns appear in therapy.

125569.q: What distinguishes a psychiatrist from a psychologist?
a: A psychiatrist is a doctor and may prescribe medicines
A psychiatrist only works with children
A psychiatrist may not hold conversations
125569.e: Psychiatrists have studied medicine and completed specialist training. Psychologists have studied psychology and do not prescribe medicines.
125569.m: Psychiatrists are doctors and may prescribe medicines.

125570.q: What is the long-established psychiatric university hospital in Zurich called?
125570.e: The Burghölzli opened in 1870 and is now part of the Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich. In the early 20th century it was a world-famous centre of psychiatry.
125570.m: The Burghölzli is the well-known psychiatric hospital in Zurich.

125571.e: Eugen Bleuler introduced the term at the beginning of the 20th century. The word means roughly “split mind”, but it does not mean a split personality.
125571.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia.

125572.q: Which group of medicines is mainly used to treat psychoses?
125572.e: Antipsychotics, also called neuroleptics, reduce symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations. They act mainly on the dopamine system.

125573.q: Under Swiss law, what is it called when a person is placed in an institution against their will for their own protection?
125573.e: Placement for care and assistance is regulated in the Civil Code. It is only allowed if the necessary treatment or care cannot be provided in any other way.
125573.m: Placement for care and assistance is a protective measure in the Civil Code.

a: A perception without an external stimulus
125574.e: In a hallucination, someone hears, sees or feels something that is not there. Voices that other people cannot hear are common, for example.
125574.m: A hallucination is a perception without a real stimulus.

125575.q: Which substance has long been used as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder?
125575.e: Lithium salts can reduce relapses into mania and depression. Because the effective dose is close to the toxic one, the blood level is checked regularly.
125575.m: Lithium stabilises mood in bipolar disorder.

125576.q: What does a psychiatric day clinic offer?
a: Treatment during the day, nights at home
125576.e: The day clinic is a partly inpatient service. Patients spend the day at the clinic with therapies and return home in the evening.
125576.m: In a day clinic you are treated during the day and sleep at home.

a: People are looked down on and excluded because of a characteristic
People are given an award for an achievement
People receive a new identity card
125577.e: In stigmatisation, a characteristic, such as an illness, is linked with negative prejudices. As a result, those affected are put at a disadvantage.
125577.m: Stigmatisation means looking down on people because of a characteristic.

125578.q: What did the Greek word “stigma” originally mean?
a: A prick or a brand mark
125578.e: In ancient Greece, a stigma was a mark that had been burnt or cut into the skin. Today it means a characteristic for which someone is looked down on.
125578.m: A stigma was originally a brand mark.

a: Those affected turn prejudices against themselves
You register yourself with the doctor
125579.e: People who take society's prejudices to heart often feel ashamed and less valuable. This can make recovery even harder.
125579.m: In self-stigmatisation, those affected turn prejudices against themselves.

125580.q: What is a common consequence of the stigmatisation of mental illness?
a: Those affected seek help later or not at all
125580.e: Out of shame and fear of rejection, many people keep their symptoms to themselves. As a result, treatment often starts late.
125580.m: Stigma stops people from seeking help.

125581.q: According to research, which measure is particularly effective in reducing prejudice against people with mental illness?
125581.e: According to the contact hypothesis, direct encounters reduce prejudice. That is why personal accounts from those affected are often used in anti-stigma programmes.

125582.q: Which wording is considered more respectful?
125582.e: This wording puts the person before the illness. That way the person is not reduced to their diagnosis.
125582.m: Respectful language puts the person before the diagnosis.

125583.q: What is the Swiss campaign called that encourages people to talk openly about mental health?
125583.e: The campaign is a project of the German-speaking cantons and the Pro Mente Sana foundation on behalf of Health Promotion Switzerland. It gives tips on how to start conversations about mental health problems.
125583.m: The campaign “Wie geht's dir?” encourages conversations about mental health.

125584.q: What is meant by structural discrimination against people with mental illness?
a: Disadvantage caused by rules and institutions
125584.e: Structural discrimination comes from laws, procedures or the way resources are shared out, not from individual prejudices. One example is poorer care compared with physical illnesses.
125584.m: Structural discrimination is built into rules and institutions.

125585.q: What can children and young people contact the Pro Juventute 147 helpline about?
125585.e: The 147 helpline is open for any topic, such as stress, bullying, family or worries about the future. No worry is too small.
125585.m: You can talk about any worry on 147.

125586.q: When can you reach the 147 helpline?
125586.e: The 147 helpline can be reached around the clock, 365 days a year. That way, young people can find support at night too.
125586.m: The 147 helpline is available day and night.

125587.q: How much does a call to the 147 helpline cost?
a: A flat rate of ten francs
It varies from canton to canton
125587.e: The helpline is free for children and young people. That way no one has to go without help for lack of money.

125588.q: Apart from by phone, how else can you reach the 147 helpline?
a: By text message, chat and email
Only in person at a counter
125588.e: Besides the phone, advice is available by text message, in a chat and by email. Many young people prefer writing to calling.
125588.m: The 147 helpline can also be reached by text, chat and email.

125589.q: What is true of conversations with the 147 helpline?
125589.e: The advice is confidential, and you do not have to give your name. This makes it easier to talk about difficult topics too.
125589.m: On 147 you can talk about your worries in confidence.

125590.q: What kind of organisation is Pro Juventute?
a: A Swiss foundation for children and young people
125590.e: Pro Juventute is a non-profit foundation. It supports children, young people and parents with advice and projects.
125590.m: Pro Juventute is a foundation for children and young people.

125591.q: What is the phone number of Die Dargebotene Hand, the Swiss helpline for adults?
125591.e: Die Dargebotene Hand can be reached on 143 and is mainly for adults. The number 145 belongs to Tox Info, 118 to the fire brigade.
125591.m: Die Dargebotene Hand has the number 143.

125592.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance service when a life is in acute danger?
125592.e: In a medical emergency such as an acute danger to life, you call the ambulance service on 144. The 147 helpline is for talking about worries, and 145 is the number of Tox Info.
125592.m: When a life is in acute danger, you dial 144.

125593.q: Which American psychiatrist is regarded as the founder of cognitive therapy?
125593.e: Aaron T. Beck first developed cognitive therapy for depression. He showed how negative thought patterns influence feelings.
125593.m: Aaron T. Beck founded cognitive therapy.

125594.q: Who developed rational emotive behaviour therapy?
125594.e: Albert Ellis believed that irrational beliefs cause distressing feelings. His method is one of the roots of cognitive behavioural therapy.
125594.m: Albert Ellis developed rational emotive behaviour therapy.

125595.q: What does Beck's cognitive triad refer to?
a: A negative view of yourself, the world and the future
125595.e: Beck described a negative view of oneself, one's surroundings and the future in depression. The therapy examines these thoughts together.
125595.m: The cognitive triad is a negative view of yourself, the world and the future.

125596.q: What is the thinking error called in which you conclude the worst possible outcome from a small problem?
125596.e: In catastrophising, one mistake immediately becomes total failure. Therapy helps to find more realistic thoughts.
125596.m: Catastrophising turns small things into disasters.

125597.q: What does the “B” stand for in Albert Ellis's ABC model?
125597.e: A is the activating event, B the belief and C the consequence. It is not the event alone but how it is judged that determines the feeling.
125597.m: In the ABC model, how an event is judged determines the feeling.

125598.q: What is the technique called in which unhelpful thoughts are recognised, checked and replaced with more helpful ones?
125598.e: In cognitive restructuring, you look for evidence for and against a thought. This leads to more balanced views.

125599.q: What is the aim of behavioural activation in depression?
a: Staying in bed as much as possible
125599.e: Depressed people often withdraw, which lowers their mood further. Planned, positive activities break this cycle.
125599.m: Behavioural activation gets mood going again through activity.

125600.q: What is the thinking error called in which only extremes such as “perfect” or “total failure” are seen?
125600.e: In black-and-white thinking, there are no shades in between. Anyone who is not perfect then sees themselves straight away as a failure.
125600.m: Black-and-white thinking has no shades in between.

125601.q: Which skill do people practise in many modern behavioural therapies by perceiving the moment consciously and without judging it?
125601.e: Mindfulness is a core element of newer methods such as Marsha Linehan's dialectical behaviour therapy. You learn to notice thoughts and feelings without reacting to them straight away.
125601.m: Mindfulness means experiencing the moment consciously and without judging.

a: The interaction between mind and body
125602.e: The term is made up of the Greek “psyche” (soul) and “soma” (body). Psychosomatics studies how mental factors influence physical complaints and the other way round.
125602.m: Psychosomatics studies the interplay between mind and body.

125603.q: Which model explains illness as the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors?
125603.e: The biopsychosocial model was made known by the psychiatrist George Engel. It adds the mind and the environment to the purely biological view.
125603.m: The biopsychosocial model connects body, mind and social environment.

125604.q: Which hormone does the adrenal cortex release in larger amounts during lasting stress?
125604.e: Cortisol provides energy and helps to cope with strain. If it stays high for a long time, it can weaken the immune system and disturb sleep.
125604.m: Cortisol is an important stress hormone.

a: Physical complaints without a sufficient physical cause being found
A broken bone after a fall
A heart disease present from birth
125605.e: Those affected really suffer from pain or other complaints, but the examinations do not explain them sufficiently. The complaints are not imagined.
125605.m: In somatoform disorders, real complaints have no sufficient physical cause.

125606.q: Which complaint is particularly often partly caused by stress and tension?
125606.e: Under stress, the neck and head muscles tense up. This can trigger a pressing headache.

125607.q: What is the effect called that arises solely from positive expectations of a treatment?
125607.e: Just expecting a remedy to help can measurably relieve complaints. Placebo means “I shall please” in Latin.
125607.m: The placebo effect comes from positive expectations.

125608.q: What is the effect called in which negative expectations cause or worsen complaints?
125608.e: People who expect side effects, for example, feel them more often, even with a dummy pill. Nocebo means “I shall harm” in Latin.
125608.m: Negative expectations can trigger complaints through the nocebo effect.

125609.q: Which researcher shaped the modern concept of stress with the “general adaptation syndrome”?
125609.e: Hans Selye described how the body reacts to lasting strain in phases: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. He made the term stress known in medicine.
125609.m: Hans Selye shaped the modern understanding of stress.

125610.q: Which two postulates form the basis of the special theory of relativity?
a: The principle of relativity and the constancy of the speed of light
Conservation of energy and conservation of momentum
The principle of inertia and the law of gravitation
The uncertainty principle and wave-particle duality
125610.e: First, the laws of nature are the same in all inertial frames. Second, the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of how the source moves.
125610.m: Special relativity is based on the principle of relativity and the constant speed of light.

125611.q: What is the region of spacetime called that a signal from an event can reach at most at the speed of light?
125611.e: In a spacetime diagram, the paths of light rays form a cone around the event. Only events inside this cone can be causally connected.
125611.m: The light cone limits what an event can influence.

a: A frame of reference without acceleration
A braking car as a frame of reference
125612.e: In an inertial frame, a body on which no forces act moves in a straight line at constant speed. The frame is at rest or moves at constant velocity.
125612.m: An inertial frame is a non-accelerating frame of reference.

125613.q: A spaceship flies at 0.5 c and launches a probe forwards at 0.5 c relative to the ship. How fast is the probe relative to the starting point?
125613.e: According to relativistic velocity addition, u = (v + w) / (1 + vw/c²). So (0.5 + 0.5) / (1 + 0.25) = 1 / 1.25 = 0.8 c.
125613.m: Velocities added relativistically never exceed the speed of light.

125614.q: Which mathematician combined space and time into a four-dimensional spacetime?
125614.e: Hermann Minkowski, a former teacher of Einstein’s at ETH Zurich, formulated the theory geometrically. Space and time form a single spacetime.
125614.m: Hermann Minkowski shaped the concept of spacetime.

125615.q: How large is the relativistic kinetic energy of a body with mass m at 0.6 c (γ = 1.25)?
125615.e: Relativistically, E_kin = (γ minus 1)mc² = (1.25 minus 1)mc² = 0.25 mc². The classical formula ½mv² would give only 0.18 mc² and is too inaccurate at this speed.
125615.m: Relativistically, kinetic energy is the total energy minus the rest energy.

125616.q: According to special relativity, which relation between energy E and momentum p applies to a photon?
125616.e: In general, E² = (pc)² + (mc²)². Because a photon has no rest mass, E = pc remains.
125616.m: For massless particles, energy equals momentum times the speed of light.

125617.q: What do you observe in the light from a source moving away from us at high speed?
a: It is shifted to longer wavelengths
It is shifted to shorter wavelengths
125617.e: In the relativistic Doppler effect, the light from a receding source is redshifted. Unlike with sound, time dilation also plays a part.
125617.m: Light from a receding source is redshifted.

125618.q: Which thought experiment, according to Einstein himself, already occupied him as a teenager?
a: Riding along behind a beam of light
Shutting a cat in a box
125618.e: Einstein wondered what a light wave would look like if you ran alongside it. This idea later led him to realise that light travels at the same speed for every observer.
125618.m: Einstein imagined following a beam of light at an early age.

125619.q: What was the Michelson-Morley experiment originally meant to detect?
a: The Earth’s motion through the ether
125619.e: People believed that light travelled in a medium at rest, the ether. The Earth’s motion was supposed to produce a measurable “ether wind”.
125619.m: The experiment looked for the ether wind.

125620.q: Which measuring instrument did Michelson and Morley use?
125620.e: The Michelson interferometer splits a beam of light into two perpendicular beams and brings them back together. Even the tiniest differences in travel time become visible.
125620.m: Michelson and Morley measured with an interferometer.

125621.q: Which motion of the Earth was supposed to cause a measurable effect in the experiment?
a: Its orbit around the Sun at about 30 km/s
The Moon’s motion around the Earth
The plate tectonics of the continents
125621.e: The Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second. Relative to an ether at rest, this should have given a clear difference in travel time.
125621.m: The Earth moves around the Sun at about 30 km/s.

125622.q: Which observation in the interferometer would have pointed to an ether wind?
a: A shift of the interference fringes when the apparatus was turned
A change in the colour of the light
125622.e: When the apparatus was turned, the travel times in the two arms should have changed. That would have shifted the light and dark fringes.
125622.m: An ether wind would have shifted the interference fringes.

125623.q: What was the apparatus mounted on so that it could be turned with little vibration?
a: On a stone slab floating in mercury
On a wooden table with wheels
125623.e: The heavy stone slab floated in a basin of mercury. This allowed it to be turned smoothly without vibrations disturbing the measurement.

125624.q: What result did the Michelson-Morley experiment produce?
a: The ether wind was exactly as large as expected
The ether wind was twice as large as expected
The light was stopped in the interferometer
125624.e: The interference fringes hardly moved when the apparatus was turned. This null result was a big surprise, as a clear effect had been expected.
125624.m: The Michelson-Morley experiment found no ether wind.

125625.q: Which statement about light follows from the result of the Michelson-Morley experiment?
a: The speed of light is the same in all directions
Light is faster in the direction of the Earth’s motion
Light is slowed down by the ether
Light only travels in a vacuum
125625.e: However the apparatus was turned, the light took the same time in both arms. In 1905, Einstein made the constancy of the speed of light a cornerstone of special relativity.
125625.m: The speed of light does not depend on the Earth’s motion.

125626.q: How did Michelson and Morley lengthen the light path in their interferometer to increase its sensitivity?
a: By reflecting it several times off mirrors
With a tunnel in a mountain
125626.e: The light was sent back and forth between mirrors several times. A longer light path makes small differences in travel time easier to measure.
125626.m: Multiple reflections lengthened the light path in the experiment.

125627.q: What does time dilation in special relativity state?
a: All clocks run at the same rate
125627.e: For an observer, less time passes on a clock moving relative to them. The effect only becomes clear at very high speeds.
125627.m: For an observer at rest, moving clocks run slow.

125628.q: With what did researchers demonstrate time dilation on passenger aircraft in 1971?
125628.e: Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew atomic clocks around the Earth and compared them with clocks on the ground. The tiny differences agreed with the theory of relativity.
125628.m: Atomic clocks on aircraft confirmed time dilation.

125629.q: What is the time shown by a clock moving along with an object, in its own rest frame, called?
125629.e: Proper time is the time measured by a clock moving with the object. It is the same in every frame of reference and is therefore especially important.
125629.m: Proper time is the time in a clock’s rest frame.

125630.q: Roughly how large is the Lorentz factor γ at a speed of 0.99 c?
125630.e: γ = 1 / √(1 minus 0.99²) = 1 / √0.0199 ≈ 1 / 0.141 ≈ 7.1. Clocks then run about seven times slower.
125630.m: Close to the speed of light, the Lorentz factor becomes very large.

125631.q: Which thought experiment is often used to derive time dilation?
125631.e: In the light clock, a pulse of light travels back and forth between two mirrors. For an outside observer, the light in the moving clock travels a longer path, so the clock ticks more slowly.
125631.m: The light clock illustrates time dilation.

125632.q: Two spaceships pass each other at constant velocity. What do the crews notice about each other’s clock?
a: Both see the other clock running slow
Only one crew sees an effect
Both see the other clock running fast
Both clocks run at the same rate
125632.e: Between two inertial frames, time dilation is symmetrical. Each side may regard itself as at rest and measures the other’s clock as running slow.
125632.m: Between inertial frames, time dilation is mutual.

125633.q: Which relation describes time dilation if Δt₀ is the proper time?
125633.e: Because γ is always at least 1, the time Δt measured in the frame at rest is greater than the proper time. So the moving clock shows less time.
125633.m: The observed time is longer than the proper time by the factor γ.

125634.q: From what speed does time dilation occur?
a: At any speed, but it is tiny in everyday life
Only from half the speed of light
Only at exactly the speed of light
Only from the speed of sound
125634.e: The Lorentz factor is greater than 1 at any speed, but only very slightly at everyday speeds. With modern atomic clocks, the effect can even be detected at cycling speed.
125634.m: Time dilation exists at any speed; in everyday life it is just tiny.

a: Moving bodies are shortened in the direction of motion
125635.e: An observer measures a body moving relative to them as shorter in the direction of motion than at rest. Nothing changes at right angles to the motion.
125635.m: Moving bodies appear shortened in the direction of motion.

125636.q: In which direction does length contraction occur?
a: Only in the direction of motion
Only at right angles to the motion
125636.e: The Lorentz transformation only changes the coordinate in the direction of motion. The dimensions at right angles to it stay the same.
125636.m: Length contraction only acts in the direction of motion.

125637.q: A spaceship is 100 m long at rest. What length does an observer measure as it flies past at 0.6 c?
125637.m: The moving length is shorter than the proper length by the Lorentz factor.

125638.q: At what speed does a rod appear shortened to half its proper length?
125638.e: Half the length means √(1 minus v²/c²) = 0.5, so v²/c² = 0.75. It follows that v = √0.75 c ≈ 0.87 c.
125638.m: To shorten something to half, you need about 87 per cent of the speed of light.

125639.q: What is the length of a body in its own rest frame called?
125639.e: Proper length is measured when the body is at rest relative to the measuring rod. In every other inertial frame, the measured length is shorter.
125639.m: The proper length is the greatest measurable length of a body.

125640.q: Which two physicists proposed a shortening of moving bodies to explain the Michelson-Morley result?
125640.e: George FitzGerald and Hendrik Antoon Lorentz each assumed such a contraction independently. Einstein later derived it from his postulates.
125640.m: FitzGerald and Lorentz were the first to propose length contraction.

125641.q: From the point of view of a fast muon, how do you explain that it reaches the ground?
a: The atmosphere is shortened for the muon
The Earth approaches the muon more slowly
The muon takes a short cut
125641.e: In the muon’s rest frame, its clock runs normally. Instead, length contraction makes the layer of atmosphere so thin that it crosses it in time.
125641.m: From the muon’s point of view, the atmosphere is shortened.

125642.q: Why do we not notice length contraction in everyday life?
a: Everyday speeds are much smaller than c
125642.e: At everyday speeds, v²/c² is tiny, so the Lorentz factor is almost exactly 1. The shortening is then immeasurably small.
125642.m: At low speeds, length contraction is unnoticeable.

125643.q: What is the Lorentz transformation used for?
a: It converts positions and times between frames moving at constant velocity
It calculates the orbits of planets
It breaks vibrations down into individual frequencies
It describes the refraction of light in lenses
125643.e: With the Lorentz transformation, you can convert coordinates from one inertial frame into another. It is named after the Dutchman Hendrik Antoon Lorentz.
125643.m: The Lorentz transformation links moving frames of reference.

125644.q: Which transformation of classical mechanics is replaced by the Lorentz transformation?
125644.e: In the Galilean transformation, time is the same for all observers. The Lorentz transformation, by contrast, takes into account the constant speed of light.
125644.m: The Lorentz transformation replaces the Galilean transformation.

125645.q: What does the Lorentz transformation give when the speed is much smaller than the speed of light?
125645.e: For v ≪ c, the Lorentz factor becomes almost 1 and the term vx/c² vanishes. Then the formulas of classical mechanics practically apply.
125645.m: At low speeds, relativity turns into classical mechanics.

125646.q: What is the Lorentz factor γ?
125646.e: The Lorentz factor is always at least 1 and grows towards infinity as v approaches c. It determines the amount of time dilation and length contraction.
125646.m: The Lorentz factor grows with speed.

125647.q: Which quantity remains unchanged under a Lorentz transformation?
a: The spacetime interval between two events
The spatial distance between two events
The time interval between two events
The kinetic energy of a body
125647.e: Distances in space and time each depend on the frame of reference. The combination c²Δt² minus Δx², by contrast, is the same in all inertial frames.
125647.m: The spacetime interval is the same in all inertial frames.

125648.q: According to special relativity, which quantity is the same for all observers moving at constant velocity?
a: The speed of light in a vacuum
125648.e: Einstein assumed that light in a vacuum travels at the same speed for every observer. Time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity follow from this.
125648.m: The speed of light is the same for all observers.

125649.q: Frame S' moves at 0.6 c (γ = 1.25) relative to S. An event has the coordinates t = 0 and x = 4 light years in S. What time value t' does it have in S'?
125649.e: t' = γ(t minus vx/c²) = 1.25 · (0 minus 0.6 · 4) years = 1.25 · (−2.4) years = −3 years. So simultaneity depends on the frame of reference.
125649.m: Events that are simultaneous in one frame are often not simultaneous in another.

125650.q: Frame S' moves at 0.6 c (γ = 1.25) relative to S. What position coordinate x' does an event with t = 0 and x = 4 light years have?
125650.e: x' = γ(x minus vt) = 1.25 · (4 minus 0) light years = 5 light years. Because t = 0, the term with v drops out.
125650.m: The Lorentz transformation links the coordinates of two inertial frames.

125651.q: What does the twin paradox describe?
a: A twin who travels fast is younger on returning
The twin on Earth is younger
125651.e: One twin flies away at almost the speed of light and comes back. On returning, less time has passed for them than for the twin on Earth.
125651.m: The travelling twin is younger on returning.

125652.q: Why is the twin paradox not a real contradiction?
a: Only the traveller changes inertial frame
Because both stay the same age
Because light is slower on the journey
125652.e: The travelling twin has to turn round and accelerate to do so. So the situation is not symmetrical, and only the twin on Earth stays in a single inertial frame.
125652.m: The twin paradox is resolved by the asymmetry of the journey.

125653.q: A twin flies at 0.8 c to a star 4 light years away and back. For the twin on Earth this takes 10 years. How much time passes for the traveller?
125653.e: The Lorentz factor is γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.64) = 1 / 0.6. For the traveller, 10 years · 0.6 = 6 years pass.
125653.m: The travelling twin experiences less time than the twin at home.

125654.q: A twin travels there and back at 0.6 c while 10 years pass on Earth. How many years does the traveller age?
125654.e: At 0.6 c, √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8. So the traveller ages 10 years · 0.8 = 8 years.
125654.m: The faster the journey, the less the traveller ages.

125655.q: Why does the twin paradox hardly matter for today’s astronauts?
a: They fly far slower than light
There is no time in space
Gravity always cancels the effect completely
125655.e: Time dilation only becomes large close to the speed of light. After half a year on the ISS, an astronaut has aged only milliseconds less.
125655.m: In today’s space flights, time dilation is tiny.

125656.q: In special relativity, which world line between two events has the longest proper time?
a: The one with the most bends
The one with the highest speed
The one with the greatest acceleration
125656.e: In a spacetime diagram, the bent world line of the traveller has less proper time than the straight one of the twin who stayed at home. That is why the twin on Earth is older.
125656.m: The unaccelerated world line has the longest proper time.

125657.q: What does the travelling twin notice about their own clock during the flight?
125657.e: In their own frame of reference, time passes quite normally for the traveller. Only the comparison after the return shows the difference.
125657.m: Your own clock runs normally for every observer.

125658.q: Does the effect in the twin paradox only affect clocks, or also the ageing of the body?
125658.e: Time dilation affects time itself and therefore all physical and biological processes. Heartbeat and cell division slow down to the same extent.
125658.m: Time dilation applies to all processes, including ageing.

125659.q: What is Einstein’s famous formula for the equivalence of mass and energy?
125659.e: The formula states that mass and energy can be converted into each other. The factor c² is very large, so a small mass contains a great deal of energy.
125659.m: Mass and energy are linked by the square of the speed of light.

125660.q: What is the difference between the mass of an atomic nucleus and the sum of the masses of its individual nucleons called?
125660.e: An atomic nucleus is lighter than its separate building blocks. According to E = mc², the missing mass corresponds to the binding energy of the nucleus.
125660.m: The mass defect corresponds to the binding energy of the nucleus.

125661.q: What is produced when an electron and a positron meet and annihilate each other?
125661.e: In pair annihilation, the entire mass of the two particles is converted into energy. Usually two gamma photons are produced.
125661.m: In pair annihilation, mass turns completely into radiation.

125662.q: According to E = mc², what happens to the mass of a body when it is heated?
125662.e: Heat added is energy and therefore also increases the mass by ΔE/c². In everyday life, however, the effect is immeasurably small.
125662.m: Any energy added also increases the mass a little.

125663.q: What was the title of Einstein’s paper in which he derived the equivalence of mass and energy?
a: “Does the Inertia of a Body Depend upon Its Energy Content?”
“The Foundation of the General Theory of Relativity”
125663.e: The short paper appeared as a supplement to special relativity. It shows that a body loses mass when it radiates energy.
125663.m: Einstein asked whether inertia depends on energy content.

125664.q: What role does E = mc² play in nuclear fission in a nuclear power station?
a: The fission products are lighter, and the mass difference becomes energy
The fission products are heavier than the uranium nucleus
125664.e: When uranium splits, the fragments together are slightly lighter than the original nucleus plus neutron. This small mass difference is released as energy.
125664.m: In nuclear fission, a small part of the mass is converted into energy.

125665.q: According to E = mc², what mass corresponds to an energy of 1 kWh (3.6 · 10⁶ J, c ≈ 3 · 10⁸ m/s)?
125665.e: m = E/c² = 3.6 · 10⁶ J / (9 · 10¹⁶ m²/s²) = 4 · 10⁻¹¹ kg. So one kilowatt hour corresponds to a tiny mass.
125665.m: Everyday amounts of energy correspond to only tiny masses.

125666.q: Roughly what share of the mass is converted into energy when hydrogen fuses into helium?
125666.e: A helium nucleus is slightly lighter than the four hydrogen nuclei it is formed from. About 0.7 per cent of the mass is released as energy.
125666.m: In hydrogen fusion, about 0.7 per cent of the mass becomes energy.

125667.q: What does the equivalence principle state?
a: Gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart locally
All bodies have the same mass
125667.e: In a closed lift, you cannot tell whether you are at rest in a gravitational field or being accelerated steadily. Einstein built his theory of gravity on this.
125667.m: According to the equivalence principle, gravity acts locally like acceleration.

125668.q: What happens to light travelling outwards from a strong gravitational field?
125668.e: Light loses energy as it climbs out of a gravitational field, and its frequency falls. This is called gravitational redshift.
125668.m: Light is redshifted as it leaves a gravitational field.

125669.q: What is the effect called in which a large mass bends the light of galaxies behind it and shows them distorted?
125669.e: Galaxy clusters act like huge lenses and produce arcs or multiple images. Astronomers use this to study very distant objects.
125669.m: Large masses can act like a lens for light.

125670.q: How does a clock at sea level behave compared with a clock on a high mountain?
125670.e: Deeper in a gravitational field, time passes more slowly; this is called gravitational time dilation. Modern atomic clocks can measure the effect with height differences of less than one metre.
125670.m: The stronger the gravity, the more slowly time passes.

125671.q: Which Swiss mathematician and fellow student helped Einstein with differential geometry for general relativity?
125671.e: Marcel Grossmann studied with Einstein at the Polytechnic in Zurich. Later he introduced him to tensor calculus, which Einstein needed for his theory of gravity.
125671.m: Marcel Grossmann helped Einstein with the mathematics of general relativity.

125672.q: What did researchers detect directly for the first time in 2015, which Einstein had predicted about a hundred years earlier?
125672.e: In 2015, the LIGO detectors measured tiny distortions of spacetime caused by two merging black holes. This confirmed an important prediction of general relativity.
125672.m: Gravitational waves were measured directly for the first time in 2015.

125673.q: What happens to radar signals that pass close to the Sun on their way to a planet and back?
a: They take a little longer than without the Sun
125673.e: The curved spacetime near the Sun measurably lengthens the travel time. This Shapiro effect is a further test of the theory.
125673.m: Near large masses, signals take longer; this is called the Shapiro effect.

125674.q: What do Einstein’s field equations of general relativity describe?
a: How mass and energy curve spacetime
How electric current flows in conductors
125674.e: One side of the equations describes the curvature of spacetime, the other the distribution of mass and energy. In short: matter tells spacetime how to curve.

125675.q: Which quantity did Einstein add to his field equations in 1917 to allow a static universe?
125675.e: Einstein added the cosmological constant Λ to his equations. After the expansion of the universe was discovered he dropped it; today it is used to describe dark energy.
125675.m: The cosmological constant was introduced by Einstein and later rediscovered.

125676.q: When were gravitational waves detected directly for the first time?
125676.e: On 14 September 2015, the LIGO detectors in the USA recorded a signal. The discovery was announced in February 2016.
125676.m: Gravitational waves were measured directly for the first time in 2015.

125677.q: Which event produced the first directly measured gravitational waves?
a: The merger of two black holes
125677.e: Two black holes of about 30 solar masses each orbited each other and merged. Part of their mass was radiated away as gravitational waves.
125677.m: The first signal came from two merging black holes.

125678.q: At what speed do gravitational waves travel?
a: At half the speed of light
125678.e: According to general relativity, disturbances of spacetime travel at the speed of light. Observations have confirmed this very precisely.
125678.m: Gravitational waves are as fast as light.

125679.q: How do detectors such as LIGO measure gravitational waves?
a: With laser interferometers that detect tiny changes in length
With huge telescope mirrors for visible light
125679.e: A gravitational wave alternately squeezes and stretches the arms, which are kilometres long. The change in length is much smaller than the diameter of a proton and is measured using light interference.
125679.m: Gravitational wave detectors measure tiny changes in length with laser light.

125680.q: Who predicted the existence of gravitational waves in theory?
125680.e: Shortly after completing his theory of gravity, Einstein worked out that disturbances of spacetime spread as waves. He himself thought they could hardly be measured.

125681.q: Which observation provided indirect evidence of gravitational waves even before 2015?
a: The shrinking orbit of a binary pulsar
125681.e: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a binary pulsar whose orbital period decreases exactly as the emission of gravitational waves requires. They received the Nobel Prize for this in 1993.
125681.m: A binary pulsar provided the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves.

125682.q: What is the name of ESA’s planned gravitational wave observatory in space?
125682.e: LISA is to consist of three satellites millions of kilometres apart. LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA, by contrast, are detectors on Earth.
125682.m: LISA is meant to measure gravitational waves in space.

125683.q: What is the typical signal of two merging objects called, whose frequency and strength rise rapidly just before the merger?
125683.e: The closer the two bodies get, the faster they orbit each other. Turned into sound, the signal is like a rising twitter, a “chirp”.
125683.m: Merging objects produce a rising chirp signal.

125684.q: How does a gravitational wave deform the space it passes through?
a: It stretches and squeezes it at right angles to the direction of travel
It only stretches it in the direction of travel
It does not change it at all
125684.e: Gravitational waves are transverse waves. At right angles to the direction of travel, space is alternately stretched in one direction and squeezed in the other.
125684.m: Gravitational waves stretch and squeeze space at right angles to their direction of travel.

125685.q: Which astrophysicist found a solution of the field equations in 1916 that sets the radius of a non-rotating black hole?
125685.e: Karl Schwarzschild found the solution shortly after Einstein’s publication. The radius named after him is r = 2GM/c².
125685.m: The Schwarzschild radius describes the size of a black hole.

125686.q: Which project published the first image of a black hole in 2019?
125686.e: The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes all over the Earth into one giant virtual telescope. The image shows the shadow of the black hole in the galaxy M87.
125686.m: The Event Horizon Telescope produced the first image of a black hole.

125687.q: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way?
125687.e: Sagittarius A* lies in the constellation Sagittarius and has about four million solar masses. The orbits of nearby stars revealed its mass.
125687.m: At the centre of the Milky Way is the black hole Sagittarius A*.

125688.q: According to a prediction from quantum theory, which radiation should black holes emit?
125688.e: Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should radiate weakly because of quantum effects at the horizon. As a result, they could evaporate over an extremely long time.
125688.m: According to Hawking, black holes should radiate weakly.

125689.q: How do stellar black holes form?
a: Through the collapse of a very massive star
Through the explosion of a planet
Through the cooling of a white dwarf
125689.e: When a very massive star has used up its fuel, its core collapses under its own gravity. This is often preceded by a supernova.
125689.m: Stellar black holes form from collapsing massive stars.

125690.q: What is the stretching of a body by extreme tidal forces near a black hole called?
125690.e: The pull on the nearer part of a body is much stronger than on the farther part. As a result, the body is stretched lengthways and squeezed from the sides.
125690.m: Tidal forces can stretch bodies near a black hole.

125691.q: What is the rotating disc of gas and dust that spirals into a black hole called?
125691.e: The inflowing matter forms a flat, rotating disc and heats up strongly through friction. That is why the surroundings of a black hole often shine brightly.
125691.m: Matter flows into a black hole through an accretion disc.

125692.q: According to the so-called no-hair theorem, which three quantities completely describe a black hole?
a: Mass, angular momentum and electric charge
125692.e: All other properties of the matter that has fallen in are lost to the outside. Only mass, angular momentum and charge remain.
125692.m: A black hole is determined solely by mass, angular momentum and charge.

125693.q: What is the boundary around a black hole called, beyond which not even light can escape?
125693.e: Inside the event horizon, you would have to be faster than light to escape. That is why no information gets out from there.
125693.m: Nothing escapes from inside the event horizon of a black hole.

125694.q: According to special relativity, how does the high orbital speed affect the clocks of GPS satellites?
a: They run about 7 microseconds slower per day
They run about 7 seconds slower per day
They run about 7 microseconds faster per day
125694.e: The satellites move at almost 4 kilometres per second. Because of time dilation, their clocks lose about 7 microseconds per day.
125694.m: The orbital speed makes GPS clocks run slower.

125695.q: According to general relativity, how does the weaker gravity at orbital height affect GPS clocks?
a: They run about 45 microseconds faster per day
They run about 45 microseconds slower per day
They run about 45 seconds faster per day
125695.e: Farther from the Earth, the gravitational field is weaker and time passes faster. The effect amounts to about 45 microseconds per day.
125695.m: At height, clocks run faster because of the weaker gravity.

125696.q: Which relativistic effect dominates for the clocks of GPS satellites?
a: The gravitational effect; the clocks run fast overall
The speed effect; the clocks run slow overall
Both cancel each other out exactly
125696.e: The orbital speed slows the satellite clocks down, while the weaker gravity speeds them up. At a height of about 20,000 km the gravitational effect is much larger, so the clocks run fast overall.
125696.m: With GPS, the gravitational effect dominates and the satellite clocks run fast.

125697.q: Without relativistic correction, roughly how large would the position error grow after one day?
125697.e: The satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds fast per day overall; multiplied by the speed of light, that gives 38 · 10⁻⁶ s · 3 · 10⁸ m/s ≈ 11,400 m. Without correction, GPS would be useless after a short time.
125697.m: Without relativity, GPS would be kilometres out after one day.

125698.q: How are the relativistic effects corrected for GPS satellites?
a: The clock frequency is set slightly lower before launch
The satellites are brought back to Earth every day
125698.e: The base frequency of the satellite clocks is reduced so that, in orbit, they run correctly as seen from the Earth. Receivers calculate further small corrections themselves.
125698.m: GPS clocks are adjusted for relativistic effects before launch.

125699.q: A GPS signal travels for about 0.07 seconds. Why does the Earth’s rotation have to be taken into account?
a: The receiver moves on with the Earth during this time
The Earth’s rotation slows the radio signal down
The Earth’s rotation changes the frequency of the atomic clocks
Otherwise the satellites would stand still
125699.e: While the signal is on its way, the receiver turns a little further with the Earth. At the equator this is over 30 metres, which would distort the position.
125699.m: With GPS, the Earth’s rotation during the signal’s travel time must also be corrected.

125700.q: Which European satellite navigation system also has to be corrected for relativity?
125700.e: Galileo is operated by the European Union and also uses atomic clocks in orbit. The same relativistic effects act on all such systems.
125700.m: The European Galileo system also needs relativistic corrections.

125701.q: Which relativistic correction does the GPS receiver calculate itself, because it changes during the orbit?
a: The correction for the slightly elliptical orbit
The correction for the lunar cycle
125701.e: On a slightly elliptical orbit, the satellite’s height and speed change periodically. As a result, the rate of its clock also varies, and the receiver corrects this by calculation.
125701.m: The shape of the satellites’ orbits requires an extra correction in the receiver.

125702.q: During which period did Albert Einstein live in today’s Einstein House in Bern?
125702.e: Einstein lived in the flat during his productive years in Bern. Several of his groundbreaking papers were written during this time.
125702.m: Einstein lived on the Kramgasse from 1903 to 1905.

125703.q: Which museum in Bern has its own permanent exhibition on Einstein’s life, in addition to the Einstein House?
125703.e: The Einstein Museum is part of the Bern Historical Museum. It presents Einstein’s life and work in detail.
125703.m: The Einstein Museum is in the Bern Historical Museum.

125704.q: Which famous theory did Einstein publish in 1905, while he was living in Bern?
125704.e: 1905 is considered Einstein’s miracle year. In Bern he wrote, among other things, the paper on special relativity while working at the patent office.
125704.m: Einstein developed special relativity in Bern.

125705.q: Which famous Bern landmark stands at the top end of the Kramgasse, just a few steps from the Einstein House?
125705.e: The Kramgasse leads from the Zytglogge towards the Nydegg Bridge. The medieval clock tower is one of the city’s best-known buildings.
125705.m: The Zytglogge is very close to the Einstein House.

125706.q: To which UNESCO World Heritage Site does the building housing the Einstein House belong?
125706.e: The Einstein House is right in the middle of Bern’s Old City with its arcades and fountains. The Old City as a whole is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
125706.m: The Einstein House is in the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Old City of Bern.

125707.q: On what occasion was Einstein’s former flat in Bern opened as a museum?
125707.e: The flat was opened as a museum on 14 March 1979, Einstein’s hundredth birthday. Since then, people from all over the world have visited the small museum.
125707.m: The Einstein House was opened for Einstein’s 100th birthday.

125708.q: Which fountain with a figure stands in the Kramgasse, the street where the Einstein House is?
125708.e: The Zähringer Fountain shows a bear in armour and recalls the founders of the city, the Dukes of Zähringen. The other fountains stand in other streets and squares of the Old City.
125708.m: The Zähringer Fountain stands in the Kramgasse.

125709.q: Which fundamental change is at the centre of the Neolithic Revolution?
a: The move to farming crops and keeping animals
The move to a culture of writing
The move to sailing the open seas
125709.e: People gradually gave up living as hunter-gatherers and produced their own food. This went together with settling down, storing supplies and new kinds of settlement.
125709.m: In the Neolithic Revolution, people became farmers and herders.

125710.q: Roughly when did the Neolithic Revolution begin in the Near East?
125710.e: At the end of the last Ice Age, about 12,000 years ago, people in the Near East began to use and grow wild cereals on purpose. In central Europe, farming only began thousands of years later.
125710.m: Farming began in the Near East about 12,000 years ago.

125711.q: Why is the site of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey so important for research?
a: Monumental buildings probably made by hunter-gatherers
The first royal tomb with written finds
The oldest known harbour on the Mediterranean
125711.e: The stone circles with T-shaped pillars were built about 11,000 years ago, apparently before fully developed farming. This challenges the idea that large buildings were only possible after people settled down.
125711.m: Göbekli Tepe shows that even hunter-gatherers built monuments.

125712.q: Which health consequence did the farming way of life of the Neolithic often bring?
a: More diseases passed on from animals
Less tooth decay because of the grain
125712.e: Living closely with domestic animals and in crowded settlements favoured zoonoses. Skeletons of early farmers also often show more tooth decay and a smaller body height than those of hunter-gatherers.
125712.m: Early farmers suffered more often from diseases that came from animals.

125713.q: Why did farming encourage social differences in society?
a: Hunting prey was shared out more evenly
Settlements became smaller and more mobile
125713.e: Harvest surpluses that could be stored could be piled up and shared out. This led to differences in wealth, specialised jobs and later elites.
125713.m: Harvest surpluses made differences in wealth and specialisation possible.

125714.q: Which settlement in central Anatolia is considered one of the largest settlements of the Neolithic?
125714.e: About 9,000 years ago, Çatalhöyük was home to several thousand people. The houses stood close together and were entered through the roofs.
125714.m: Çatalhöyük is one of the largest settlements of the Neolithic.

125715.q: Which tool is typical of the Neolithic and was used to clear forest?
125715.e: With polished stone axes in wooden handles, the first farmers cleared forest for fields and houses. Polished stone tools are a hallmark of the Neolithic.
125715.m: The first farmers cleared forest with polished stone axes.

125716.q: Why is the area from the Persian Gulf to the Levant called the “Fertile Crescent”?
a: The fertile land curves in an arc round the Syrian Desert
The moon looks especially big there
The fields were laid out in the shape of a crescent
The area belonged to the Ottoman Empire, whose symbol was the crescent
125716.e: On the map, the fertile river valleys and hill country form an arc round the desert. One of the first kinds of farming arose there about 11,000 years ago.
125716.m: The Fertile Crescent is an arc of fertile land round the Syrian Desert.

125717.q: Which two rivers shape the eastern part of the Fertile Crescent?
125717.e: The Euphrates and Tigris flow through Mesopotamia, the “land between the rivers”. Their water later made large irrigation cultures possible.
125717.m: The Euphrates and Tigris form the heart of Mesopotamia.

125718.q: Which present-day country does NOT lie in the area of the Fertile Crescent?
125718.e: The Fertile Crescent stretches from the Levant through south-eastern Anatolia to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf. The Arabian Peninsula with its deserts is not part of it.
125718.m: The Fertile Crescent curves round the Syrian Desert to the north.

125719.q: Which cereal is one of the first crops of the Fertile Crescent?
125719.e: Barley, einkorn and emmer were the first to be domesticated in the Near East. Maize comes from America, while rice and millet were mainly grown in Asia and Africa.
125719.m: Barley is one of the oldest cereals of the Near East.

125720.q: Which pulse is one of the founder crops of the Fertile Crescent?
125720.e: Lentils, peas and chickpeas were domesticated in the Near East. The soya bean comes from East Asia, and the peanut and common bean from America.
125720.m: The lentil is one of the oldest crops of the Near East.

125721.q: Which farm animals were first domesticated in the area of the Fertile Crescent?
125721.e: Sheep and goats became domestic animals in Anatolia and the Zagros Mountains about 10,000 years ago or earlier. Llamas and alpacas come from the Andes, the horse from the steppes of Eurasia.
125721.m: Sheep and goats are among the first farm animals of the Near East.

125722.q: Which feature of the wild plants in the Fertile Crescent made early farming easier?
125722.e: The climate with wet winters and dry summers favoured annual plants with large seeds that could be stored. The geographer Jared Diamond saw this as one reason for early farming in this region.
125722.m: Large-seeded annual wild grasses made it easier to start farming.

125723.q: Which mountain range forms the eastern edge of the Fertile Crescent?
125723.e: The Zagros Mountains in present-day Iran and Iraq form the eastern edge. Very early evidence of goat keeping has been found in their foothills.
125723.m: The Zagros Mountains form the eastern edge of the Fertile Crescent.

125724.q: Which animal is considered the oldest domestic animal of humans?
125724.e: The dog descends from the wolf and was domesticated even before farming was invented. Estimates go back more than 15,000 years.
125724.m: The dog is humans’ oldest domestic animal.

125725.q: Which feature is typical of domesticated cereals compared with the wild form?
a: Ripe ears no longer fall apart
The seeds are scattered far and wide
125725.e: In wild cereals, the stalk of the ear breaks when ripe so that the seeds fall out. Without meaning to, farmers mainly harvested plants with a firm stalk and sowed them again.
125725.m: Domesticated cereals keep their grains in the ripe ear.

125726.q: What is the whole set of features called that distinguishes crops from their wild forms?
125726.e: The domestication syndrome includes, for example, larger seeds, ripening at the same time and the loss of natural seed dispersal. Similar changes appeared independently in many crops.
125726.m: The domestication syndrome sums up typical features of crops.

125727.q: Which wild cat is considered the ancestor of the domestic cat?
125727.e: Genetic studies show that the domestic cat descends from the African wildcat (Felis lybica) of North Africa and the Near East. Cats probably joined the first farmers because mice were attracted to the grain stores.
125727.m: The domestic cat descends from the African wildcat.

125728.q: Which naturalist published a work in 1868 on the variation of animals and plants under domestication?
125728.e: In “The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication”, Darwin described the changes in domestic animals and crops. He used artificial selection as a model for natural selection.
125728.m: Darwin used breeding as a model for natural selection.

125729.q: According to current knowledge, where was rice of the subspecies japonica domesticated?
a: In the Yangtze valley in China
In the Nile valley in Egypt
125729.e: Archaeological and genetic findings point to the Yangtze area in China. There, wild rice turned into cultivated rice over thousands of years.
125729.m: Rice was domesticated on the Yangtze in China.

125730.q: Why could many crops hardly survive without humans?
a: They no longer spread their seeds themselves
125730.e: A maize cob, for example, does not drop its grains; if it germinates as a whole, the seedlings compete crowded together. In crops, humans take over seed dispersal.
125730.m: Many crops depend on humans to sow them.

125731.q: What is the deliberate selection by humans of animals and plants for further breeding called?
125731.e: In artificial selection, humans decide which individuals reproduce. Over generations, desired features become stronger.
125731.m: In artificial selection, humans choose the animals and plants for breeding.

125732.q: How many sets of chromosomes does einkorn have?
125732.e: Einkorn is diploid with 14 chromosomes. It is therefore considered the genetically simplest of the cultivated wheat species.
125732.m: Einkorn is the diploid wheat species.

125733.q: In which region was einkorn domesticated, like the other early cereals?
a: In the Fertile Crescent in the Near East
In the Yangtze valley in China
In the Po Valley in northern Italy
125733.e: Genetic comparisons point to the Karacadağ mountains in south-eastern Turkey. They lie in the northern Fertile Crescent, where farming began over 10,000 years ago.
125733.m: Einkorn comes from the Fertile Crescent.

125734.q: In which famous find was einkorn shown to be part of the last meal?
125734.e: In the stomach of the glacier mummy, which is about 5,300 years old, researchers found remains of einkorn and game meat, among other things. Ötzi lived in the late Neolithic.
125734.m: Ötzi had eaten einkorn before he died.

125735.q: Why is einkorn one of the hulled cereals?
a: The grains stay enclosed when threshed
It only grows on marshy soils
It is only used as animal feed
125735.e: In hulled cereals, the grains are still held tightly in their husks after threshing. They have to be dehulled in an extra step.
125735.m: Hulled cereals have to be dehulled after threshing.

125736.q: What is the scientific name of cultivated einkorn?
125736.e: “Monococcum” roughly means “single-grained”. Triticum aestivum is bread wheat, Triticum durum is durum wheat and Hordeum vulgare is barley.
125736.m: The scientific name of einkorn is Triticum monococcum.

125737.q: What colour is einkorn flour because of its high carotenoid content?
125737.e: Einkorn contains a lot of lutein, a yellow pigment from the carotenoid group. That is why flour and pasta made from einkorn are strikingly yellow.
125737.m: Einkorn flour is yellowish because of its carotenoids.

125738.q: Why is einkorn hardly grown on a large scale any more?
a: It gives a much smaller yield than bread wheat
Growing it is banned in Europe
125738.e: Einkorn has small grains, has to be dehulled and gives a much smaller yield than modern wheat. Today it is grown again in small amounts for speciality products.
125738.m: Einkorn gives a low yield and has therefore become rare.

125739.q: How many grains does a spikelet of emmer typically contain?
125739.e: Emmer usually forms two grains per spikelet and is therefore also called “Zweikorn” (two-grain) in German. It is one of the oldest kinds of wheat.
125739.m: Emmer usually has two grains per spikelet.

125740.q: Which kind of wheat developed from emmer and is used today mainly for pasta?
125740.e: Durum wheat (Triticum durum), like emmer, is tetraploid and developed from cultivated emmer. Its grains can be threshed free of their husks.
125740.m: Durum wheat for pasta descends from emmer.

125741.q: How did hexaploid bread wheat, from which most bread is baked today, come about?
a: By a cross between a tetraploid wheat and a wild grass
By a cross between rye and barley
By targeted genetic engineering in the 20th century
By doubling the chromosomes of maize
125741.e: About 8,000 years ago, tetraploid cultivated wheat crossed by chance with a goat grass. A third set of chromosomes was added, and hexaploid bread wheat was the result.
125741.m: Bread wheat came from a cross between wheat and a wild grass.

125742.q: In which region was emmer first grown?
a: In the foothills of the Alps
125742.e: Wild emmer grows in the Near East. There, about 10,000 years ago, it became one of the first crops.
125742.m: Emmer comes from the Fertile Crescent.

125743.q: In which ancient civilisation was emmer the most important wheat?
125743.e: In Ancient Egypt, bread and beer were made from emmer. Finds from tombs show how important it was.
125743.m: In Ancient Egypt, emmer was the most important wheat.

125744.q: How many sets of chromosomes does emmer have?
125744.e: Emmer combines the chromosome sets of two wild grass species and is therefore tetraploid. Its genome includes 28 chromosomes.
125744.m: Emmer is a tetraploid wheat species.

125745.q: Which kind of wheat is called “Zweikorn” (two-grain) in German because it has two grains per spikelet?
125745.e: Emmer usually forms two grains per spikelet. Einkorn has only one, while spelt and durum wheat are other forms of wheat.
125745.m: Emmer usually has two grains per spikelet.

125746.q: What is the formation of a species by combining the chromosome sets of two different species called, as in emmer?
125746.e: Wild emmer came from a cross between Triticum urartu and a goat grass, in which the chromosome sets of both parents were kept. In autopolyploidy, by contrast, the set of the same species is multiplied.
125746.m: Allopolyploidy combines the chromosome sets of different species.

125747.q: Which wild plant does maize descend from?
125747.e: Genetic studies show that maize developed from a subspecies of teosinte. Although they are closely related, the plants look very different.

125748.q: In which present-day country was maize domesticated from teosinte?
125748.e: Domestication took place in the south of present-day Mexico. From there, maize spread across the whole of America.
125748.m: Maize was domesticated in present-day Mexico.

125749.q: How did teosinte turn into today’s maize over time?
a: Through a single cross with wheat
Through genetic engineering in the 20th century
125749.e: Over many generations, farmers chose plants with larger grains that were easier to harvest. This artificial selection changed teosinte step by step into maize.
125749.m: Maize is the result of long selection by humans.

125750.q: Roughly how long ago was maize domesticated?
125750.e: Genetic dating and finds of starch grains point to a start about 9,000 years ago. Large cobs only developed over thousands of years.
125750.m: Maize was domesticated about 9,000 years ago.

125751.q: What finally confirmed that maize descends from teosinte?
125751.e: Genetic studies showed that maize is most closely related to a teosinte subspecies from Mexico. The Nobel Prize winner George Beadle had already argued for this origin.
125751.m: Genome comparisons confirmed that maize descends from teosinte.

125752.q: How do teosinte grains clearly differ from maize grains?
a: They are enclosed in a hard case
They are much bigger than maize grains
They sit on a thick cob
They are coloured blue and soft
125752.e: Teosinte grains are enclosed in a hard fruit case. A change in the gene tga1 exposed the grain in maize.
125752.m: Teosinte grains have a hard case, maize grains are exposed.

125753.q: How does the growth of teosinte differ from that of maize?
a: Teosinte is heavily branched, maize has one main stalk
Teosinte is a tree, maize a grass
Teosinte grows under water, maize on land
Teosinte climbs up trees, maize stands on its own
125753.e: Teosinte forms many side shoots. In maize, a change in the gene tb1 suppresses the side shoots, so that one strong main stalk forms.
125753.m: Maize grows unbranched, teosinte heavily branched.

125754.q: Roughly how many grains does an ear of teosinte carry?
125754.e: An ear of teosinte consists of a few grains lying one behind the other. A modern maize cob, on the other hand, carries several hundred grains.
125754.m: An ear of teosinte has only about a dozen grains or fewer.

125755.q: What is meant by the Columbian Exchange?
a: The exchange of plants, animals and diseases between America and the Old World
A trade agreement between Spain and Portugal
Swapping gold for spices in India
A prisoner exchange after the conquest of Mexico
125755.e: After 1492, potatoes and maize, for example, came to Europe, while horses, wheat and smallpox came to America. The historian Alfred W. Crosby coined the term in 1972.
125755.m: The Columbian Exchange linked the plants, animals and diseases of both worlds.

125756.q: Which plant came from America to Europe through the Columbian Exchange?
125756.e: The tomato comes from Central and South America and became known in Europe after 1492. Wheat, sugar cane and coffee travelled in the opposite direction.
125756.m: The tomato came from America to Europe.

125757.q: Which animal came from Europe to America and changed the lives of many peoples of the prairie?
125757.e: Horses had died out in America and came back with the Spanish. Many prairie peoples became bison hunters on horseback.
125757.m: The horse came back to America with the Europeans.

125758.q: What was the main cause of the massive population decline of the Indigenous peoples of America after 1492?
a: Crop failures caused by volcanic eruptions
Wars between the Incas and the Aztecs
125758.e: People in America had no resistance to smallpox, measles and flu. Epidemics killed a large part of the population, often even before direct contact with Europeans.
125758.m: Introduced epidemics devastated the Indigenous peoples of America.

125759.q: Which spice from America shapes Hungarian cooking today?
125759.e: Paprika belongs to the genus Capsicum from America and spread to Hungary via the Mediterranean region and the Ottoman Empire. Today it is seen as the national spice there.

125760.q: Which American root crop became a staple food in Africa?
125760.e: Cassava comes from South America and was brought to Africa by the Portuguese. Yams and taro, on the other hand, are plants of the Old World.
125760.m: Cassava came from South America to Africa.

125761.q: Which Old World plant was grown on plantations in the Caribbean and drove the transatlantic slave trade?
125761.e: Sugar cane comes from Asia and was grown on a huge scale in the Caribbean and Brazil. Millions of people were taken from Africa by force to work on the plantations.
125761.m: Growing sugar cane was closely linked with the slave trade.

125762.q: Where does the cocoa plant originally come from?
