125762.e: Cocoa was already used in Mesoamerica by the Olmecs, Maya and Aztecs. West Africa is the largest producer today, but it is not the plant’s home.
125762.m: Cocoa comes from America, even though it mainly grows in West Africa today.

125763.q: Which bird came from America to Europe through the Columbian Exchange?
125763.e: The turkey was domesticated in Mexico and came to Europe in the 16th century. Chickens, guinea fowl and pheasants come from the Old World.

125764.q: In which fields did Nikolai Vavilov do research?
125764.e: Vavilov was a Russian botanist and geneticist. He studied the origin and diversity of crops.
125764.m: Nikolai Vavilov was a botanist and geneticist.

125765.q: What did Nikolai Vavilov discover about the origin of crops?
a: They come from a few centres of origin with great diversity
They arose everywhere in the world at the same time
They all descend from a single wild plant
125765.e: Vavilov found that there are regions where a crop and its wild relatives are especially diverse. That is probably where it was first grown.
125765.m: Crops come from a few centres of origin.

125766.q: Which opponent in Soviet biology contributed greatly to Vavilov’s persecution?
125766.e: Lysenko rejected classical genetics and had Stalin’s support. Vavilov was arrested in 1940.
125766.m: Lysenko’s influence led to Vavilov’s persecution.

125767.q: What did Nikolai Vavilov die of?
125767.e: Vavilov was sentenced to death, but the sentence was changed to imprisonment. He died in prison in 1943 as a result of hunger.
125767.m: Vavilov died of hunger as a prisoner.

125768.q: What did Nikolai Vavilov build up in Leningrad?
a: One of the largest seed collections in the world
The world’s first nuclear research centre
A museum of minerals and ores
125768.e: Vavilov’s institute collected seeds from all over the world to preserve the diversity of crops for breeding. The collection still exists in St Petersburg today.
125768.m: Vavilov created a huge seed collection.

125769.q: What did staff at Vavilov’s institute do during the Siege of Leningrad?
a: They went hungry rather than eat the seeds
They burnt the collection for heating
They sowed everything in the city parks
125769.e: Several staff members died of hunger, although they were guarding tonnes of edible seeds and tubers. They wanted to keep the collection for the future.
125769.m: The guardians of the seed collection stood firm even when starving.

125770.q: Under which Soviet ruler was Nikolai Vavilov arrested and sentenced?
125770.e: Vavilov was arrested under Stalin in 1940 because he defended classical genetics. He was only rehabilitated after Stalin’s death.

125771.q: Why did Nikolai Vavilov go on many research trips to lots of countries?
a: To collect seeds and wild forms
125771.e: On expeditions in Asia, Africa, Europe and America he collected crops and their wild relatives. These finds formed the basis of his theory.
125771.m: Vavilov collected plants worldwide on expeditions.

125772.q: What is meant by the gene centre of a crop?
a: The region with the greatest genetic diversity
A lab where genes are changed
An area where no crops grow
A part of the cell nucleus with many genes
125772.e: According to Vavilov, a crop’s diversity is greatest where it has been grown the longest. Gene centres are therefore often seen as regions of origin.
125772.m: In the gene centre, a crop’s genetic diversity is greatest.

125773.q: Why are gene centres important for plant breeding?
a: Wild relatives provide genes, for example for resistance
Plants grow there without any water
There are no pests or diseases there
All forms of breeding are banned there
125773.e: Gene centres have old local varieties and wild relatives with features that modern varieties lack. Breeders cross them in, for example for resistance to diseases.
125773.m: Gene centres are treasure chests for breeding.

125774.q: Which crop has its gene centre in the highlands of Ethiopia?
125774.e: Coffea arabica comes from the mountain forests of Ethiopia, where wild coffee plants still grow today. Vavilov counted Ethiopia among the important gene centres.

125775.q: Which crop comes from the East Asian gene centre in China?
125775.e: The soya bean was domesticated in north-eastern China. The chickpea comes from the Near East, the sunflower and potato from America.
125775.m: The soya bean comes from China.

125776.q: Where is the global seed vault that keeps seed samples from all over the world safe?
125776.e: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault lies in a mountain near Longyearbyen in the permafrost. It keeps backup copies from seed banks all over the world.
125776.m: The global seed vault is on Svalbard.

125777.q: Which Swiss foundation works to preserve old crop varieties and livestock breeds?
125777.e: ProSpecieRara preserves rare varieties and breeds by passing on seeds and animals to nurseries and farms. Pro Juventute, Pro Senectute and Pro Helvetia have other tasks.
125777.m: ProSpecieRara preserves old varieties and breeds in Switzerland.

125778.q: What is the loss of genetic diversity in crops and livestock called?
125778.e: When a few high-yield varieties push out old local varieties, genes are lost for ever. This process is called genetic erosion.
125778.m: Genetic erosion means the loss of genetic diversity.

125779.q: Where is the gene centre of the cultivated apple and its wild ancestor?
a: In the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia
In the Alps of central Europe
125779.e: The wild apple Malus sieversii grows in the forests of the Tian Shan, for example in Kazakhstan. It is considered the most important ancestor of the cultivated apple.
125779.m: The cultivated apple comes from the Tian Shan in Central Asia.

125780.q: Since which year have the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps been a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
125780.e: In 2011, UNESCO added a selection of pile dwelling sites to the World Heritage List. Many of them are in Switzerland.
125780.m: The pile dwellings around the Alps have been World Heritage since 2011.

125781.q: In how many countries are the sites of the World Heritage “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps”?
125781.e: The sites are in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. Of the 111 sites, 56 are in Switzerland, about half.
125781.m: The pile dwelling World Heritage is spread across six countries.

125782.q: Where were remains of pile dwellings spotted at low water in the winter of 1853/54, starting the “pile dwelling fever”?
125782.e: The low water level uncovered piles and finds in Obermeilen. After that, pile dwellings were discovered at many Swiss lakes.
125782.m: The find at Obermeilen on Lake Zurich started the pile dwelling fever.

125783.q: Which Zurich antiquarian interpreted the finds from Obermeilen as pile dwellings?
125783.e: Ferdinand Keller imagined villages on platforms above the water. His interpretation shaped the picture of the pile dwellers for a long time.
125783.m: Ferdinand Keller founded the pile dwelling theory.

125784.q: Why have especially many plant remains survived in pile dwelling settlements?
a: No air in the wet lake bed
A dry climate like in the desert
125784.e: In waterlogged ground there is no oxygen, so wood, seeds and textiles hardly rot. That is why wetland settlements provide lots of evidence of early farming.
125784.m: The oxygen-poor lake bed preserves plant remains.

125785.q: Which method can often date wood from pile dwelling settlements to the exact year?
125785.e: Dendrochronology compares the tree-ring pattern of a piece of wood with a reference curve. This often makes it possible to find the year a tree was felled.
125785.m: Tree rings reveal the year the pile dwelling wood was felled.

125786.q: Which fibre plant did the pile dwellers grow for cords and textiles?
125786.e: Flax seeds, fibres and remains of fabric have been found in pile dwelling settlements. Flax provided both fibres and oily seeds.
125786.m: The pile dwellers used flax for textiles.

125787.q: How does modern research correct the romantic picture of pile dwellings?
a: Many houses stood on shores that were flooded at times
The houses floated on large rafts
The villages were only lived in during winter
The piles were carved from stone
125787.e: Many settlements lay on the shore, which flooded during high water. The houses were therefore raised on piles, but did not stand in the middle of the lake.
125787.m: Many pile dwellings stood on the lakeshore and not in open water.

125788.q: Which archaeology museum in Hauterive (NE) shows important finds from pile dwelling settlements?
125788.e: The Laténium on Lake Neuchâtel is one of the largest archaeology museums in Switzerland. It also shows finds from the lakeshore settlements.
125788.m: The Laténium in Hauterive shows pile dwelling finds.

125789.q: Which group of islands in Indonesia was known as the “Spice Islands”?
125789.e: Cloves and nutmegs grew on the Moluccas and were highly prized in Europe. The struggle for these islands shaped colonial history.
125789.m: The Moluccas are the famous Spice Islands.

125790.q: On which coast of India was the most important growing area for black pepper?
125790.e: Black pepper comes from the humid forests of the Malabar Coast in south-west India. Ports such as Calicut and Cochin were therefore the goal of European sailors.
125790.m: Pepper comes from the Malabar Coast in south-west India.

125791.q: Which city controlled a large part of the spice trade with the Levant in the late Middle Ages?
125791.e: Venetian merchants bought spices in Alexandria and Beirut and sold them on all over Europe. This trade made Venice rich.
125791.m: Venice became rich through the spice trade.

125792.q: Which trading company was founded in 1602 and soon controlled the spice trade with Indonesia?
125792.e: The Dutch VOC was given wide-ranging rights, for example to wage war. It gained a monopoly on nutmeg and cloves.
125792.m: The Dutch VOC controlled the trade in nutmeg and cloves.

125793.q: From which part of the plant is saffron obtained?
a: From the stigmas of the crocus flower
From the roots of the crocus
From the seeds of the crocus
From the corm of the crocus
125793.e: Each flower of Crocus sativus gives only three stigma threads, which are picked by hand. That is why saffron is one of the most expensive spices.
125793.m: Saffron consists of the stigmas of the saffron crocus.

125794.q: Which spice is obtained from the bark of a tree and used to come mainly from Sri Lanka?
125794.e: Ceylon cinnamon consists of the dried inner bark of the cinnamon tree. The island was for a long time the most important place it came from.

125795.q: Which small nutmeg island did the Dutch keep in the Treaty of Breda in 1667, while England kept New Amsterdam?
125795.e: The island of Run belongs to the Banda Islands, the home of the nutmeg. New Amsterdam later became a world city as New York.
125795.m: For the nutmeg island of Run, the Dutch gave up New Amsterdam.

125796.q: Who was mockingly called a “pepper sack” (German “Pfeffersack”) in the late Middle Ages?
125796.e: Pepper was so expensive that traders made great fortunes from it. The nickname mocked their wealth.
125796.m: A “pepper sack” was a rich merchant.

125797.q: Which spice from Mexico is grown today mainly on Madagascar, where it is pollinated by hand?
125797.e: Outside Mexico, the natural pollinators of the vanilla orchid are missing. That is why every flower has to be pollinated by hand, which makes vanilla very expensive.
125797.m: Outside Mexico, vanilla has to be pollinated by hand.

125798.q: What are the potatoes of the Andean peoples called that are preserved by frost and sun?
125798.e: The tubers are left out in the frost at night, dried during the day and squeezed. This way chuño keeps for years and was an important supply in the Inca Empire.
125798.m: Chuño is an ancient way of preserving potatoes.

125799.q: Who first brought the potato to Europe in the 16th century?
125799.e: The Spanish brought the tuber from South America in the second half of the 16th century. At first it was seen in many places as a botanical curiosity.
125799.m: The Spanish brought the potato to Europe.

125800.q: Which Prussian king promoted potato growing in 1756 with the so-called “Potato Order”?
125800.e: Frederick II, known as Frederick the Great, ordered the potato to be grown in order to prevent famines. Many farmers were suspicious of the new plant at first.
125800.m: Frederick the Great promoted the potato in Prussia.

125801.q: Which French pharmacist made the potato popular in France?
125801.e: In the 18th century, Parmentier promoted the potato with experiments and banquets. Several potato dishes still bear his name today.
125801.m: Antoine Parmentier made the potato popular in France.

125802.q: Which pathogen caused the great famine in Ireland from 1845?
125802.e: The water mould Phytophthora infestans causes late blight and destroyed several harvests. Ireland depended heavily on a few potato varieties.
125802.m: Late blight caused the Irish famine.

125803.q: Which poisonous substance builds up in green patches and sprouts of potatoes?
125803.e: Solanine is an alkaloid of the nightshade family. Green patches and sprouts should therefore be cut away generously.
125803.m: Green patches on potatoes contain poisonous solanine.

125804.q: Which pest introduced from North America eats the leaves of potato plants in Europe?
125804.e: The yellow and black striped Colorado potato beetle comes from North America and spread across Europe in the 20th century. Beetles and larvae can strip fields bare.
125804.m: The Colorado potato beetle is a pest introduced from North America.

125805.q: Why are potatoes in farming usually propagated from tubers rather than seeds?
a: The offspring are exactly like the variety
The plant does not form flowers
125805.e: Planting tubers produces genetically identical clones of the variety. That keeps the features the same, but makes whole fields vulnerable to the same diseases.
125805.m: Potatoes grown from tubers are clones of their mother plant.

125806.q: Where does the German word “Kartoffel” (potato) come from?
125806.e: The tubers reminded people of truffles, “tartufolo” in Italian. Via “Tartuffel”, this became the German word “Kartoffel”.
125806.m: The German word Kartoffel goes back to the Italian word for truffle.

125907.q: Where do you stick the AED pads on adults in the standard position?
a: Below the right collarbone and on the left side of the chest
Both pads next to each other on the breastbone
One on the stomach and one on the lower back
One pad on each upper arm
125907.e: This way the current flows diagonally through the heart. The devices also show the position on the pads with a picture.
125907.m: The AED pads place the heart between them.

125908.q: In ventricular fibrillation without defibrillation, roughly how does the chance of survival change per minute?
a: It falls by about 7 to 10 per cent
It stays the same for the first 10 minutes
It falls by about 50 per cent
125908.e: Without treatment, the chance of survival drops considerably every minute. Chest compressions slow this loss but do not replace the shock.
125908.m: In ventricular fibrillation, every minute until the first shock counts.

125909.q: What do you pay attention to when sticking AED pads on a person with an implanted pacemaker?
a: Do not stick the pad directly over the device
Switch off the pacemaker first with a magnet
Do not use the AED at all
Stick the pads on the back
125909.e: A pacemaker usually lies below the left or right collarbone and can be felt as a bulge. The pad is stuck next to it, a few centimetres away.
125909.m: A pacemaker is no reason not to use the AED.

125910.q: What should you do if a person's chest is wet before you stick on the AED pads?
a: Moisten the pads with water as well
Choose a shock with double the energy
Stick the pads on the clothes
125910.e: On wet skin the pads stick poorly and the current can flow away over the surface. A quick dry is enough.
125910.m: The AED pads always go on dry, bare skin.

125911.q: Why must nobody touch the person while the AED is analysing and delivering a shock?
a: Movements disturb the analysis and the current can hit the helpers
Because otherwise the battery runs flat
Because otherwise the device changes language
Because the pads would then fall off
125911.e: The AED must be able to measure the heart rhythm without disturbance. During the shock, the current could also jump to the helpers.
125911.m: During analysis and shock, nobody touches the person.

125912.q: What do helpers do immediately after an AED shock?
a: Carry on with chest compressions at once
Feel for the pulse for one minute
Put the person in the recovery position
125912.e: Even after a successful shock, the heart often does not yet pump enough. That is why compressions continue straight away until the device announces the next analysis.
125912.m: After the shock, compressions continue without a break.

125913.q: How should gasping breaths in an unconscious person be interpreted?
a: As a sign of cardiac arrest
As a sign of normal recovery
As a sign of deep sleep
125913.e: Gasping consists of rare, slow breaths without effective gas exchange. It does not count as normal breathing, so you start resuscitation immediately.
125913.m: Gasping is not normal breathing and calls for immediate chest compressions.

125914.q: According to the ERC guidelines, with how many rescue breaths do you begin resuscitating a child?
125914.e: In children, cardiac arrest is usually the result of a lack of oxygen. That is why they first receive oxygen through five rescue breaths.
125914.m: In children, resuscitation starts with five rescue breaths.

125915.q: Which medicine does the ambulance service give as standard during resuscitation?
125915.e: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and so increases the pressure with which blood flows to the heart and brain. It is injected into a vein or into the bone.
125915.m: Adrenaline is the most important medicine in resuscitation.

125916.q: What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in adults?
125916.e: Narrowed coronary arteries and heart attacks often lead to ventricular fibrillation. This rhythm suddenly stops the heart's pumping.
125916.m: Sudden cardiac death is usually caused by a disease of the coronary arteries.

125917.q: In the classic chain of rescue, which link comes directly after the emergency call?
125917.e: Several minutes often pass between the alarm and the arrival of the professionals. Laypeople bridge this time with first aid.
125917.m: After the emergency call, helpers give first aid until the ambulance service arrives.

125918.q: How many links does the European Resuscitation Council's chain of survival have?
125918.e: The links are early recognition and emergency call, early chest compressions, early defibrillation and further treatment by professionals. Each link increases the chance of survival.
125918.m: The chain of survival in cardiac arrest has four links.

a: Several injuries at the same time, of which one or their combination is life-threatening
A single minor injury on several days
A chronic disease of several organs
125919.e: In polytrauma, several regions of the body or organ systems are injured. What matters is that the injuries together threaten life.
125919.m: Polytrauma is a life-threatening multiple injury.

125920.q: Where does the ambulance service in Switzerland take polytrauma patients whenever possible?
a: Always to the nearest regional hospital
125920.e: Severely injured people are treated in a few large centres where all specialities are available around the clock. A longer transport, for example by helicopter, is accepted for this.
125920.m: Severely injured people belong in a trauma centre.

125921.q: Which three conditions form the so-called lethal triad in a severely injured patient?
a: Hypothermia, acidosis and a clotting disorder
High blood pressure, diabetes and being overweight
125921.e: Hypothermia and acidification of the blood make blood clotting worse. As a result the patient bleeds more, which makes the other two conditions even worse.
125921.m: Hypothermia, acidosis and clotting disorders make each other worse in severely injured people.

125922.q: What does the term “golden hour” mean in trauma care?
a: The first hour after the accident, in which quick treatment achieves a particularly great deal
The hour before sunset with good visibility for helicopters
The time when operations are cheapest
The first hour of rest after an operation
125922.e: The term stresses that severely injured people should reach a suitable hospital as quickly as possible. The exact length is more of a guiding idea than a fixed limit.
125922.m: For severely injured people, the time until final treatment is what counts most.

125923.q: What does the “B” stand for in the ABCDE approach of emergency medicine?
125923.e: The approach checks, in order, the airway, breathing, circulation, neurological state and the undressed body. What kills fastest is treated first.
125923.m: In the ABCDE approach, breathing comes straight after the airway.

125924.q: Why does the ambulance service put a pelvic binder on an accident victim?
a: To reduce internal bleeding if a broken pelvis is suspected
To support the spine when lifting
125924.e: With an unstable pelvic fracture, a lot of blood can be lost inside the pelvis. The binder presses the bones together and reduces the space for bleeding.
125924.m: A pelvic binder stabilises the pelvis and slows internal bleeding.

125925.q: What is the aim of “damage control surgery” in severely injured people?
a: First only control bleeding and contamination, with the final repair following later
Fully repair all injuries at once in one long operation
125925.e: A long operation would overwhelm the weakened body. After a short emergency operation, the patient is stabilised in intensive care and the surgery is completed later.
125925.m: In severely injured people, life is saved first with a short operation, and everything is repaired later.

125926.q: How do you position a person with anaphylaxis who is mainly short of breath but conscious?
a: Sitting or with the upper body raised
Head down with the feet raised
125926.e: Breathing is easier when sitting, because the breathing muscles work better. If the circulation is weak, however, you lay the person flat.
125926.m: If someone is short of breath, let them sit upright.

125927.q: In an allergic reaction, which signs point to life-threatening anaphylaxis?
a: Shortness of breath and circulatory weakness
Slight redness at the sting site
125927.e: In anaphylaxis, not only the skin but also the airways and circulation are affected. Then an immediate call to 144 is needed.
125927.m: Shortness of breath and circulation problems turn an allergy into an emergency.

125928.q: In which period is the chance of survival highest for avalanche victims who are completely buried?
a: On the day after the avalanche
125928.e: Most buried people survive the first few minutes. After that the survival curve drops steeply, because many run out of air.
125928.m: In an avalanche, quick rescue in the first few minutes is what counts.

125929.q: What do most avalanche victims who are recovered dead after a short time die of?
125929.e: Once it stops moving, the snow packs down like concrete and blocks the mouth and nose. Without an air space, a lack of oxygen sets in quickly.
125929.m: The greatest danger under an avalanche is suffocation.

125930.q: Why do all avalanche transceivers send on the same frequency?
a: So that every device can locate every other one
So that they use less power
So that they do not interfere with mobile phones
So that they can also be used as radios
125930.e: All avalanche transceivers work internationally on 457 kilohertz. This way, any device can find a buried person, no matter which brand they are wearing.
125930.m: All avalanche transceivers work on the same frequency.

125931.q: Which emergency equipment is standard on ski tours away from secured pistes?
a: Avalanche transceiver, avalanche shovel and avalanche probe
Foil blanket, mobile phone and map
125931.e: With the transceiver you locate the buried person, with the probe you confirm their position and with the shovel you dig them out. If any one of these is missing, the rescue takes much longer.
125931.m: Transceiver, shovel and probe always belong together.

125932.q: Why is rescue by companions so crucial in avalanche accidents?
a: Because it is much faster than an organised rescue on the spot
Because it is cheaper than a helicopter mission
Because rescue services are not allowed to fly into the mountains
Because only companions know the victims
125932.e: Even a helicopter usually needs much longer for the alarm and the flight than the first critical minutes. The companions are already there.
125932.m: In avalanches, it is often the companions who save the lives of those buried.

125933.q: What do you uncover as early as possible when recovering an avalanche victim?
a: The head with the mouth and nose
125933.e: As soon as the airway is clear, the person can breathe. During the rescue, you also look out for a possible air pocket in front of the face.
125933.m: With avalanche victims, the head and airway are uncovered first.

125934.q: Below which core body temperature is it called hypothermia?
125934.e: The normal core temperature is about 37 degrees. If it falls below 35 degrees, a person is considered hypothermic.
125934.m: Hypothermia begins below a core temperature of 35 degrees.

125935.q: According to the Swiss staging system, what characterises stage I hypothermia?
125935.e: In the first stage, the person is awake and shivers strongly. Shivering produces heat and is a protective mechanism.
125935.m: Someone who is shivering strongly and thinking clearly is mildly hypothermic.

125936.q: Below roughly which core temperature does shivering usually stop?
125936.e: As the body cools further, the energy reserves run out and the muscles no longer work effectively. A lack of shivering is therefore a warning sign.
125936.m: If a hypothermic person stops shivering, it becomes dangerous.

125937.q: Why do you move a severely hypothermic person as gently as possible and keep them horizontal?
a: Because otherwise ventricular fibrillation can be triggered
Because otherwise they fall asleep immediately
125937.e: The cold heart is very easily irritated. Jerky movements and cold blood from the limbs can trigger a dangerous rhythm.
125937.m: Hypothermic people are kept still and lying flat.

125938.q: What does the saying “Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead” mean?
a: That you keep resuscitating hypothermic people without signs of life
That the dead must always be warmed up
That you only resuscitate in summer
125938.e: Cold greatly reduces the brain's need for oxygen. That is why even people with a long cardiac arrest in deep hypothermia have a chance of survival.
125938.m: In severe hypothermia, resuscitation is not given up too soon.

125939.q: How is a deeply hypothermic person in cardiac arrest most effectively rewarmed in hospital?
a: With a heart-lung machine or ECMO
With warm tea through a stomach tube
With infrared lamps on the skin
125939.e: In extracorporeal rewarming, the blood is warmed outside the body and enriched with oxygen. At the same time, the machine takes over the pumping work of the heart.
125939.m: In hypothermia with cardiac arrest, a heart-lung machine helps.

125940.q: Why do small children cool down faster than adults?
a: Because their body surface is larger in relation to their volume
Because their heart beats more slowly
125940.e: The body loses heat through its surface, while heat is produced and stored in its volume. A small body has relatively a lot of surface and therefore loses heat quickly.
125940.m: Small children need especially good protection from the cold.

125941.q: Why does alcohol increase the risk of hypothermia?
a: Because it widens the blood vessels in the skin, so more heat is lost
Because it heats the body up strongly from inside
125941.e: The feeling of warmth on the skin is deceptive, because heat flows out through the widened vessels. Alcohol also clouds your judgement of the danger.
125941.m: Alcohol only seems to warm you and in fact encourages cooling down.

125942.q: Which language does the word “triage” come from?
125942.e: The verb “trier” means to sort or select. In German medical services it is also called “Sichtung”.
125942.m: Triage means sorting patients by urgency.

125943.q: Which of Napoleon's military surgeons is regarded as the founder of modern triage?
125943.e: Larrey had the wounded treated according to how serious their injuries were and not according to rank. He also introduced fast transport carts for the wounded.
125943.m: Modern triage goes back to Napoleon's surgeon Larrey.

125944.q: What does the colour red mean in triage after a major incident?
125944.e: People marked red are acutely life-threateningly injured but have a good chance of survival with immediate help. Yellow stands for urgent cases, green for minor ones.
125944.m: In triage, red means treat immediately.

125945.q: In the START system, which category do all people who can walk on their own receive?
125945.e: People who can walk usually have no immediately life-threatening injury. They are sent to a gathering point and assessed more closely later.
125945.m: In the START system, people who can walk are first considered slightly injured.

125946.q: After a major incident, an injured person is breathing more than 30 times a minute. Which category do you put them in under the START system?
125946.e: Very fast breathing shows a serious disturbance of breathing or circulation. Such people need help immediately.
125946.m: If an injured person breathes very fast, they must be treated immediately.

125947.q: Above which capillary refill time is a person considered critical in the START system?
125947.e: You press on a fingernail bed and measure how quickly it turns pink again. Slow refilling points to shock.
125947.m: A slow return of colour to the nail bed points to shock.

125948.q: What does the Manchester Triage System in the emergency department set for each level of urgency?
a: A maximum waiting time until first seeing a doctor
125948.e: The system divides patients into five colour levels. Red means immediately, blue may wait the longest.
125948.m: The Manchester Triage System works with five colour levels.

125949.q: What does the German abbreviation MANV stand for in emergency services?
125949.e: A mass casualty incident occurs when there are more injured people than available rescue resources. Triage then becomes the central task of the first emergency teams.
125949.m: In a mass casualty incident, triage is essential.

125950.q: In which city is Tox Info Suisse based?
125950.e: The centre works closely with the University of Zurich. From there it gives advice to the whole of Switzerland.
125950.m: Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich.

125951.q: When can the Tox Info Suisse emergency number be reached?
a: Only on weekdays during office hours
125951.e: Poisonings happen at any time of day. That is why experts answer the calls without a break.
125951.m: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night.

125952.q: Which age group among children is most often affected in poisoning enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
125952.e: Toddlers explore their surroundings with their mouths. That is why they often swallow household products, parts of plants or medicines.
125952.m: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept out of reach of toddlers.

125953.q: What should you not do if a child has swallowed a corrosive cleaning product?
125953.e: When vomiting, the corrosive liquid would damage the oesophagus a second time. It could also get into the lungs.
125953.m: After swallowing cleaning products, never make someone vomit yourself.

125954.q: Which group of products is most often involved in enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
125954.e: Medicines are found in almost every household and get mixed up, taken in too high a dose or found by children. Household products come next.
125954.m: Most poisoning enquiries are about medicines.

125955.q: What should you have ready if possible when calling Tox Info Suisse?
125955.e: The packaging shows the name and the ingredients. This lets the expert assess the risk accurately.
125955.m: In a poisoning, keep the product's packaging ready.

125956.q: Which remedy is used in many poisonings to bind toxic substances in the gut?
125956.e: Activated charcoal has a huge inner surface to which many substances stick. An expert decides whether it makes sense to use it.
125956.m: Activated charcoal binds many poisons before they enter the blood.

125957.q: How is the Swiss Samaritan Association organised at grassroots level?
125957.e: The clubs work largely on a voluntary basis and are grouped into cantonal associations. They offer courses and first aid services in their region.
125957.m: Samaritan work depends on local clubs with volunteers.

125958.q: Which course must people in Switzerland have attended before applying for a learner's permit for driving a car?
a: The first aid for children course
125958.e: The emergency first aid course teaches how to behave at the scene of an accident, positioning and chest compressions. Providers include the Samaritan clubs.
125958.m: Anyone who wants to learn to drive first attends the emergency first aid course.

125959.q: What role does the Interverband für Rettungswesen (IVR) play in Switzerland?
a: It is the umbrella association for rescue services
It is the police emergency call centre
It is a private ambulance company
It is the Federal Office for Civil Protection
125959.e: In the IVR, organisations and experts from the rescue services work together. It campaigns for a uniform quality of rescue.
125959.m: The IVR is the umbrella association of Swiss rescue services.

125960.q: What is the Interverband für Rettungswesen called in French?
125960.e: The French abbreviation is IAS. In French-speaking Switzerland the association is known by this name.
125960.m: In French-speaking Switzerland, the IVR is called Interassociation de sauvetage.

125961.q: What does the IVR award to ambulance services that meet its quality guidelines?
125961.e: Ambulance services are checked for equipment, staff and procedures. The recognition shows that they meet the Swiss-wide standards.
125961.m: Ambulance services recognised by the IVR meet uniform quality standards.

125962.q: Besides ambulance services, which facilities are also recognised according to IVR guidelines?
125962.e: The emergency call centres take calls, send out rescue resources and guide laypeople over the phone. Uniform quality requirements apply to them too.
125962.m: The 144 emergency call centres also follow Swiss-wide guidelines.

125963.q: At which level of education are paramedics trained in Switzerland?
a: At a college of higher education (Höhere Fachschule)
125963.e: The qualification is called qualified paramedic HF. The training combines college and practical work in the ambulance service.
125963.m: In Switzerland, paramedics are trained at colleges of higher education.

125964.q: Which qualification do patient transport attendants earn in Switzerland?
a: A federal diploma of higher vocational education
A course certificate from the employer
125964.e: The professional examination leads to the federal diploma. Patient transport attendants mainly work on planned and less urgent patient transports.
125964.m: Patient transport attendants qualify with a federal diploma.

125965.q: Which target for response time do the IVR guidelines set for ambulance services?
a: On the scene within 15 minutes in 90 per cent of call-outs
On the scene within 2 minutes in all call-outs
Within 1 hour in 50 per cent of call-outs
125965.e: The response time is the time it takes for the ambulance service to reach the scene. It is an important figure for planning ambulance stations.
125965.m: Ambulance services should reach most emergencies within a quarter of an hour.

125966.q: When is a tourniquet used in first aid?
a: For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that cannot be stopped any other way
For every small cut on a finger
For a bruise without a wound
125966.e: A tourniquet stops the blood flow to the whole limb. It is the right tool when pressure and a pressure bandage are not enough or there is no time for them.
125966.m: A tourniquet is meant for life-threatening bleeding from arms and legs.

125967.q: Where is a tourniquet applied when the wound is known?
a: A few centimetres above the wound, towards the body, not over a joint
Below the wound, towards the hand or foot
125967.e: Above the wound, it cuts off the supply to the bleeding site. Over a joint, the blood vessel cannot be reliably compressed.
125967.m: The tourniquet goes above the wound and never on a joint.

125968.q: What must always be written down after applying a tourniquet?
a: The skin colour of the helper
125968.e: How long the limb has been tied off is important for treatment in hospital. The time is often written directly on the tourniquet or on the person's forehead.
125968.m: With a tourniquet, the time is always written down.

125969.q: What is the turning rod called that is used to tighten a modern tourniquet?
125969.e: Turning the rod tightens the band so much that the artery is compressed. The rod is then secured in a holder.
125969.m: A tourniquet is tightened with a turning rod called a windlass.

125970.q: Who is allowed to loosen a tourniquet once it has been applied?
a: Anyone, as soon as the bleeding has stopped
Nobody, it stays on until healing is complete
125970.e: When it is loosened, the bleeding can start again and toxic substances from the limb get into the circulation. That is why professionals decide.
125970.m: Only professionals loosen a tourniquet once it has been applied.

125971.q: Where do you apply a tourniquet if the exact source of bleeding cannot be seen?
a: As high up the limb as possible, close to the body
Exactly in the middle of the limb
125971.e: Following the principle “high and tight”, this covers all possible bleeding sites below it. Later, professionals can place the tourniquet more precisely.
125971.m: If the source of bleeding is unclear, the tourniquet goes high and tight on the limb.

125972.q: How can you tell that a tourniquet is tight enough?
a: The bleeding stops and no pulse can be felt below it
The skin below turns red and warm
The injured person feels no pain
The band can still be moved easily
125972.e: A tourniquet that is too loose only traps blood in the veins and can even make the bleeding worse. It must completely cut off the flow through the arteries.
125972.m: A tourniquet is only right when the bleeding really stops.

125973.q: Why is a thin cord unsuitable as an improvised tourniquet?
a: It cuts in and damages skin and nerves
125973.e: A narrow band puts the pressure on a small area. It injures the tissue underneath and often still does not fully compress the artery.
125973.m: A tourniquet needs a wide band, not a thin cord.

125974.q: Roughly how long is a correctly applied tourniquet considered acceptable without serious damage being expected?
125974.e: After that, the risk of muscle and nerve damage rises considerably. That is why quick transport to hospital is important.
125974.m: A tourniquet is only a stopgap until treatment in hospital.

125975.q: With which heart finding does an AED not deliver a shock?
125975.e: In asystole, there is no electrical activity at all that a shock could reorganise. Only chest compressions and medicines help here.
125975.m: A flat line cannot be treated with an electric shock.

125976.q: What do you do with a medicine patch that is stuck where an AED pad needs to go?
a: Remove it and wipe the skin
Stick the pad directly over it
125976.e: A patch under the pad can block the flow of current and cause burns. It only takes seconds to pull it off.
125976.m: No patch may be stuck under an AED pad.

125977.q: What do special child pads or a child mode on an AED do?
a: They extend the analysis time to ten minutes
They switch off the voice prompts
They deliver several shocks at the same time
125977.e: Children need a smaller amount of current than adults. If there are no child pads, the adult pads are used anyway.
125977.m: On a child, an AED may be used with reduced energy.

125978.q: How often should several helpers ideally take turns doing chest compressions?
125978.e: Chest compressions are tiring, and the depth of the compressions drops unnoticed as you tire. The changeover should happen with as short a pause as possible.
125978.m: Helpers take turns regularly during chest compressions.

125979.q: What is the longest that checking an unconscious person's breathing should take?
125979.e: You tilt the head back and look, listen and feel for breathing movements, breathing sounds and airflow. If you are unsure, you start chest compressions.
125979.m: Checking breathing takes no longer than ten seconds.

125980.q: Roughly what proportion of normal heart output does good chest compression achieve?
a: About a quarter to a third
125980.e: Chest compressions only partly replace the heart's pumping. But this is enough to supply the brain and heart with some oxygen for a while.
125980.m: Chest compressions keep an emergency circulation going until the heart beats again.

125981.q: During resuscitation, how can you tell that the heart is beating on its own again?
a: A pulse and normal breathing return
125981.e: When the heart beats by itself again, a pulse can be felt and the person often starts breathing normally again. Experts call this return of spontaneous circulation.
125981.m: When pulse and breathing return, the heart is beating on its own again.

125982.q: After successful resuscitation, what is deliberately avoided in intensive care during the first few days?
125982.e: A raised body temperature makes brain damage after a lack of oxygen worse. That is why the temperature is monitored and carefully controlled.
125982.m: After resuscitation, a controlled body temperature protects the brain.

125983.q: What does the classic chain of rescue start with?
a: The arrival of the emergency doctor
125983.e: Immediate measures include securing the scene of the accident, rescuing people from the danger zone and chest compressions. They are carried out by the first people on the scene.
125983.m: The chain of rescue begins with the people who are first at the scene.

125984.q: What is it called when the emergency call centre guides laypeople through chest compressions over the phone?
125984.e: The dispatcher counts out the rhythm and gives instructions. As a result, many more laypeople start resuscitation.
125984.m: In cardiac arrest, the emergency call centre helps with resuscitation over the phone.

125985.q: What is the job of first responders, who are alerted by smartphone app in many cantons?
a: They start resuscitation before the ambulance service arrives
They replace the emergency doctor in hospital
They direct traffic at the scene of the accident
125985.e: Volunteers trained in resuscitation who are nearby are called out at the same time as the ambulance service. They are often on the scene faster.
125985.m: In cardiac arrest, first responders bridge the time until the ambulance service arrives.

125986.q: At least how far away do you set up the warning triangle on Swiss motorways?
125986.e: Because of the high speeds, vehicles behind need a long braking distance. On other roads, 50 metres is usually enough.
125986.m: On the motorway, the warning triangle stands at least 100 metres before the accident.

125987.q: What is the top priority for helpers at the scene of an accident?
125987.e: Anyone who puts themselves in danger can become an additional victim and can no longer help anyone. That is why you first secure the scene and watch out for traffic, fire or electricity.
125987.m: Anyone who helps protects themselves first.

125988.q: Which grip do you use to quickly pull an unconscious person out of a danger zone, for example out of a car?
125988.e: You reach under the armpits, grab one of the person's forearms and pull them out of the danger zone on your own thighs. The grip is named after the Austrian Franz Rautek.
125988.m: With the Rautek manoeuvre, even a weaker person can rescue someone who is unconscious.

125989.q: What do you do with an unconscious motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet?
a: Just close the visor with tape
Bend the head with the helmet sharply forwards
125989.e: With the helmet on, the airway cannot be checked and kept clear. If possible two people remove it, stabilising the head and neck at the same time.
125989.m: If a motorcyclist is unconscious, the helmet is removed.

125990.q: Which life-threatening chest injury is relieved in an emergency with a needle?
125990.e: In a tension pneumothorax, air collects under pressure in the chest and squeezes the lungs and heart. The needle lets the air escape and buys time until a drain is inserted.
125990.m: A tension pneumothorax must be relieved immediately.

125991.q: Where do you inject an adrenaline auto-injector in anaphylaxis?
a: Into the outer side of the thigh
Into a vein on the back of the hand
Under the skin of the stomach
Into the crook of the arm
125991.e: The large thigh muscle has a good blood supply and is easy to reach. In an emergency you can even inject through trousers.
125991.m: The adrenaline pen is placed on the outer thigh.

125992.q: What do you do if anaphylaxis does not improve about 5 minutes after the first dose of adrenaline?
a: Give a second dose of adrenaline
Give the person a glass of milk
Leave the person to rest alone
125992.e: That is why many people with allergies carry two auto-injectors. The second dose is given into the other thigh.
125992.m: If the first dose of adrenaline does not help, a second one follows.

125993.q: What is anaphylaxis called that only occurs when someone does sport after eating a particular food?
125993.e: Only the combination of the food and physical exertion triggers the reaction. A well-known trigger is wheat.
125993.m: Some types of anaphylaxis also need physical exertion as a trigger.

125994.q: Which foods particularly often trigger anaphylaxis in children?
125994.e: Nuts are among the most common triggers of severe allergic reactions. Even tiny traces can be enough.
125994.m: Nuts are common triggers of anaphylaxis.

125995.q: Why does a person in anaphylactic shock quickly need a lot of intravenous fluid?
a: Because fluid leaks out of the leaky blood vessels into the tissue
Because they have too much salt in their blood
Because otherwise the adrenaline will not dissolve
125995.e: Messenger substances make the vessel walls leaky and widen the vessels. As a result, the circulation suddenly lacks a lot of volume.
125995.m: In anaphylaxis, the circulation loses fluid to the tissue.

125996.q: After the bite of which animal can alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to red meat, develop?
125996.e: The bite sensitises the body to the sugar alpha-gal, which is also found in mammal meat. The reaction typically only occurs hours after eating.
125996.m: A tick bite can trigger a delayed allergy to red meat.

125997.q: Why is adrenaline for anaphylaxis injected into the muscle and not under the skin?
a: Because it gets into the blood faster from the muscle
Because it turns into crystals under the skin
Because the skin contains no blood
Because it costs less that way
125997.e: Muscles have a good blood supply, while adrenaline under the skin narrows the vessels there and so slows down its own absorption. That is why injecting into the muscle is standard.
125997.m: Adrenaline for anaphylaxis goes into the muscle.

125998.q: Which number do you dial in a poisoning if the person is unconscious or breathing badly?
125998.e: When life is in danger, the ambulance service is needed immediately. If necessary, the emergency call centre can consult Tox Info Suisse itself.
125998.m: In a life-threatening poisoning, you call the ambulance service first.

125999.q: Which events do many Samaritan clubs organise together with the Swiss Red Cross blood donation service?
125999.e: The clubs provide helpers for registering, looking after and feeding the donors. This way, blood is collected regularly in many municipalities.
125999.m: Samaritan clubs help with many blood donation drives.

126000.q: What aim has the Samaritan movement pursued since its beginnings in the 19th century?
a: Laypeople should be able to give first aid in accidents
Only doctors should be allowed to treat injured people
Hospitals should be replaced by clubs
Injured people should only be cared for by the army
126000.e: The Samaritan movement wants ordinary people to be able to help properly in accidents until professionals arrive. The name goes back to the parable of the Good Samaritan.

126001.q: Which course do Samaritan clubs offer in which you practise chest compressions and defibrillation?
126001.e: BLS stands for Basic Life Support, the basic measures of resuscitation. Because knowledge fades, regular refresher courses are recommended.
126001.m: In a BLS-AED course you learn how to help in cardiac arrest.

126002.q: What is the maximum age of the emergency first aid course certificate when applying for a learner's permit?
126002.e: If the course was longer ago, it has to be repeated. This is so that the knowledge is still reasonably fresh when you start driving.
126002.m: An emergency first aid course that is too old must be repeated before the learner's permit.

126003.q: In triage after a major incident, what does the category blue mean?
a: Expectant treatment, because there is hardly any chance of survival under the circumstances
Immediate treatment because of danger to life
Slightly injured and able to walk
126003.e: This difficult category is only used when there are not enough resources for everyone. Those affected are looked after and reassessed when capacity becomes free.
126003.m: The category blue is only given when rescue resources are lacking.

126004.q: What is the threshold frequency for a metal with a work function of 2.28 eV (h = 6.626 · 10^-34 J·s, e = 1.602 · 10^-19 C)?
126004.e: The threshold frequency is f = W/h. With W = 2.28 · 1.602 · 10^-19 J = 3.65 · 10^-19 J, it follows that f = 3.65 · 10^-19 J / 6.626 · 10^-34 J·s ≈ 5.5 · 10^14 Hz.
126004.m: Below the threshold frequency, light does not release electrons from the metal.

126005.q: Light of 400 nm falls on a metal with a work function of 2.3 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons (h·c ≈ 1240 eV·nm)?
126005.e: The photon energy is 1240 eV·nm / 400 nm = 3.1 eV. The work function is subtracted from this: 3.1 eV minus 2.3 eV = 0.8 eV.
126005.m: The photon energy minus the work function gives the greatest kinetic energy of the electrons.

126006.q: In the photoelectric effect, what changes when you increase the light intensity above the threshold frequency?
a: The maximum energy of the individual electrons
The work function of the metal
126006.e: At the same frequency, more intensity means more photons per second. But each photon still gives the same energy to one electron.
126006.m: Brighter light releases more electrons, but not faster ones.

126007.q: In the stopping voltage method, the photocurrent just becomes zero at a stopping voltage of 1.5 V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
126007.e: The fastest electrons are stopped exactly when their kinetic energy equals e·U. With U = 1.5 V, this gives 1.5 eV.
126007.m: The stopping voltage measures the greatest kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

126008.q: Which quantity is given by the slope of the line when you plot the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons against the light frequency?
126008.e: According to the equation E_kin = h·f − W, the line is equally steep for all metals. Only the intercept depends on the work function.
126008.m: In the photoelectric effect, the slope of the line is the same for every metal.

126009.q: Which physicist was the first to observe, in 1887, that UV light makes it easier for sparks to form between electrodes?
126009.e: Hertz noticed the effect during his experiments with electromagnetic waves. He did not yet have an explanation for it.
126009.m: Heinrich Hertz discovered the external photoelectric effect more or less by chance.

126010.q: In which year did Albert Einstein publish his light quantum hypothesis to explain the photoelectric effect?
126010.e: 1905 is considered Einstein’s “miracle year”, in which he also published special relativity. At the time he was working at the patent office in Bern.
126010.m: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect during his time in Bern.

126011.q: Which observation in the photoelectric effect contradicts classical wave theory particularly clearly?
a: Electrons are released practically without delay even with very weak light
126011.e: According to wave theory, with weak light the energy would first have to build up in an electron over a longer time. With light quanta, by contrast, an electron receives the energy in one go.
126011.m: In the photoelectric effect, a single light quantum gives its energy to an electron immediately.

126012.q: What happens when a negatively charged zinc plate is exposed to UV light?
126012.e: The UV light releases electrons from the zinc, so the negative charge decreases. This does not work with visible light, because its photons have too little energy.
126012.m: UV light can discharge a negatively charged zinc plate.

126013.q: While explaining which radiation did Max Planck introduce the quantum of action in 1900?
a: The radiation of a black body
126013.e: Planck found a formula for the spectrum of a black body that could only be derived with quantised packets of energy. He himself first saw this as a mathematical trick.
126013.m: The quantum of action came from the study of thermal radiation.

126014.q: What did Max Planck receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for?
a: For the discovery of energy quanta
For the discovery of the electron
126014.e: With the idea that energy is only given off in certain portions, Planck laid the foundation of quantum physics. That is why he is considered its founder.
126014.m: Max Planck was honoured for discovering energy quanta.

126015.q: What is the failure of the classical radiation formula, which predicted infinite radiated power at short wavelengths, called?
126015.e: According to the Rayleigh-Jeans law, the radiated power grows without limit towards small wavelengths. Only quantisation resolved this contradiction.
126015.m: The ultraviolet catastrophe showed the limits of classical physics.

126016.q: What condition did Max Planck set in 1900 for the energy of an oscillator with frequency f?
a: The energy is a whole-number multiple of h·f
The energy can take any value
The energy is always exactly zero
The energy is proportional to the oscillator’s temperature
126016.e: An oscillator can only take in or give off energy in whole packets of size h·f. With this assumption, his radiation formula matched the measurements.
126016.m: According to Planck, an oscillator’s energy only comes in whole packets.

126017.q: What rest mass does a photon have?
a: One thousandth of the electron’s mass
126017.e: A photon can never be at rest and always moves at the speed of light in a vacuum. Its energy and momentum come entirely from its motion.

126018.q: To which class of particles does the photon belong?
126018.e: The photon has spin 1. Particles with whole-number spin are called bosons and can occupy the same state any number of times.

126019.q: What momentum does a photon with a wavelength of 500 nm have (h = 6.626 · 10^-34 J·s)?
126019.e: With p = h/λ, it follows that 6.626 · 10^-34 J·s / 5.0 · 10^-7 m ≈ 1.3 · 10^-27 kg·m/s. Such momenta are used by solar sails, for example.
126019.m: The shorter a photon’s wavelength, the greater its momentum.

126020.q: Roughly how many photons per second does a laser with 1 mW output and a wavelength of 633 nm emit?
126020.e: One photon has E = h·c/λ ≈ 3.1 · 10^-19 J. The number per second is 10^-3 W / 3.1 · 10^-19 J ≈ 3.2 · 10^15.
126020.m: Even a weak laser emits an unimaginable number of photons.

126021.q: From which Greek word does the name “photon” come?
126021.e: The name was coined in 1926 and became established for the light quantum. The same word is also found in photography and photosynthesis.
126021.m: The name photon comes from the Greek word for light.

126022.q: What wavelength does a photon with an energy of 1 eV have (h·c ≈ 1240 eV·nm)?
126022.e: From λ = h·c/E, it follows that 1240 eV·nm / 1 eV = 1240 nm. This radiation is in the near infrared.
126022.m: Photons with little energy have a long wavelength.

126023.q: What is the antiparticle of the photon?
126023.e: The photon is electrically neutral and has no other charge that could be reversed. That is why it is its own antiparticle.
126023.m: The photon is its own antiparticle.

126024.q: Which physicist formulated the principle of complementarity to interpret wave-particle duality?
126024.e: According to Bohr, the wave picture and the particle picture exclude each other in a single experiment. But both are needed to describe the behaviour of quantum objects completely.
126024.m: The wave and particle pictures complement each other but never appear at the same time.

126025.q: With which large molecules did Anton Zeilinger’s group demonstrate interference in 1999?
a: With fullerenes made of 60 carbon atoms
126025.e: The football-shaped C60 molecules are much larger than electrons and still showed wave properties. The experiment showed that duality is not limited to the tiniest particles.
126025.m: Even large molecules can behave like waves.

126026.q: Why does an electron microscope achieve a much higher resolution than a light microscope?
a: Because the wavelength of the electrons is much smaller
Because electrons are heavier than atoms
126026.e: Resolution is limited by the wavelength. Fast electrons have wavelengths far below one nanometre, much smaller than those of visible light.
126026.m: The smaller the wavelength, the finer the details in the microscope.

126027.q: For a single photon, what does the brightness at a point of an interference pattern indicate?
a: The probability that it lands there
The speed of the photon there
126027.e: A single photon lands at a random place. Only many photons together form the pattern that matches the probability distribution.
126027.m: The interference pattern shows where a photon is likely to land.

126028.q: Which observation on the screen shows the particle nature in the double-slit experiment?
a: Each particle produces a single point-like hit
The pattern has light and dark fringes
The fringes become wider over time
126028.e: A wave would spread over the whole screen. In fact, however, the detector registers each quantum object at exactly one point.
126028.m: Single hits reveal the particle, the overall pattern the wave.

126029.q: At which Swiss research facility are neutrons produced for diffraction experiments on materials?
a: At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen
126029.e: PSI operates a spallation neutron source, SINQ. There, the neutrons are diffracted like waves by crystal lattices.
126029.m: At the Paul Scherrer Institute, the wave nature of neutrons is put to use.

126030.q: Which formula is used to calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a particle?
126030.e: The wavelength is Planck’s constant divided by the momentum. The greater the momentum, the shorter the wavelength.
126030.m: The matter wavelength falls as momentum rises.

126031.q: Which experiment confirmed the wave nature of electrons in 1927 through diffraction by a nickel crystal?
126031.e: Davisson and Germer found diffraction maxima exactly where they were expected according to the de Broglie wavelength. This proved the hypothesis experimentally.
126031.m: Electrons are diffracted by crystals just like X-rays.

126032.q: What de Broglie wavelength does an electron with a speed of 1.0 · 10^6 m/s have (m = 9.11 · 10^-31 kg)?
126032.m: Slow electrons have wavelengths in the range of the distances between atoms.

126033.q: What de Broglie wavelength does a tennis ball of 57 g at 50 m/s have?
126033.e: With p = 0.057 kg · 50 m/s = 2.85 kg·m/s, it follows that λ = 6.626 · 10^-34 J·s / 2.85 kg·m/s ≈ 2.3 · 10^-34 m. That is immeasurably small.
126033.m: For everyday objects, the matter wave is far too small to notice.

126034.q: How does the de Broglie wavelength of a slow particle change when its speed doubles?
126034.e: At non-relativistic speeds, momentum is proportional to speed. Because λ is inversely proportional to momentum, it halves.
126034.m: Double the speed means half the matter wavelength.

126035.q: Which particle has the smaller de Broglie wavelength at the same speed?
126035.e: The proton is about 1836 times heavier than the electron and so has correspondingly more momentum at the same speed. Its wavelength is therefore about 1836 times smaller.
126035.m: At the same speed, heavier particles have shorter matter waves.

126036.q: Which idea made Louis de Broglie famous and earned him the Nobel Prize?
a: Particles such as electrons also have wave properties
Light consists of particles with a fixed mass
Electrons orbit the nucleus on any paths at all
126036.e: In his doctoral thesis in 1924, de Broglie proposed that matter also has a wave nature. After experiments had confirmed the diffraction of electrons, he received the Nobel Prize in 1929.
126036.m: De Broglie realised that particles also have wave properties.

126037.q: How does the idea of matter waves explain the allowed orbits in Bohr’s atomic model?
a: A whole number of wavelengths fits on an allowed orbit as a standing wave
The electrons are held on their orbit by photons
The orbits are set by the nucleus’s magnetic fields
The electrons only vibrate on the innermost orbit
126037.e: Only if the wave does not cancel itself out after one orbit can it exist stably. This gives certain orbit radii.
126037.m: Allowed electron orbits correspond to standing matter waves.

126038.q: Why are thermal neutrons well suited for studying crystal structures?
a: Their wavelength is in the range of the distances between atoms
They carry a strong electric charge
They move at the speed of light
They are completely swallowed by crystals
126038.e: Diffraction is clear when the wavelength and the lattice spacing are of similar size. Thermal neutrons have wavelengths of a few tenths of a nanometre.
126038.m: For diffraction, the wavelength must match the distance between atoms.

126039.q: According to Heisenberg, what is the minimum value of the product of position uncertainty and momentum uncertainty?
126039.e: Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2. An arbitrarily small product of the two uncertainties is therefore impossible.
126039.m: Position and momentum can never both be pinned down as sharply as you like at the same time.

126040.q: An electron is confined to a region of 1 · 10^-10 m. What is its minimum velocity uncertainty (ħ = 1.055 · 10^-34 J·s, m = 9.11 · 10^-31 kg)?
126040.e: From Δp ≥ ħ/(2Δx), it follows that Δp ≥ 5.3 · 10^-25 kg·m/s. Divided by the mass, this gives Δv ≥ 5.8 · 10^5 m/s.
126040.m: Electrons confined in an atom cannot stand still.

126041.q: In which year did Werner Heisenberg publish the uncertainty principle?
126041.e: At the time, Heisenberg was working with Niels Bohr in Copenhagen. The principle became a cornerstone of the Copenhagen interpretation.
126041.m: The uncertainty principle dates from the founding years of quantum mechanics.

126042.q: Why do spectral lines have a natural width?
a: Because excited states only have a finite lifetime
Because light is slowed down in glass
126042.e: According to the energy-time uncertainty, a short lifetime leads to an uncertainty in the energy. That is why the frequency of the emitted light is not completely sharp either.
126042.m: Short-lived states have an uncertain energy.

126043.q: Is Heisenberg’s uncertainty caused by inaccurate measuring instruments?
a: No, it is a fundamental property of nature
Yes, better instruments can remove it
Yes, it disappears in a vacuum
No, it only occurs with light
126043.e: Even with perfect instruments, the uncertainty remains. It follows from the fact that quantum objects do not have sharp values for position and momentum at the same time.
126043.m: Uncertainty is not a measuring error but a law of nature.

126044.q: Why does helium not become solid at normal pressure even at absolute zero?
a: Because of its zero-point energy, which follows from the uncertainty principle
Because it is heavier than air
126044.e: The light helium atoms keep so much zero-point motion that the weak attractive forces cannot form a solid lattice. Helium only becomes solid under high pressure.
126044.m: At normal pressure, helium stays liquid right down to absolute zero.

126045.q: What did Werner Heisenberg receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for?
126045.e: In 1925, Heisenberg developed matrix mechanics, the first complete form of quantum mechanics. The prize honoured this fundamental work.
126045.m: Heisenberg is one of the founders of quantum mechanics.

126046.q: What does Heisenberg’s thought experiment with a gamma-ray microscope show?
a: Short-wave light for an exact position measurement gives the electron a strong push
Electrons are invisible in the microscope
126046.e: The shorter the wavelength, the more exact the position, but the greater the photon’s momentum. This momentum is transferred to the electron in an uncontrolled way during the collision.
126046.m: A more exact position measurement disturbs the momentum more.

126047.q: In which year did Erwin Schrödinger publish his wave equation?
126047.e: The equation appeared in a series of papers in the journal “Annalen der Physik”. It quickly became the standard tool of atomic physics.
126047.m: The Schrödinger equation was created in the mid-1920s.

126048.q: At which university was Erwin Schrödinger a professor when he set up his wave equation?
126048.e: Schrödinger taught in Zurich for several years. Later he moved to Berlin as Max Planck’s successor.
126048.m: The Schrödinger equation was developed in Zurich.

126049.q: In which resort in the Grisons did Schrödinger work on his wave equation around the turn of the year 1925/26?
126049.e: Schrödinger spent the Christmas holidays in Arosa. There he developed important parts of his wave mechanics.
126049.m: Part of quantum mechanics was created in the mountains of the Grisons.

126050.q: According to Max Born, what is the meaning of the square of the absolute value |ψ|² of the wave function?
a: It is the probability density of finding the particle at a place
It is the electric charge of the particle
It is the temperature of the system
It is the mass of the particle
126050.e: The wave function itself cannot be measured directly. Only its absolute square gives the probability for a measured value at each place.
126050.m: The square of the wave function gives the probability of where the particle is.

126051.q: What follows from the Schrödinger equation for an electron bound in an atom?
a: It can only take certain energy values
It moves on a fixed circular orbit
126051.e: For a bound particle, the Schrödinger equation only has meaningful solutions at certain energies. This explains the energy levels and spectral lines of atoms.
126051.m: Bound particles can only have certain energies.

126052.q: By what factor is the energy of the third level of a particle in an infinitely deep potential well greater than that of the ground state?
126052.e: In the potential well, E_n is proportional to n². For n = 3, this gives 3² = 9.
126052.m: In a potential well, the energies grow with the square of the quantum number.

126053.q: What is the 1935 thought experiment “Schrödinger’s cat” meant to illustrate?
a: The problem of applying superposition states to everyday-sized objects
The effect of radioactive radiation on animals
The refraction of light in glass
126053.e: If the superposition of an atom were transferred to the cat, it would be alive and dead at the same time until the measurement. Schrödinger wanted to show how strange this interpretation seems in everyday life.
126053.m: Schrödinger’s cat shows the puzzle of superposition on a large scale.

126054.q: With whom did Erwin Schrödinger share the Nobel Prize in Physics?
126054.e: Both were honoured for new forms of atomic theory. The Englishman Dirac had developed a relativistic quantum theory of the electron.
126054.m: Schrödinger and Dirac received the Nobel Prize together.

126055.q: Which mathematical property of the Schrödinger equation allows solutions to be superposed into new solutions?
126055.e: With a linear equation, any sum of solutions is again a solution. The superposition principle of quantum mechanics is based on this.
126055.m: Because the Schrödinger equation is linear, quantum states can be superposed.

126056.q: To which particles does the Pauli principle apply?
126056.e: Fermions include electrons, protons and neutrons. Bosons such as photons, by contrast, may occupy the same state more than once.
126056.m: The Pauli principle applies to fermions.

126057.q: In which decade were the foundations of modern quantum mechanics laid with the Pauli principle and the Schrödinger equation?
126057.e: Pauli formulated the exclusion principle in 1925, Schrödinger his equation in 1926. Quantum mechanics as it is taught today came into being in these years.
126057.m: The Pauli principle dates from the 1920s.

126058.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy a single orbital?
126058.e: The electrons of an orbital agree in three quantum numbers. They must therefore differ in the spin quantum number, which can only take two values.
126058.m: An orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spin.

126059.q: According to the Pauli principle, what is the maximum number of electrons that fit in the shell with principal quantum number n = 3?
126059.e: The maximum is 2n². With n = 3, this gives 2 · 9 = 18.
126059.m: The capacity of an electron shell grows with the square of the principal quantum number.

126060.q: Why can’t all the electrons in an atom fall into the innermost shell?
a: Because the innermost shell is positively charged
126060.e: Each state may only be occupied by one electron. Once the innermost shell is full with two electrons, further electrons must move into higher shells. This gives the structure of the periodic table.
126060.m: The Pauli principle forces electrons into different shells.

126061.q: What did physicists jokingly call the “Pauli effect”?
a: That experiments often failed when Pauli was present
That Pauli always found the right solution
That electrons glowed in Pauli’s laboratory
That Pauli never carried out an experiment
126061.e: Pauli was a pure theorist, and colleagues liked to tell how equipment broke near him. Pauli himself was amused by this legend.
126061.m: The Pauli effect is an anecdote, not a physical effect.

126062.q: What spin quantum number does an electron have?
126062.e: The electron is a spin-1/2 particle. That is why it belongs to the fermions.

126063.q: Into how many beams did the beam of silver atoms split in the Stern-Gerlach experiment of 1922?
126063.e: The non-uniform magnetic field deflected the atoms up or down depending on the orientation of their magnetic moment. Classically, a continuous broadening would have been expected.
126063.m: The Stern-Gerlach experiment showed that orientation in a magnetic field is quantised.

126064.q: Can you imagine the spin of an electron as the rotation of a small ball?
a: No, it is a purely quantum mechanical property
Yes, the electron spins like the Earth
Yes, but only in a magnetic field
No, because the electron is not magnetic at all
126064.e: A spinning ball the size of an electron would have to move faster than light at its surface. Spin is an internal angular momentum with no classical counterpart.
126064.m: Spin is an angular momentum without any real rotation.

126065.q: Which particles belong to the fermions because of their half-integer spin?
126065.e: Electrons have spin 1/2 and are therefore fermions. Photons and gluons have spin 1, the Higgs boson spin 0; they are all bosons.
126065.m: Particles with half-integer spin are called fermions.

126066.q: What spin does the Higgs boson have?
126066.e: The Higgs boson is the only known elementary particle without spin. It was detected at CERN in 2012.
126066.m: The Higgs boson is a particle without spin.

126067.q: What is the ferromagnetism of iron mainly based on?
a: On the electron spins being aligned in the same direction
On the magnetic field of the atomic nucleus
On electric currents in the metal
On the gravity of the atoms
126067.e: The spins carry a magnetic moment. In ferromagnetic materials, they line up in parallel in regions called Weiss domains.
126067.m: Iron is magnetic because many electron spins line up in the same direction.

126068.q: How many different results can a measurement of an electron’s spin component along an axis give?
126068.e: A measurement always finds exactly one of two values. These are called “spin up” and “spin down” for short.
126068.m: The spin component of an electron has only two possible values.

126069.q: Which device was greatly improved thanks to spin-dependent giant magnetoresistance (Nobel Prize 2007)?
126069.e: The resistance of thin layered systems depends strongly on their magnetisation. This made it possible to build tiny read heads, and hard disks store much more data.
126069.m: Giant magnetoresistance made large hard disk storage possible.

126070.q: What is meant by the tunnel effect?
a: A particle overcomes an energy barrier even though, classically, its energy is not enough
A particle is accelerated in a tunnel
Light is guided in an optical fibre
A particle decays into two particles
126070.e: The wave function reaches into the barrier and is not zero behind it. That is why there is a probability of finding the particle on the other side.
126070.m: Quantum objects can pass through barriers that are classically impossible to overcome.

126071.q: With an otherwise identical barrier, how does the tunnelling probability depend on the mass of the particle?
a: Heavier particles tunnel much less often
126071.e: The mass appears in the exponent of the tunnelling probability. That is why electrons tunnel easily, atoms much less easily and everyday objects practically never.
126071.m: The heavier a particle, the less often it tunnels.

126072.q: Which data storage uses electrons tunnelling through a thin insulating layer when writing?
126072.e: The electrons tunnel onto an insulated gate and stay stored there even without power. This is how USB sticks and SSDs work.
126072.m: Flash memory holds data with tunnelled electrons.

126073.q: Which microscope shows individual atoms by measuring the tiny current that flows through the gap between a fine tip and the sample?
126073.e: Electrons tunnel through the narrow gap, and the current depends very strongly on the distance. Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer developed the device at IBM in Rüschlikon and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986.
126073.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope uses the tunnel effect.

126074.q: Why can nuclear fusion take place inside the Sun even though, classically, the temperature is not high enough?
a: Because protons tunnel through the Coulomb barrier
Because the Sun is made of iron
Because light squeezes the protons together
126074.e: The average energy of the protons is not enough to overcome the electric repulsion. Thanks to the tunnel effect, they still occasionally get close enough together.
126074.m: Without the tunnel effect, the Sun would not shine.

126075.q: Which type of radioactive decay is explained by the tunnel effect?
126075.e: An alpha particle is trapped in the nucleus by an energy barrier. It can only leave by tunnelling, as George Gamow explained in 1928.
126075.m: Alpha particles tunnel out of the atomic nucleus.

126076.q: How does the wave function of a particle behave inside a barrier that is higher than its energy?
a: It oscillates with a larger amplitude
126076.e: Inside the barrier, the Schrödinger equation has decaying solutions. If the barrier is thin enough, something is left at the other end.
126076.m: In a barrier, the wave function falls quickly but does not disappear completely.

126077.q: How does the tunnelling probability change when a barrier becomes twice as thick?
126077.e: The wave function decreases exponentially inside the barrier. That is why the tunnelling probability falls with thickness much more than just by half.
126077.m: Even slightly thicker barriers make tunnelling much rarer.

126078.q: Which three physicists published the well-known paradox about entanglement in 1935?
126078.e: In the EPR paradox, they argued that quantum mechanics was incomplete. The debate about it later led to testable experiments.
126078.m: The EPR paradox questioned the completeness of quantum mechanics.

126079.q: What did Albert Einstein dismissively call entanglement?
126079.e: Einstein was bothered that a measurement on one particle is immediately linked to the result on its distant partner. He suspected hidden variables behind it.
126079.m: Einstein mistrusted spooky action at a distance.

126080.q: What did experiments with entangled particles show about Bell’s inequality?
a: Quantum mechanics predicts the results correctly
Einstein was right about hidden variables
126080.e: In 1964, John Bell set up an inequality that every theory with local hidden variables must satisfy. Entangled particles violate it in experiments, exactly as quantum mechanics predicts.

126081.q: Which three researchers received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments with entangled photons?
a: Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger
Peter Higgs, François Englert and Alain Aspect
Roger Penrose, Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel
Michel Mayor, Didier Queloz and James Peebles
126081.e: Their experiments violated Bell’s inequality ever more clearly. In doing so, they laid foundations for quantum information.
126081.m: In 2022, the Nobel Prize was awarded for experiments on entanglement.

126082.q: Can entangled particles be used to send information faster than the speed of light?
a: Yes, as fast as you like
Yes, but only over short distances
Yes, if the particles are charged
126082.e: The individual measurement results are random. Only the comparison, which has to go through a normal channel, reveals the correlation.
126082.m: Entanglement does not allow any message to travel faster than light.

126083.q: What is transferred from one place to another in quantum teleportation?
a: The quantum state of a particle
The particle itself with its mass
126083.e: With the help of an entangled pair and a classical message, the state is recreated at the destination. The original state is destroyed in the process.
126083.m: In quantum teleportation, a state travels, not matter.

126084.q: In which Swiss region did Nicolas Gisin’s group demonstrate entanglement between photons more than 10 kilometres apart at the end of the 1990s?
126084.e: The researchers sent the photons through telecommunications optical fibres to two places near Geneva. The experiment showed that entanglement is preserved even over large distances.
