126772.m: Arber's restriction enzymes are the scissors of genetic engineering.

126773.q: Which Swiss scientist received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1978?
126773.e: Werner Arber was honoured in 1978 for discovering restriction enzymes. Rolf Zinkernagel received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1996, and Wüthrich and Dubochet the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
126773.m: Werner Arber received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1978.

126774.q: Which canton does Werner Arber come from?
126774.e: Arber was born in Gränichen in the canton of Aargau in 1929. He studied at ETH Zurich.
126774.m: Werner Arber is a Nobel laureate from Aargau.

126775.q: In which city did Werner Arber teach as professor of microbiology from 1971?
126775.e: After his time in Geneva, Arber became a professor at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel in 1971.

126776.q: On which organisms did Arber study the restriction of foreign DNA?
126776.e: Bacteriophages are viruses that attack bacteria. Arber showed that bacteria cut up the phage DNA that has entered them.
126776.m: Bacteria defend themselves against viruses with restriction enzymes.

126777.q: How do bacteria protect their own DNA from their own restriction enzymes?
126777.e: The bacteria attach methyl groups to the recognition sites of their own DNA. This way the enzyme does not recognise their own DNA as a target.
126777.m: Methylation marks the body's own DNA as protected.

126778.q: At which places do type II restriction enzymes cut DNA?
a: At particular, often palindromic base sequences
126778.e: Each enzyme recognises a short, particular base sequence that often reads the same on both strands. It cuts reliably there.
126778.m: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at precisely defined recognition sites.

126779.q: For which field did Arber's discoveries create an important basis?
126779.e: With restriction enzymes, pieces of DNA can be cut out precisely and put together in new ways. This made recombinant DNA technology possible.
126779.m: Without restriction enzymes there would be no modern genetic engineering.

126780.q: Which office did Werner Arber take on in 2011?
a: President of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences
126780.e: Arber became the first Protestant president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences in the Vatican.
126780.m: Werner Arber headed the Pontifical Academy of Sciences.

126781.q: Which Greek island did Hippocrates, after whom the oath is named, come from?
126781.e: Hippocrates of Kos lived in the 5th and 4th centuries BC and is regarded as the founder of scientific medicine.
126781.m: Hippocrates came from the island of Kos.

126782.q: In which language was the Hippocratic Oath originally written?
126782.e: The oath comes from ancient Greece and has been handed down in the Hippocratic Corpus.
126782.m: The Hippocratic Oath is an ancient Greek text.

126783.q: By which god does the doctor swear first in the Hippocratic Oath?
126783.e: The oath begins with “I swear by Apollo the Physician” and then calls on Asclepius, Hygieia and Panacea.
126783.m: The Hippocratic Oath begins with swearing by Apollo.

126784.q: Which Latin principle is often linked with the oath but does not actually appear in it in that form?
126784.e: “First, do no harm” sums up the spirit of the oath. But the Latin phrase only came about much later.
126784.m: The principle of doing no harm is older than the Latin phrase for it.

126785.q: Which medical duty that still applies today is already contained in the Hippocratic Oath?
126785.e: The doctor promises to keep silent about everything he sees or hears during treatment. Today the duty of confidentiality is also laid down in law.
126785.m: Medical confidentiality has its roots in the Hippocratic Oath.

126786.q: Which text is considered the modern version of the doctor's pledge today?
126786.e: The Declaration of Geneva was adopted in 1948 and has been revised several times since. It takes over the basic ideas of the Hippocratic Oath.
126786.m: The Declaration of Geneva is the modern form of the doctor's oath.

126787.q: According to the Hippocratic Oath, how should the person taking the oath treat their teacher?
126787.e: The oath requires you to regard your teacher as equal to your parents and to support him if necessary. You should also teach his sons free of charge.
126787.m: In the Hippocratic Oath, the teacher is on the same level as the parents.

126788.q: What does the doctor promise in the Hippocratic Oath about deadly drugs?
a: Not to give them to anyone, even if asked
To give them only to adults
To give them only in war
To give them only with the city's permission
126788.e: The doctor swears not to give a deadly drug to anyone, even when asked to, and not to give any such advice.
126788.m: The oath forbids the doctor to give a deadly drug.

126789.q: From which language does the abbreviation “SI” for the International System of Units come?
126789.e: SI stands for “Système international d'unités”. French was the traditional language of international metrology.
126789.m: The abbreviation SI comes from French.

126791.q: Which international treaty of 1875, also signed by Switzerland, forms the basis of the SI?
126791.e: With the Metre Convention of 1875, the countries committed themselves to common units of measurement. Switzerland was among the first to sign.
126791.m: The Metre Convention of 1875 is the cornerstone of the International System of Units.

126792.q: What is the unit coulomb in SI base units?
126792.e: Charge is current times time, Q = I·t. So one coulomb is the charge that flows at 1 A in 1 s.
126792.m: One coulomb is one ampere second.

126793.q: What is the SI unit pascal in base units?
126793.e: Pressure is force per area: (kg·m/s²) divided by m² gives kg/(m·s²).
126793.m: One pascal is one newton per square metre.

126794.q: What does it mean that the SI is a coherent system of units?
a: Derived units are formed without numerical factors
All units have names of the same length
Every unit is named after a person
126794.e: In a coherent system, derived units are simply products and quotients of the base units, for example 1 J = 1 N·m without a factor.
126794.m: In the coherent SI, no numerical factors are needed when converting derived units.

126795.q: Which of the following units is not an SI unit but is accepted for use with the SI?
126795.e: The litre equals one cubic decimetre and is accepted for use with the SI. The kelvin, mole and candela are SI base units.
126795.m: The litre is allowed but is not one of the actual SI units.

126796.q: How many base units does the International System of Units have?
126796.e: The seven base units are the second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
126796.m: The SI rests on seven base units.

126797.q: Which SI base unit belongs to the amount of substance?
126797.e: The amount of substance indicates how many particles there are. Its unit is the mole.
126797.m: The amount of substance is measured in moles.

126798.q: Which SI base unit belongs to luminous intensity?
126798.e: The candela measures the luminous intensity of a source in a particular direction. The lux and lumen are units derived from it.
126798.m: Luminous intensity is the only base quantity tuned to human vision, and it is measured in candelas.

126799.q: Which SI base unit belongs to thermodynamic temperature?
126799.e: The kelvin is the base unit of temperature. The degree Celsius is a unit derived from it.
126799.m: The SI base unit of temperature is the kelvin.

126800.q: Which SI base unit belongs to electric current?
126800.e: Electric current is a base quantity with the unit ampere. The volt, coulomb and ohm are derived units.
126800.m: Among the electrical units, only the ampere is a base unit.

126801.q: Which of the following units is not an SI base unit?
126801.e: The newton is derived from the kilogram, metre and second. The other three are base units.
126801.m: The newton is a derived unit.

126802.q: Which SI base unit is the only one with a prefix in its name?
126802.e: The name kilogram contains the prefix “kilo”. For historical reasons, the base unit is not the gram but the kilogram.
126802.m: The kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix in its name.

126803.q: By how many kelvin does the temperature rise when water warms from 20 °C to 35 °C?
126803.e: A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size; only the zero point is shifted. The difference is 35 minus 20 = 15 K.
126803.m: Temperature differences are the same size in kelvin and degrees Celsius.

126804.q: What is the unit volt in SI base units?
126804.e: A volt is one joule per coulomb. Substituting the base units of energy and charge gives kg·m²/(s³·A).
126804.m: A volt is one watt per ampere.

126805.q: Which constant of nature has defined the kilogram since 2019?
126805.e: Since 2019 the numerical value of the Planck constant h has been fixed exactly. Together with the second and the metre, it defines the kilogram.
126805.m: Today the kilogram depends on the Planck constant.

126806.q: What material was the International Prototype of the Kilogram made of, which defined the kilogram until 2019?
126806.e: The cylinder was 90 % platinum and 10 % iridium and about 39 mm tall. This alloy is very hard and hardly corrodes.
126806.m: Until 2019 a metal cylinder in Sèvres was the standard for every kilogram.

126807.q: Why did scientists no longer want to tie the kilogram to a prototype?
a: Its mass changed slightly compared with its copies
It was too heavy for scales
126807.e: Comparisons showed that the masses of the prototype and its copies had drifted apart by up to about 50 micrograms over a century. A constant of nature does not change.
126807.m: An object can change, a constant of nature cannot.

126808.q: Which constant has defined the ampere since 2019?
126808.e: The value of the elementary charge e is fixed exactly. One ampere therefore corresponds to a certain number of elementary charges per second.
126808.m: Since 2019 the ampere counts elementary charges per second.

126809.q: How was the mole defined before the redefinition of 2019?
a: By the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12
126809.e: A mole used to contain as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. Since 2019 the number of particles itself has been fixed instead.
126809.m: The mole used to depend on the mass of carbon-12.

126810.q: Where was the International Prototype of the Kilogram kept?
126810.e: The cylinder was kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris. Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined by the Planck constant.
126810.m: The original kilogram is in Sèvres near Paris.

126811.q: In which unit is the total luminous flux of a lamp given, as printed on LED lamp packaging?
126811.e: The lumen measures how much light a lamp gives off in total. The candela measures luminous intensity in one direction, the lux the illuminance on a surface.
126811.m: How bright a lamp is overall is shown in lumens on the packaging.

126812.q: Since 2019, how many defining constants with exactly fixed values form the basis of the SI?
126812.e: The seven defining constants include the speed of light, the Planck constant and the elementary charge. Their numerical values are exact.
126812.m: Since 2019 seven fixed constants have determined the whole SI.

126813.q: How is the metre defined today?
a: By the distance light travels in a vacuum in a fraction of a second
As one ten-millionth of the meridian
By a platinum bar in Paris
126813.e: A metre is the distance light travels in a vacuum in a precisely fixed fraction of a second. The other answers describe older definitions.
126813.m: Today the metre is defined by the speed of light.

126814.q: Since which year has the value of the speed of light been fixed exactly by the definition of the metre?
126814.e: In 1983 the metre was redefined using the speed of light. Since then c has not been a measured value but a fixed one.
126814.m: Since 1983 the speed of light has had an exact value.

126815.q: Roughly how long does a radio signal take to travel from the Earth to the Moon, about 384,000 km away?
126815.m: A signal to the Moon takes just over a second.

126816.q: Roughly how far does light travel in one year?
126816.e: A year has about 3.16·10^7 seconds. Multiplied by about 300,000 km/s, this gives about 9.46·10^12 km.
126816.m: A light year is a distance, not a length of time.

126817.q: Who, in 1676, was the first to estimate the speed of light using the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons?
126817.e: Rømer noticed that the eclipses of the moon Io came later when the Earth was further from Jupiter. This meant light has a finite speed.
126817.m: Ole Rømer was the first to show that light has a finite speed.

126818.q: What did the Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 find?
a: The speed of light was the same in all directions
Light was faster in the direction of the Earth's motion
126818.e: The experiment looked for a difference in the speed of light caused by the Earth's motion. It found none, which argued against a stationary luminiferous ether.
126818.m: The speed of light does not depend on the Earth's motion.

126819.q: Roughly how far does light travel in a vacuum in one nanosecond?
126819.e: s = c·t = 3.0·10^8 m/s · 1·10^-9 s = 0.3 m. That is about 30 cm.
126819.m: In one nanosecond light travels about the length of a ruler.

126820.q: What is the approximate mass of 1 mol of water (H2O)?
126820.e: The molar mass comes from 2 · 1 g/mol for hydrogen and 16 g/mol for oxygen, about 18 g/mol in total.
126820.m: One mole of water weighs about 18 grams.

126821.q: How many water molecules are there in 2 mol of water?
126821.e: N = n·N_A = 2 mol · 6.022·10^23 /mol, so about 1.2·10^24 molecules.
126821.m: You get the number of particles by multiplying the amount of substance by the Avogadro constant.

126822.q: What is the approximate mass of one carbon-12 atom if the molar mass is 12 g/mol?
126822.e: m = M/N_A = 12 g/mol divided by 6.022·10^23 /mol, so about 1.99·10^-23 g.
126822.m: The mass of an atom is the molar mass divided by the Avogadro constant.

126823.q: Which scientist is the Avogadro constant named after?
126823.e: Amedeo Avogadro was an Italian physicist of the early 19th century who studied the number of particles in gases.
126823.m: The Avogadro constant recalls an Italian scientist.

126824.q: Which constant do you get when you multiply the Avogadro constant by the elementary charge?
126824.e: F = N_A·e is the charge of one mole of elementary charges, about 96,485 C/mol. It is important for electrolysis.
126824.m: The Faraday constant is the charge of one mole of elementary charges.

126825.q: Which constant results from the product of the Avogadro constant and the Boltzmann constant?
126825.e: R = N_A·k_B, about 8.314 J/(mol·K). The gas constant is the Boltzmann constant applied to one mole.
126825.m: The gas constant links the Boltzmann constant with the mole.

126826.q: Before 2019, which objects were used in the international Avogadro Project to determine the Avogadro constant very precisely?
126826.e: Scientists effectively counted the atoms in almost perfect spheres of silicon-28. Volume, mass and lattice spacing were measured extremely precisely.
126826.m: Perfectly shaped silicon spheres helped to determine the Avogadro constant.

126827.q: What amount of substance corresponds to about 3.011·10^23 particles?
126827.m: The amount of substance is the number of particles divided by the Avogadro constant.

126828.q: What is the relative measurement uncertainty in the value (50.0 ± 0.5) cm?
126828.e: Relative uncertainty is the absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value: 0.5 cm / 50.0 cm = 0.01, so 1 %.
126828.m: The relative uncertainty compares the uncertainty with the measured value.

126829.q: Which kind of measurement errors can be reduced by repeating a measurement many times and averaging?
126829.e: Random errors scatter in both directions and partly cancel out when averaged. Systematic errors shift all values by the same amount.
126829.m: Averaging helps against random errors but not against systematic ones.

126830.q: Which example leads to a systematic measurement error?
a: Different reaction times when stopping a timer
126830.e: A wrongly set scale shows the same amount too much or too little at every measurement.
126830.m: Systematic errors act in the same direction in every measurement.

126831.q: How does the uncertainty of the mean change if you take four times as many measurements?
126831.e: The standard uncertainty of the mean falls with 1 over the square root of n. The square root of 4 is 2, so it halves.
126831.m: To halve the uncertainty you need four times as many measurements.

126832.q: The length and width of a rectangle have relative uncertainties of 2 % and 3 %. Using the maximum error estimate, what is the relative uncertainty of the area?
126832.e: For a product, the maximum error estimate adds the relative uncertainties: 2 % + 3 % = 5 %.
126832.m: For products, in the worst case you add the relative uncertainties.

126833.q: What does the value g = (9.81 ± 0.05) m/s² mean?
a: The true value very probably lies between 9.76 and 9.86 m/s²
The value varies by 0.05 m/s² over the course of the day
The value definitely lies between 9.81 and 9.86 m/s²
126833.e: The measurement uncertainty gives a range around the measured value in which the true value probably lies. How uncertainties are stated is set out internationally in a guide called the GUM.
126833.m: A measured value is only complete with its uncertainty.

126834.q: What is the best way to estimate the random scatter of a measurement?
a: By repeating it several times and analysing the results statistically
By one single, especially careful measurement
By looking up the textbook value
126834.e: From a series of measurements you can calculate the mean and the standard deviation. Experts call an uncertainty found in this way “Type A”.
126834.m: Series of measurements show how much values scatter.

126835.q: What does it mean when measurements are precise but not accurate?
a: They scatter little but lie away from the true value
They scatter widely around the true value
They match the true value exactly
126835.e: Precision describes how little the values scatter. Accuracy (trueness) describes how close the mean is to the true value.
126835.m: Precise values lie close together, accurate values hit the target.

126836.q: How many significant figures does the number 3.060 have?
126836.e: The zero between 3 and 6 counts, and the zero at the end shows the precision. So there are four figures.
126836.m: Zeros between other digits are always significant.

126837.q: How many significant figures does the value 2.5·10^3 have?
126837.e: In scientific notation only the digits before the power of ten count, here 2 and 5.
126837.m: The power of ten does not change the number of significant figures.

126838.q: What is the correctly rounded result of 2.5 · 3.41?
126838.e: 2.5 · 3.41 = 8.525. When multiplying, the result follows the factor with the fewest significant figures, here two, so 8.5.
126838.m: When multiplying, the least precise factor sets the number of figures.

126839.q: What is the correctly rounded result of 12.1 + 0.256?
126839.e: 12.1 + 0.256 = 12.356. When adding, the smallest number of decimal places counts, here one, so 12.4.
126839.m: When adding, the number with the fewest decimal places sets the result.

126840.q: How do you write 1200 so that it is clear three significant figures are meant?
126840.e: With 1200 it is unclear whether the zeros are significant. 1.20·10^3 clearly shows three figures.
126840.m: Scientific notation makes the number of significant figures clear.

126841.q: What is the correctly rounded result of 7.20 ÷ 2.4?
126841.e: 7.20 ÷ 2.4 = 3. The divisor 2.4 has only two significant figures, so you write 3.0.
126841.m: When dividing, too, the least precise value sets the number of figures.

126842.q: How many significant figures does a counted number such as “12 pupils” have?
a: As many as you like, it is exact
126842.e: Counted quantities and defined numbers are exact. They do not limit the precision of a result.
126842.m: Exact numbers have unlimited significant figures.

126843.q: How many nanometres are there in a micrometre?
126843.e: Micro means 10^-6 and nano 10^-9. The difference is three powers of ten, so 1000.
126843.m: A micrometre has a thousand nanometres.

126844.q: Which factor does the prefix “giga” stand for?
126844.e: Giga stands for one billion. A gigawatt is therefore one billion watts.

126845.q: Which two prefixes for very large numbers were introduced in 2022?
126845.e: In 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures introduced ronna for 10^27 and quetta for 10^30, plus ronto and quecto for the reciprocals.
126845.m: The largest SI prefixes today are ronna and quetta.

126846.m: From kilometres to millimetres is six powers of ten.

126847.q: What is the difference between the symbols “Mm” and “mm”?
126847.e: Capital M stands for mega (10^6), small m for milli (10^-3). Whether a prefix is written in capitals or small letters is binding.
126847.m: With prefixes, capital or small letters decide the meaning.

126849.q: Which factor does the prefix “femto” stand for?
126849.e: Femto means one quadrillionth. Very short laser pulses, for example, are measured in femtoseconds.

126850.q: Which binary prefix means exactly 2^10, that is 1024?
126850.e: In the SI, kilo always means 1000. For 1024 the binary prefix kibi was introduced, as in 1 KiB = 1024 bytes.
126850.m: A kibibyte has 1024 bytes, a kilobyte 1000 bytes.

126851.q: Which atoms does the atomic clock use that defines the second internationally?
126851.e: The second is defined as exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from a transition in the caesium-133 atom.
126851.m: The second is counted with a caesium atomic clock.

126852.q: Since which year has the second been defined by atomic oscillations instead of the Earth's motion?
126852.e: The General Conference on Weights and Measures introduced the atomic second in 1967. Before that it was defined by the year and therefore by the Earth's motion.
126852.m: Since 1967 the atomic clock has set the length of the second.

126853.q: Which longwave transmitter broadcasts the time for radio-controlled clocks in Central Europe?
126853.e: DCF77 transmits from Mainflingen near Frankfurt am Main. Its signal is controlled by atomic clocks and can also be received in Switzerland.
126853.m: Radio-controlled clocks get their time from the DCF77 transmitter.

126854.q: Why are optical atomic clocks more accurate than caesium clocks?
a: They use a much higher oscillation frequency
126854.e: Optical clocks count oscillations of light instead of microwaves. With more oscillations per second, time can be divided more finely.
126854.m: The higher the frequency, the more finely a clock can measure time.

126855.q: Roughly what position error results if a GPS clock is wrong by 1 microsecond?
126855.e: Radio signals travel at the speed of light: 3·10^8 m/s · 1·10^-6 s = 300 m.
126855.m: Satellite navigation only works with extremely precise clocks.

126856.q: What is a leap second for?
a: To adjust atomic time to the irregular rotation of the Earth
To make up for leap years
126856.e: The Earth does not rotate quite evenly. Leap seconds kept Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) close to solar time.
126856.m: Leap seconds match atomic time to the Earth's rotation.

126857.q: What is the name of the time scale that is averaged from many atomic clocks around the world?
126857.e: TAI is calculated by the BIPM from the data of hundreds of atomic clocks in many countries. Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is derived from it.
126857.m: International Atomic Time comes from many clocks around the world.

126858.q: In which country did the first working caesium atomic clock start operating in 1955?
126858.e: Louis Essen and Jack Parry built it at the National Physical Laboratory in England.
126858.m: The first caesium atomic clock ticked in England.

126859.q: Where is the Federal Institute of Metrology based?
126859.e: The institute is in Wabern, in the municipality of Köniz near Bern.
126859.m: Swiss measurement science is based in Wabern near Bern.

126860.q: What is the short name of the Federal Institute of Metrology?
126860.e: The abbreviation METAS is used in all the national languages.
126860.m: Switzerland's national metrology institute is called METAS.

126861.q: What is one of the main tasks of METAS?
a: To provide the national measurement standards
126861.e: METAS provides the national standards for the units. This means measurements in Switzerland can be traced back to the SI.
126861.m: METAS makes sure that measurements in Switzerland are correct.

126862.q: What is the task of METAS regarding time?
a: It determines and distributes Switzerland's legal time
It works out the public holidays
126862.e: METAS runs atomic clocks and provides the official Swiss time, which is matched to Coordinated Universal Time.
126862.m: Official Swiss time comes from the atomic clocks of METAS.

126863.q: Who carries out the verification of measuring instruments such as shop scales or petrol pumps in Switzerland?
a: Cantonal verification officers supervised by METAS
126863.e: Measuring instruments used in trade must be verified. The cantonal verification offices carry this out, and METAS supervises them.
126863.m: Verified scales protect customers from wrong quantities.

126864.q: Why is a national metrology institute such as METAS important for trade and industry?
a: Because everyone measures with the same precise units
Because it sets the prices of goods
Because it invents new units for every company
Because it collects taxes on measuring devices
126864.e: METAS makes sure that a kilogram or a metre is measured the same way throughout Switzerland and matches the international SI. Only then are measurements comparable and fair.
126864.m: Uniform units make measurements comparable and fair.
